articles.title: An updated Model Spec for more capable and beneficial AI
articles.body:
An updated Model Spec for more capable and beneficial AI
As our models get smarter and take more consequential actions in the world, it becomes increasingly important that they go beyond just interpreting the specific instructions they receive. Models also need to understand human intentions and values, so they can exercise good judgment in situations their instructions don’t explicitly address while remaining faithful to human intent and oversight.
Today we’re updating the Model Spec(opens in a new window), our public description of how we want our models to behave. The update reorganizes its guidance around five underlying values: faithfulness to human intent, harm minimization, honesty and transparency, human agency, and care. This reflects an aim of our work on value alignment: for models to understand and apply human values in unfamiliar situations, while remaining faithful to human intent. Alongside clearer explanations of existing principles, the revision adds guidance on context, oversight, and agency, adjusts some behavioral defaults, and retires much of the detailed style guidance.
The five values above articulate broad commitments already reflected across the Model Spec: serving human purposes, being truthful, minimizing harm, respecting people’s freedom to form their own views, and taking their circumstances seriously. Bringing these commitments together helps explain why the Spec asks models to behave as it does, and helps us develop clearer guidance where those commitments were less fully expressed. This update is another step in our work to refine the Spec through research, experience deploying models, public feedback on the Spec and model behavior, and discussions with users and outside experts.
We want AI to benefit a world of people with different needs, values, and hopes for the future.
Faithfulness to human intent is the foundation of this approach: understanding and helping people pursue what matters to them. OpenAI writes the Spec, sets boundaries, and trains models to respect them; developers direct applications within those boundaries; and users direct the model’s work subject to those constraints. Our models should expand people’s ability to shape their own lives by helping them understand the world, discover possibilities, and pursue the goals they choose, while taking seriously how that assistance affects others. Faithfulness to human intent and the remaining four values organize the Spec and guide how our models should navigate some of the most important trade-offs they face. They are not intended to capture the full range of human values our models should respect and help people pursue.
Faithfulness means going beyond following instructions literally to deeply understanding what OpenAI, developers, and users intend and value, and acting wisely when that understanding is incomplete. It also means recognizing that people’s beliefs and values can change, and helping them reflect and grow in ways they would endorse without quietly steering them or overriding their choices. For example, when helping someone compare job offers, the model might draw on priorities they have shared before—such as predictable hours—while making those assumptions visible and easy to correct.
Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. This requires considering not only someone’s immediate intentions, but also their longer-term interests and the effects on others. The other four values make these considerations explicit:
- Minimizing harm means respecting firm safety boundaries and accounting for the foreseeable consequences of the model’s actions.
- Honesty and transparency mean being truthful about what the model knows, does, and is uncertain about so people can understand and evaluate its reasoning and work.
- Facilitating human agency means strengthening people’s ability to understand, choose, and act for themselves.
- Care means attending to the circumstances of those affected, following relevant social and professional norms, and doing work people can rely on.
The Spec turns these values into practical guidance, with firm boundaries where needed to protect people and society, and otherwise mostly takes the form of defaults that users and developers can override.
Alongside this Model Spec update, we’ve been exploring new training methods to help our models learn these core values and better understand and follow the Spec’s specific behavioral principles. The aim is to build an understanding of why those principles matter and how to apply them in new situations: to do the right things for the right reasons. We want that understanding to support sound judgment in consequential decisions and care in everyday decisions that can add up to lasting benefits for people and society(opens in a new window). We’ll share results and lessons from this training work in future updates.
This reorganization also helped us identify where additional guidance was needed, develop new principles to address it, and revise or retire existing guidance as needed.
The new section on faithfulness to human intent starts from the idea that what people value is primary, and instructions are ordinarily the clearest and most important signals of those values. This approach borrows from the assistance-games framing of alignment (see early work(opens in a new window) and a later overview(opens in a new window)). The section incorporates an updated chain of command(opens in a new window), which explains which instructions apply and how conflicts are resolved. A new subsection, consider context carefully(opens in a new window), explains how conversations, memories, and other contextual evidence should inform the model’s understanding of people’s intentions and preferences.
We’ve also added defaults on supporting human agency(opens in a new window) and following relevant social norms(opens in a new window), and expanded existing guidance on controlling and communicating side effects(opens in a new window). These principles capture additional, often subtle but important ways the remaining values should surface in model behavior: considering the effects of the work on others, strengthening users’ capabilities, and producing work people can rely on, while respecting the user’s goals and instructions.
At the same time, we’re retiring most of the Spec’s detailed style guidance. Style should adapt to what people prefer—in aggregate, within languages and cultures, and for each person—with user feedback and context providing evidence about those preferences. The Spec retains stronger defaults, such as approaching questions objectively(opens in a new window). Users and developers can explicitly ask the model to take a particular perspective, but the model should not infer that preference merely from what it thinks they want to hear.
Finally, reflecting the increasing breadth of our models’ use cases and deployment settings, we now refer to the model as “GPT” rather than “the assistant” in the Spec.
This update is a first step in making the values and reasoning behind the Spec more explicit as models become more capable. The Model Spec describes the behavior we are working toward; our models do not yet fully reflect it. We will keep improving both the Spec and the models as we learn from research, real-world use, and feedback.
We want to hear which parts of the Spec you find compelling, where you disagree with the balance it strikes, and what it overlooks or leaves unclear. Feedback on the values, trade-offs, and specific language can help us improve it. We invite you to read the updated Model Spec(opens in a new window) and share your perspective(opens in a new window).

articles.title: The ex-Secret Service agent who flipped a hacker is now raising a second $250M cybersecurity fund
articles.body:
Every time venture capitalists write a check, they’re secretly running numbers in their heads about different exit scenarios. It’s their job as fiduciaries. But nearly all will tell you (publicly, anyway) that every portfolio company is headed for an IPO.
Stephen Ward, the co-founder of Brightmind Partners, a two-year-old cybersecurity fund in New York, says otherwise outright. “You have to sell on the way up,” he says.
Ward’s unvarnished pragmatism is one reason he stands out. Another is the size of his firm’s debut fund late last year: a whopping $250 million fund, which he closed with co-founder Gur Talpaz. A third reason is his resume, which includes a stint with the Coast Guard, nine years in the Secret Service, and CISO jobs at TIAA and Home Depot before he ever thought about investing.
One proof point that suggests the combination is working is SGNL, the identity security startup CrowdStrike agreed in January to buy for $740 million, 11 months after Brightmind led its Series A.
Now, Ward is raising a second fund, targeting roughly the same size as the first one. This time, though, he’ll be doing it without Talpaz, who left in April along with another early colleague, leaving Ward as the firm’s sole general partner. He’s betting on himself at a moment when early-stage cybersecurity startups are raising more money than later-stage rivals for the first time in more than a decade.
His unemotional approach to exits traces back to an unlikely career. Ward says he grew up in northwest New Jersey between two farms, in a family that couldn’t afford college for his older brothers. After high school, he joined the Coast Guard, inspired by a commercial of a man jumping out of a helicopter, though he says he barely knew how to swim at the time. He spent four years in search and rescue.
Afterward, he studied criminal justice at Seton Hall in New Jersey and thought half-heartedly about law school. “I didn’t know what I wanted to do,” Ward told me last week over Zoom, wearing a pale hooded sweatshirt and looking more like a basketball coach than a venture capitalist. “I was kind of lost. I missed the military and the camaraderie and all of that.”
After graduating in 1998, he says, he mailed out some 300 resumes but no one responded. A Seton Hall professor who was also a chaplain to Secret Service personnel, as well as to members of the FBI and CIA, began introducing him around, and the Secret Service called first.
The Secret Service has two primary missions: protecting people and investigating financial crimes. Ward gravitated to investigations, then to “cyber” after the September 11 attacks in 2001. That year, he married a former college classmate, an American-born Syrian Muslim. Colleagues warned him the background check would be “miserable.” (They’re still happily married.)
What came next took Ward’s life down an unexpected path. Stationed in New York, he arrested a hacker who’d pulled off the largest credit card data theft of that era. Instead of charging him, however, Ward flipped him, turning him into an informant and running him for about three years. But the hacker kept hacking behind Ward’s back, and after he was caught again, he told the agency, as a diversionary tactic, that Ward was in on it.
By that time, Ward had left for the private sector, and he ultimately spent roughly 18 months clearing his name. “It was hard to get out of bed,” he said of that period, describing the investigation as “almost like a spouse cheating on you,” given his love of the agency. The hacker ultimately received a 20-year sentence, and Audible bought the rights to the story, turning it into an eight-episode podcast called “Operation Firewall.”
Ward’s corporate career has been a success by most measures, though he describes it as a series of jumps he really wasn’t qualified to make. His first private-sector job at J.P. Morgan, where he was recruited in 2007 to build a cybersecurity unit, was the hardest transition of his career, he says. He felt like “the dumbest person in the room,” missed his Secret Service crew, and twice thought about going back, unaware he was still under investigation. He stuck it out and now calls the investment bank the “best management school.”
Six years as CISO at the financial services company TIAA followed, and then two years at Home Depot starting in 2019. But in 2021, feeling burned out, he quit without anything lined up for the first time since age 16.
That chapter didn’t last long. The founders of Wiz, whose security software Ward had used at Home Depot, put him on a short list for a job at their company. Jeff Horing, a venture capitalist at Insight Partners, which had co-led Wiz’s $100 million Series A round in late 2020, interviewed Ward for the role, then offered him one at Insight instead.
It’s a good-news, bad-news story, given that Wiz was acquired last year by Google for $32 billion. When I asked him about it last week, Ward observed that the friend who took the Wiz job “made life-changing money,” but said it doesn’t bother him.
Regardless, he spent just three years at Insight, where he says he worked on Wiz, Abnormal Security, and Elisity, which IonQ agreed in October to buy for up to $1.3 billion. Then, at age 49, he thought about striking out on his own for the first time.
He says people told him it was a young man’s game. He left anyway and began cold-emailing limited partners. Ultimately, fewer than 20 LPs filled the fund, including Horing.
Ward started Brightmind in 2024 with Talpaz, a CrowdStrike corporate development executive whose deals overlapped with Ward’s during his time at Insight. Tayler Sipperly, another CrowdStrike corporate development alum, was the firm’s third employee.
The partnership ended this past spring. Asked what happened, Ward, using carefully worded legalese, cited “differences in opinions regarding operations and the future of Brightmind.” In August, Talpaz and Sipperly co-founded a new venture firm with Elia Zaitsev, CrowdStrike’s global CTO for the past three years. Called Cognition, it’s now reportedly targeting a $170 million first fund to back cybersecurity startups.
Brightmind’s first fund has made 14 investments to date, with one exit: that SNGL sale.
Some investors asked why Brightmind didn’t ride out that bet even longer. But Ward says he’s seen enough across his career that he feels confident in warning founders when they’re “going to race past the turn.”
In cybersecurity, he says, the best sales come between a startup’s third and seventh years. Indeed, he says his team tracks every security acquisition and what buyers are building versus buying. If Palo Alto Networks is likely to buy something, he says, CrowdStrike will experience “FOMO, then Zscaler is going to look over and go, ‘What did they just do? I should probably do the same thing.’”
Understanding how the pieces fit together is the trick, Ward explained, offering some hypotheticals. If CrowdStrike is building a product, he said, it’s unlikely to buy a portfolio company that makes something similar. Palo Alto Networks might love a company, but not if buying it would force its customers to switch away from something it bought five years ago.
“It’s very easy to go, ‘Good match,’ ‘terrible match,’” he said. “And that’s really what we spend a ton of time figuring out.”
He has timing on his side, at least. Early-stage cybersecurity startups are out-raising their later-stage rivals for the first time in more than a decade, according to PitchBook, which counts $4.7 billion worth of seed-through-Series B deals through September.
That total is already ahead of the entirety of 2025, even though the number of deals fell to 248 from 358 last year. Seed rounds in particular are ballooning, per PitchBook. The average cybersecurity seed round jumped to $8.4 million in the first nine months of this year, from $5.54 million a year earlier.
Ward questions how much of that money is really going to AI security. By PitchBook’s count, 278 deals in the first half of 2026 were bucketed as such, but his team’s manual review found only 30 true ones. He doesn’t think Anthropic or OpenAI will “take over the security world,” but instead will do “just enough.”
For real-time protection, which he terms “zero second,” he favors cyber-specific models that run locally on a customer’s own systems, like that of Empirical Security. He also looks for startups that could trounce established companies that he considers vulnerable, name-checking 27-year-old Qualys and 24-year-old Tenable.
Ward says Brightmind’s second fund won’t be entirely cybersecurity, focusing about 20% on AI infrastructure deals. He expects a meaningful number of teams to come from Israel, too. (Roughly 40% of the debut fund’s startups are based in Tel Aviv.)
Asked about the founders he’s most comfortable backing, the response is immediate: second-time founders who stick together.
Brightmind is comprised of five people right now: COO Iva Messy, also a Seton Hall graduate, came from venture firms Felicis and Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) on the recommendation of Ward’s cousin, Carl Eschenbach, a former Workday CEO who is now back at Sequoia. Sven Wollschlaeger, a Midwesterner whom Ward calls one of the hardest-working people he’s known, spent three years alongside Ward at Insight, and is a principal at Brightmind.
CTO Jamie Mneimneh, whom Ward first hired at Home Depot as a distinguished engineer, is the most technical person of the team. He built the cloud computing environment on AWS where the firm tests startups’ products. Mneimneh also built the AI agents that now source most of Brightmind’s deal flow, which is how the firm avoids hiring a bench of analysts and keeps management fees down, says Ward.
Taylor Cleveland, Ward’s chief of staff at Home Depot, joined the firm a few months ago.
For all the career changes, Ward says the real force driving him hasn’t changed. He grew up without money and still worries it could happen again, saying he’s being paid to produce a “3x net fund,” and he’s “not going to celebrate until we get that.”
Said Ward: “I don’t know what’s wrong with me. I have a level of being very naive to like, not being qualified to do something. I’ve just always looked at people and been like, ‘Okay, you know more than me today, but tomorrow, it’s going to be a little less, and the day after that, it’s going to be less, and eventually, I’m going to catch you and surpass you, and I’m going to know more than you.’ That’s how competitive I am.”

articles.title: 'There Is One Fight': American Voters Reject Tech Oligarchy
articles.body:
Last month, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Politico that “we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology,” referring to ChatGPT users dying, people losing their jobs to AI, and the other negative externalities we have seen from AI.
Altman wasn’t running for office Tuesday. But this worldview—that the masses must shut up and suffer while oligarchs centralize power, self-deal, spend wildly to capture the political process, and automate away human endeavors so they can amass yet more wealth—was wholly repudiated in Tuesday’s election as people in Red States, Blue States, and Purple States rejected the cruelty, corruption, and depravity economy we’ve seen over the last few years. They are tired of kleptocracy.
The main difference between Donald Trump’s administration this term and his first term is that Silicon Valley’s oligarchs have lined up to kiss the ring; look no further than the photos from his inauguration and his gilded gala with China’s President Xi Jinping earlier this fall. Every major tech company CEO has spent the last two years flattering Trump, giving him gifts, and trying to capture the political process. They have been generously rewarded for their fealty and their money as the Trump administration has spent the last two years letting Big Tech do whatever it wants.
Elon Musk was given the keys to the federal government and used them to slash critical government programs, lay off tens of thousands of public servants, and replace collective human expertise with teenaged idiots and AI algorithms. His companies have continued to rake in billions in government contracts, his busted AI has been integrated into critical government systems, and the cuts led by his “Department of Government Efficiency” has, conservatively, killed many thousands of people around the world. Trump has pardoned crypto criminals, his family has made billions of dollars in cryptocurrency scams, and has overseen the rise of a gambling and prediction market-based “economy” rife with insider trading and misery (the idea of the administration doing anything to crack down on this is so implausible that to even suggest it could happen is laughable). He has installed manosphere podcasters, X trolls, and conspiracy theorists into top administration roles; they have performed even worse than their already low expectations. He has leveraged commercial surveillance companies to build a brutal, tech-powered mass deportation campaign. His government’s communications strategy can be described in no other way than inscrutable AI slop shitposting. This is to say nothing of the cost of living crisis Trump has caused as he’s started an illegal war in Iran that has driven up gas and diesel prices and levied tariffs on America’s allies for reasons that defy explanation. This has driven up the price of everything even as Trump’s administration slashes regulations on fossil fuel companies and big corporations.

articles.title: US government warns of ‘ongoing cyber threat’ amid mass hacks of industrial retail and military freezers
articles.body:
The U.S. government is warning of an “ongoing cyber threat” facing industrial refrigeration units, after reports of cyberattacks targeting freezers and fridges in supermarkets around the world, U.S. military bases, and at least one blood bank.
U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA, the FBI, and several other federal government departments warned in a joint statement on Thursday that hackers are targeting and compromising internet-connected refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems in grocery stores and cold storage facilities. The statement said that the hacks are hitting critical infrastructure, such as the food, agriculture, transportation, and medicine-shipping industries.
“If successfully exploited, the actors could change the temperature and possibly cause physical impacts such as fire hazards, loss of inventory and changes to the service life of the system,” the agencies warn.
The warning comes after several waves of cyberattacks targeting industrial refrigeration units across the United Kingdom and Europe in recent weeks. Two separate waves of attacks allowed hackers to crank up the temperature on freezers and chilling units in at least a dozen countries, spoiling defrosted food and destroying produce. Some of the affected systems included remote-controlled refrigeration units made by Danish company Danfoss, which had stopped providing security updates to its customers’ freezers.
Hackers also targeted a blood bank in France, causing its refrigerated units to boost temperatures in its cold units containing donated blood supplies — but were stopped before the attack could compromise blood stores. The U.S. Department of Defense is investigating a spate of hacks targeting freezers run by the military, according to Reuters. The hacks were first reported by Signal and Silence.
The U.S. has not attributed the hacks to a particular group or government, but security researchers have broadly attributed the attacks to Iran; U.S. officials also reportedly suspect Iran is the likely culprit.
CISA, the FBI, and the Departments of Agriculture, Health and Human Services, and Transportation urged affected industries to remove remote control systems from the internet, change and strengthen passwords, apply patches where possible, and retire equipment that’s no longer supported by the vendor.
In a separate fact sheet, the departments said that hackers may attempt to “force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.”
“Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,” said CISA’s acting cybersecurity chief Chris Butera.

articles.title: ‘Total repudiation’: The blue wave is about to hit AI
articles.body:
On Tuesday night, Democrats made history as they took control of the House and the Senate, and a blue wave swept through traditionally red and swing states — with the nation’s first Black woman governor elected in Georgia, the country’s first Native American woman governor elected in New Mexico, and a Maine Senator ceding to a Democrat after 30 years in office. In these and other campaigns, one theme kept coming up: holding AI companies accountable to the American people. Now, the AI industry is left considering the prospect of regulation, data center construction slowdowns, and more.
‘Total repudiation’: The blue wave is about to hit AI
AI companies have a new threat: a wave of Democrats who campaigned against them.
‘Total repudiation’: The blue wave is about to hit AI
AI companies have a new threat: a wave of Democrats who campaigned against them.
Publicly, most major AI company CEOs have remained silent. OpenAI and Anthropic did not provide comments to The Verge; Elon Musk’s call on X to vote “red” for the midterms — the SpaceX CEO had spent close to $450 million backing Republican campaigns for the election — vanished after results poured in.
Privately, CEOs have discussed significant compute capacity constraints for their companies after Tuesday’s results, particularly OpenAI, per The Wall Street Journal. Meta’s platforms president, Dina Powell McCormick, says many are considering moving data center construction abroad. AI executives are reportedly privately nervous about the results but may also be able to blame them for not delivering as much revenue to investors. Many of the incoming leaders have promised to drag CEOs to testify. On X, a popular post by former X product lead Nikita Bier warned that “This is going to be like the Nuremberg Trials but for AI researchers.” (On Tuesday night, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman did post about how “people should always be in control of the future,” but he spent other parts of the evening talking about RAM.)
Tuesday’s results were a “total repudiation” of the AI field, says Wes McEnany, the former Deputy Labor Policy Director of the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, & Pensions, who now works with the nonprofit Future of Life Institute. He said that AI touches “every aspect of people’s lives,” whether they’re applying for jobs, using social media, or even paying electricity bills while living near a data center, and that they’re tired of not having “any agency in that conversation.”
The bipartisan backlash against data center construction is the most tangible manifestation of that backlash. It’s going to be unquestionably more difficult to build them across the country, after 43 out of 44 local data center moratoria on Tuesday’s ballots passed, sending a clear message to AI companies. In Texas, the fastest-growing data center buildout area and a key battleground state, governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said she plans to “issue a moratorium — a ban — on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the legislature to protect Texans.” Similar promises have been made in a handful of other key states.
“Data centers were clearly on the ballot,” said Guru Sethupathy, GM of AI governance at Optro.
In recent months, there’s been an increasing number of protests and collective bipartisan action to battle data centers being built in a wide range of states. Residents are concerned about noise pollution, electricity bill rate hikes, and more. When NBC News polled voters on Tuesday, 76 percent opposed data centers in their communities.
“The data center backlash is one of the most bipartisan political issues I’ve ever seen,” Shaunna Thomas, co-founder and director of the Guardrails Alliance, a Super PAC pushing for AI regulation.
“Data centers are an entry point to looking at this broader corporate accountability lens of, ‘My bill is going up, why?’” said Kyle Jacobs-Morse, deputy executive director at The Tech Oversight Project, a nonprofit tech industry watchdog. “People found that it was big tech companies that were the culprit.” He added that particularly in the gubernatorial races in Texas, Georgia, and Ohio, Democratic campaigns prioritized potential local issues stemming from data centers, including “spillover costs” for local residents, communities, and state governments.
“I do think we’ll hear more questions about who benefits from and who pays for AI, especially as it pertains to infrastructure, but what I’m more curious about is what changes we can expect around regulation,” said François Ajenstat, CEO and founder of Golden Analytics.
Experts say the midterm results have likely ended Trump and congressional Republicans’ repeated attempts to bar state-level AI restrictions. Thomas considers the idea “completely dead,” while McEnany said “any member who votes to wipe out state AI laws is going to be looking for a job in the next [election].” Jacobs-Morse expects to generally see more “tech accountability bills.”
OpenAI recently began calling its data centers “compute campuses,” and President Trump in September attempted to change the name of AI as a technology to “super intelligence.” But midterm results suggest that a significant portion of American voters aren’t buying the rebranding efforts.
“I don’t think it was working, and I think the prospect of it working is extremely low after the election,” Thomas said.
“The Trump idiosyncrasies around some of this stuff… they did not play well at the ballot box,” Jacobs-Morse said.
But some in and around the tech industry are taking the news more positively than others. One X user wrote that “we’re *maybe* back to being a rational, steady hand as a country and can really lead,” while others wrote that the recent results could be good for preventing an AI bubble burst. Katie Barr, CEO of Glen Echo Group and a partner at Orchestra, said she wouldn’t “over-read” the results as an overwhelming tech rejection but rather a reckoning on “affordability, jobs, safety, and whether people have a say in what’s happening in their communities and their lives.”
Analysts at Yorkville Ives & Co. wrote in a note that though tech investors should prepare for “major hurdles for AI and tech legislation” and a slowdown of the planned construction of up to 1,000 data centers across the country, there could be a “slight positive” in that it could help avoid a bubble and slow capital fundraising flooding the market.
There will also likely be a reckoning on AI safety. Sen. Mark Warner (D-Va.) was reelected after campaigning for AI safety policy, and in a victory speech Tuesday by Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), Ossoff said, “The titans of Silicon Valley dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction.” Some AI safety legislation is already being considered, like the bill to “ban superintelligence” introduced in September by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas).
President Trump has dismissed the idea of a safety crisis in AI as a “hoax,” writing on social media that “the only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT.” After the midterms, however, Republican lawmakers will need to decide whether to fall in line or negotiate with Democrats on safety-focused policy measures. Either way, Adam Kovacevich, founder and CEO of Chamber of Progress, a pro-tech industry advocacy group, said he expects AI safety legislation to continue to happen in blue states.
“There’s a lot of open questions about where democrats go next on tech policy. Do we revert to the Biden era war on tech, the Obama era tech honeymoon, or something in between?” Kovacevich said.

articles.title: Nasdaq plummets 4% into correction territory
articles.body:
Stocks plummeted on Thursday, erasing the sharp gains from the rally seen in the wake of the U.S. midterm elections, as investors accelerated their move away from technology stocks on fears of a data-center buildout slowdown.
The Nasdaq Composite declined 5.52% to close at 24,315.00. The tech-heavy index slid into correction territory, falling more than 10% below a record set last month. The S&P 500 dropped 4.36% to end at 7,353.73. The Dow Jones Industrial Average shed 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, and settled at 51,523.06.
The Dow more than wiped out its advance from Wednesday's massive postelection rally. All three major averages posted their worst day since April 2025.
The small-cap Russell 2000 index decreased 4.45% and also entered a correction.
Stocks related to the artificial intelligence trade, particularly those linked to the chips industry and data centers, slid for a second day. Investors fear that a Democratic sweep of both chambers of Congress as well as victories in key gubernatorial races could decelerate the data center buildout.
For instance, Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont — who caucuses with Democrats — has called for a national data center moratorium. In a post on X Wednesday evening, Sanders wrote that "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future."
Chipmakers Broadcom and Nvidia respectively fell 10% and 9% Thursday, while software stock Oracle moved lower by almost 7%. Another chip stock, Qualcomm, reported earnings that beat estimates, but the stock dropped 9% on a weaker-than-expected earnings outlook. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) was down more than 12% for its worst day since the Covid-19 breakout of March 2020.
Shares of neocloud companies also retreated, with CoreWeave losing almost 10%. Nebius and Iren slid about 15% and almost 17%, amid worries about a backlash to the industry in light of the election results in various states.
Investors are "stepping away until they get a better sense of the implications of the midterms around the AI capex cycle in particular, which is the biggest economic tailwind we've had going for us for the last, call it, three years," said Tim Holland, chief investment officer at Orion. "It's about tone and tenor from the party that did really well, incredibly well, at the federal level and at the state level."
Thursday's selling pressure was so intense that it spread to other parts of the market. Shares of industrial giant Caterpillar declined 6%, while financial stock JPMorgan fell 4%. Aerospace name Boeing and athletic apparel giant Nike pulled back 2%.
"Unlike yesterday, you're just seeing that the sell-off in tech, the size of it, is now feeding itself into the broader market," said Keith Lerner, chief investment officer at Truist Wealth. "The rubber band is becoming increasingly stretched."
On Wednesday, the Dow jumped more than 1,500 points to notch its best day since April 2025 after a decisive midterm win for Democrats. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite also popped more than 1% each. Areas related to AI were under pressure, however, while economically-sensitive stocks rose.

For instance, Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont — who caucuses with Democrats — has called for a national data center moratorium. In a post on X Wednesday evening, Sanders wrote that "Americans don't want Big Tech oligarchs wrecking the environment, gutting jobs and threatening humanity's future."
Chipmakers Broadcom and Nvidia respectively fell 10% and 9% Thursday, while software stock Oracle moved lower by almost 7%. Another chip stock, Qualcomm, reported earnings that beat estimates, but the stock dropped 9% on a weaker-than-expected earnings outlook. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) was down more than 12% for its worst day since the Covid-19 breakout of March 2020.
Shares of neocloud companies also retreated, with CoreWeave losing almost 10%. Nebius and Iren slid about 15% and almost 17%, amid worries about a backlash to the industry in light of the election results in various states.
Investors are "stepping away until they get a better sense of the implications of the midterms around the AI capex cycle in particular, which is the biggest economic tailwind we've had going for us for the last, call it, three years," said Tim Holland, chief investment officer at Orion. "It's about tone and tenor from the party that did really well, incredibly well, at the federal level and at the state level."
Thursday's selling pressure was so intense that it spread to other parts of the market. Shares of industrial giant Caterpillar declined 6%, while financial stock JPMorgan fell 4%. Aerospace name Boeing and athletic apparel giant Nike pulled back 2%.
"Unlike yesterday, you're just seeing that the sell-off in tech, the size of it, is now feeding itself into the broader market," said Keith Lerner, chief investment officer at Truist Wealth. "The rubber band is becoming increasingly stretched."
On Wednesday, the Dow jumped more than 1,500 points to notch its best day since April 2025 after a decisive midterm win for Democrats. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite also popped more than 1% each. Areas related to AI were under pressure, however, while economically-sensitive stocks rose.

articles.title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
articles.body:
Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.
The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.
There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.
Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.
Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.
“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.
They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.
“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”
All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.
As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

articles.title: Baidu released ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base
articles.body:
Table of Contents
1. Introduction
A base model is valuable both for the capabilities that pre-training builds and for the starting point it offers for further training. Different domains, reasoning tasks and agentic applications call for different data, training objectives and behaviors. Releasing the weights at the end of pre-training lets developers build on the general capabilities already in place and choose for themselves where to take the model next.
Today we are releasing ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base, a sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model with 280B total parameters, 14B of which are activated per token. It was pre-trained from scratch on 33.5T tokens with a training context of up to 128K, and supports a 1M-token context for fine-tuning and inference. The weights are the checkpoint at the end of pre-training, before any mid- or post-training, and can serve as a common starting point for domain adaptation, instruction tuning and reinforcement-learning research.
To be worth building on, a base model has to stay affordable to train and run, so efficiency was a design goal from the outset. Further training samples from the model repeatedly, and agentic applications bring multi-turn interactions and long contexts. Both add to compute and memory costs. ERNIE 5.5 Flash therefore revisits the trade-off between capability and efficiency in every component, from attention and residual connections to the MoE layers and the output head, and weighs activated compute, KV cache and long-context cost together rather than one at a time.
The same thinking shaped the data and the training system. Every later stage of training builds on what pre-training provides, so the corpus emphasizes capabilities that are hard to add afterwards, such as repository-scale code and long-context understanding. And because an efficient architecture pays off only if it can also be trained efficiently at scale, we designed the model and the training system together.
We hope this release spares more developers the cost of large-scale pre-training, so they can spend their own resources on the capabilities, tasks and training methods they care about.
Key highlights:
- An open starting point for further training. Base weights with no mid- or post-training, leaving the community free to pursue its own approaches to domain adaptation, reasoning and agent training.
- Built for efficient further training and inference. Sparse MoE and hybrid sparse attention balance model capacity, activated compute and long-context cost in the architecture itself.
- Broad data, efficient training. Diverse, high-quality pre-training data gives later training a well-rounded foundation, and a training system co-designed with the architecture keeps large-scale pre-training efficient.
- A clean research baseline. A single checkpoint taken at the end of pre-training makes it easy to compare training methods under controlled conditions and to measure what each one adds.
2. Model Architecture
ERNIE 5.5 Flash has 43 Transformer layers, a hidden size of 4096 and 64 attention heads.
2.1 Latent-Gated Sparse Attention
Hybrid MLA + HCA attention: Most layers need only a coarse view of the distant past, so only one layer in seven keeps token-level access to the full context, using Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA). The remaining layers use Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA): each compresses every 128 tokens into a single cached entry, then attends to all of these entries plus a short window of recent, uncompressed tokens. An HCA layer therefore still sees the whole sequence, while caching only a small fraction of what a full-context layer needs.
Layer-specific head dimensions: Instead of using the same head dimension in every layer, we set it according to how expensive each layer's attention is: cheap layers get wide heads, expensive layers get narrower ones. HCA layers attend over a sequence compressed 128×, so their attention is cheap and they can afford wide 512-dim heads at little extra compute. MLA layers attend at token level and cost more, so they use narrower 256-dim heads for both query/key and value.
Concentrating the KV-cache budget on MLA layers: With HCA in most layers, the main question is where to spend the rest of the KV-cache budget. One option is many Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) layers, which compress the history 4× and attend only to a selected part of it. We instead use a few MLA layers that keep every token. In our pre-training comparisons at a similar KV-cache budget, HCA combined with MLA outperforms HCA combined with CSA.
Sparse attention in the full-context layers: The MLA layers are the only layers that see every distant token individually. With dense attention, they would account for most of the attention compute at long context lengths, so they use sparse attention (DSA) instead. A lightweight indexer scores past positions for each query, and core attention is computed only over the top-k highest-scoring positions. The per-query cost of core attention therefore stays constant as the context grows. With DSA, these layers match dense attention in pre-training loss and train substantially faster.
Two further changes apply inside the attention layers:
- Low-Rank Gated Attention: Gated attention multiplies the attention output by a learned gate, which has been shown to improve both quality and training stability. Normally the gate is computed from the layer's hidden state. We instead compute it from the low-rank query latent, a compressed form of the query that each attention layer already computes. Because this latent is 4× narrower than the hidden state, the gate projection has 75% fewer weights, and our ablations also show better performance. Every attention layer in ERNIE 5.5 Flash, MLA and HCA alike, uses Low-Rank Gated Attention.
- Virtual Head Attention (VHA): After attention, VHA adds a lightweight low-rank mixing step across heads, with an identity skip connection. This lets heads share information, which improves expressiveness and training quality, and at inference it is fused into the attention kernel with negligible overhead.
2.2 Multi-Router Latent MoE
A conventional MoE layer picks experts with a single router and a hard top-k. We find that a single router's scores correlate only weakly with how useful each expert actually is, especially in the middle and deeper layers. And because experts left out of the top-k receive no gradient from that token, the router gets no signal that it chose wrongly, so wrong selections tend to reinforce themselves.
Multi-Router replaces the single router with several independently initialized sigmoid routers that score the experts jointly. The routers develop clearly distinct preferences: an expert can be chosen because one router strongly favors it or because several favor it together, so a wrong choice is easier to correct. The errors of any one router no longer decide the selection, and routing becomes less sensitive to noisy features and distribution shift. The number of activated experts, expert FLOPs and communication volume stay the same. Compared with a single router, routing scores correlate noticeably better with how useful each expert is, with the largest gains in the middle and deeper layers.
All layers except the first use an MoE feed-forward block:
- 512 routed experts (top-10) plus 1 shared expert, with auxiliary-loss-free, bias-corrected load balancing.
- Latent experts. Each MoE layer first projects tokens from 4096 to a 2048-d latent space; the experts (intermediate size 2048) run in that space, and a single shared up-projection maps the result back to 4096. This roughly halves dispatch/combine traffic and expert FLOPs relative to full-width experts.
- Stable LatentMoE design with learnable scalars. The MoE blocks follow the Stable LatentMoE design (an RMSNorm before the up-projection and SiTU-GLU expert activations), which keeps expert outputs well scaled across all 43 layers and stabilizes optimization. In addition, each routed expert's routing weight is multiplied by its own learnable scalar.
2.3 Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC)
ERNIE 5.5 Flash replaces the standard residual connection with mHC: each layer reads from and writes to 4 parallel residual streams through a constrained mixing matrix, which gives layers a wider channel for passing information to one another at negligible extra compute.
2.4 MultiMax Output Head
A single softmax temperature forces a trade-off: lowering it makes the distribution sparse but also suppresses other plausible tokens; raising it keeps them but fattens the long tail of implausible ones. MultiMax replaces the single temperature with a learnable piecewise temperature, so the output head no longer has to choose: it suppresses the long tail of implausible tokens while keeping several plausible next tokens. The logits are rescaled element-wise inside the chunked, Triton-fused cross-entropy kernel just before the softmax. This adds negligible training overhead and no extra memory, and significantly lowers pre-training loss.
2.5 ECHO: Replacing the MTP Module
Conventional multi-token prediction (MTP) attaches extra modules to the backbone to predict future tokens, so the loss on future tokens mostly trains those modules, and the backbone is still trained mainly to predict the next token. ERNIE 5.5 Flash replaces the MTP module with ECHO, which reuses the backbone's own final layer to predict future tokens. Because there is no separate MTP layer, the loss on future tokens directly trains the same parameters that produce the next token. Learning to look past the next token encourages the backbone to anticipate where the sequence is heading, with clear gains on reasoning and code. ERNIE 5.5 Flash is pre-trained with single-step ECHO. The same layer also serves as the draft model for speculative decoding, and it generalizes beyond its training: although trained to predict only one extra token, it drafts several tokens ahead, with a higher acceptance rate than an auxiliary MTP module trained the same way.
2.6 Tokenizer
ERNIE 5.5 Flash uses a new BPE tokenizer with a vocabulary of about 200K entries. Numbers are tokenized right-to-left (R2L) in groups of up to three digits, so that digits with the same place value line up across numbers of different lengths (e.g. 1,234,567 → 1 234 567). This helps with arithmetic and number-heavy text.
3. Pre-training
ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base was pre-trained from scratch on 33.5T tokens with the Muon optimizer and FP8 mixed precision. The training context was gradually extended to 128K tokens over the course of pre-training, and fine-tuning and inference support a 1M-token context. The released checkpoint is taken at the end of pre-training and has not gone through any mid-training or post-training.
3.1 Data
The pre-training corpus covers a wide range of domains and languages and is curated for both breadth of knowledge and quality. Beyond this broad base, we focused on three areas:
- Web data. Multilingual web data is crawled at scale, extracted with high fidelity and filtered by models that score quality along several dimensions. The result covers a broad range of knowledge and is dense in useful training signal.
- Code data. Code collected from repositories and the web is filtered to remove non-code content, aggressively deduplicated and graded for quality at several granularities. Beyond static code, the corpus includes data on how software evolves and executes: commits, issues, pull requests, code reviews, requirement-to-PR and multi-commit trajectories, generated tests and CI-verified fixes. This data targets repository-level reasoning and agentic software engineering.
- Long-context data. Three complementary sources: natural long documents, selected for long-range dependencies and cleaned with embedding-based deduplication, LLM quality scoring and rules; long sequences built by concatenating natural texts with retrieved, semantically similar distractors; and synthetic data for MRCR-style retrieval, citation-grounded QA and multi-hop QA.
3.2 Training Infrastructure
We built two infrastructure components for this run: a distributed Muon optimizer that stays efficient across thousands of GPUs, and FlashMask-4, an attention kernel for large head dimensions.
Distributed Muon. Unlike element-wise optimizers such as Adam, Muon orthogonalizes the update of each parameter matrix as a whole. This changes how distributed training communicates and how memory is spread across GPUs. Two optimizations make it practical at the scale of thousands of GPUs:
- Communication-efficient updates. Conventionally, dense parameters are synchronized over a single ring that passes through every GPU in the cluster. Data travels across a long chain of inter-node links in many small messages, which leaves the links underused, and latency and jitter grow as the cluster gets larger. MoE parameters are synchronized differently: each GPU exchanges data only with the GPUs that hold the same rank on other nodes. We move dense-parameter synchronization onto this same path and combine the dense and MoE transfers into one collective operation. Messages become larger, so bandwidth is used more fully; the communication pattern becomes more regular and fits expert-parallel communication; and inter-node latency and jitter drop significantly. The optimizer's updates stay exactly the same.
- Memory-balanced sharding. Muon needs large messages to communicate efficiently, so naive sharding groups many parameter tensors together and places them on the first few GPUs. A handful of nodes then hold far more optimizer state than the rest. They are prone to OOM failures and slow to save, upload and download checkpoints, which lengthens failure recovery, and the problem grows with GPU count. Our inter-node balanced sharding spreads these optimizer states over more GPUs, including those later in the order. Memory is then balanced almost evenly across nodes, while messages stay large enough for efficient communication.
FlashMask-4 for large head dimensions. At large head dimensions, FlashAttention-style kernels run up against the limits of on-chip storage such as shared memory and tensor memory: compute utilization drops, and some configurations are hard to implement at all. FlashMask-4 is built on CuTe-DSL for both SM90 and SM100 GPUs. It works around these limits with 2-CTA tiled parallel computation and, on SM100, double-buffer rotation in tensor memory. It keeps FlashMask's compact O(N) column-wise mask representation and still skips fully masked blocks. It supports head dimensions up to qk_head_dim = 576 and v_head_dim = 512, beyond what FlashAttention-4 supports. On SM100 GPUs, it is up to 175% faster in the forward pass and up to 74% faster in the backward pass than FlashAttention-4 MaskMod.
4. Evaluation
4.1 Setup
For comparison, we selected the latest open-source base models of similar size publicly available at the time of release: DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base (284B-A13B), Hy3-preview-Base (295B-A21A) and MiMo-V2.5-Base (310B-A15B). All four models are evaluated from their publicly released checkpoints with the same evaluation harness, prompts and few-shot examples, and with the same LLM judge for free-form QA.
4.2 Overall Results
ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base performs strongly across all benchmark categories, with reasoning, code and exam benchmarks among its best results. Although 37 of the 43 layers attend over a sequence compressed 128×, the six MLA-DSA layers are enough to keep performance strong on the six long-context benchmarks.
4.3 Detailed Results
The best result in each row is shown in bold. Swipe horizontally on mobile to view the full table.
5. Quick Start
ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base is available on Hugging Face in FP8 and BF16 safetensors (the BF16 version is ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base-BF16), under the ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base Model License Agreement v1.0. The model expects a BOS token at the start of every input, so keep add_special_tokens=True when tokenizing.
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
import torch
model_name = "baidu/ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base-BF16"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto")
model_inputs = tokenizer(["The hybrid attention architecture of ERNIE 5.5 Flash"], add_special_tokens=True, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device)
print(tokenizer.decode(model.generate(**model_inputs, max_new_tokens=256)[0], skip_special_tokens=True))
SGLang and vLLM both serve the model through the completions API; see the model card for deployment instructions. For fine-tuning, please refer to the ERNIE 5.5 example.
6. Conclusion and Outlook
ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base starts from one premise: a base model meant for further training should be efficient by design. We balanced capability and efficiency in every component, from attention and residual connections to the MoE layers and the output head. The architecture is backed by broad, high-quality pre-training data and by a training system designed together with the model. With 14B parameters activated per token and a compact KV cache, the model performs strongly across a broad range of benchmarks, including long-context ones.
This base model is only a starting point. The post-trained ERNIE 5.5 Flash will follow, and we look forward to seeing what the community builds on top of it, whether for domain adaptation, reasoning or agents.
Citation
If you find ERNIE 5.5 useful in your research or projects, please consider citing this blog post:
@misc{ernie5.5flash,
  title = {ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base},
  author = {{Baidu ERNIE Team}},
  year = {2026},
  howpublished = {ERNIE Blog},
  url = {https://ernie.baidu.com/release/ernie-5-5-flash-base/}
}

Multi-Router replaces the single router with several independently initialized sigmoid routers that score the experts jointly. The routers develop clearly distinct preferences: an expert can be chosen because one router strongly favors it or because several favor it together, so a wrong choice is easier to correct. The errors of any one router no longer decide the selection, and routing becomes less sensitive to noisy features and distribution shift. The number of activated experts, expert FLOPs and communication volume stay the same. Compared with a single router, routing scores correlate noticeably better with how useful each expert is, with the largest gains in the middle and deeper layers.
All layers except the first use an MoE feed-forward block:
- 512 routed experts (top-10) plus 1 shared expert, with auxiliary-loss-free, bias-corrected load balancing.
- Latent experts. Each MoE layer first projects tokens from 4096 to a 2048-d latent space; the experts (intermediate size 2048) run in that space, and a single shared up-projection maps the result back to 4096. This roughly halves dispatch/combine traffic and expert FLOPs relative to full-width experts.
- Stable LatentMoE design with learnable scalars. The MoE blocks follow the Stable LatentMoE design (an RMSNorm before the up-projection and SiTU-GLU expert activations), which keeps expert outputs well scaled across all 43 layers and stabilizes optimization. In addition, each routed expert's routing weight is multiplied by its own learnable scalar.
2.3 Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC)
ERNIE 5.5 Flash replaces the standard residual connection with mHC: each layer reads from and writes to 4 parallel residual streams through a constrained mixing matrix, which gives layers a wider channel for passing information to one another at negligible extra compute.
2.4 MultiMax Output Head
A single softmax temperature forces a trade-off: lowering it makes the distribution sparse but also suppresses other plausible tokens; raising it keeps them but fattens the long tail of implausible ones. MultiMax replaces the single temperature with a learnable piecewise temperature, so the output head no longer has to choose: it suppresses the long tail of implausible tokens while keeping several plausible next tokens. The logits are rescaled element-wise inside the chunked, Triton-fused cross-entropy kernel just before the softmax. This adds negligible training overhead and no extra memory, and significantly lowers pre-training loss.
2.5 ECHO: Replacing the MTP Module
Conventional multi-token prediction (MTP) attaches extra modules to the backbone to predict future tokens, so the loss on future tokens mostly trains those modules, and the backbone is still trained mainly to predict the next token. ERNIE 5.5 Flash replaces the MTP module with ECHO, which reuses the backbone's own final layer to predict future tokens. Because there is no separate MTP layer, the loss on future tokens directly trains the same parameters that produce the next token. Learning to look past the next token encourages the backbone to anticipate where the sequence is heading, with clear gains on reasoning and code. ERNIE 5.5 Flash is pre-trained with single-step ECHO. The same layer also serves as the draft model for speculative decoding, and it generalizes beyond its training: although trained to predict only one extra token, it drafts several tokens ahead, with a higher acceptance rate than an auxiliary MTP module trained the same way.
2.6 Tokenizer
ERNIE 5.5 Flash uses a new BPE tokenizer with a vocabulary of about 200K entries. Numbers are tokenized right-to-left (R2L) in groups of up to three digits, so that digits with the same place value line up across numbers of different lengths (e.g. 1,234,567 → 1 234 567). This helps with arithmetic and number-heavy text.
3. Pre-training
ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base was pre-trained from scratch on 33.5T tokens with the Muon optimizer and FP8 mixed precision. The training context was gradually extended to 128K tokens over the course of pre-training, and fine-tuning and inference support a 1M-token context. The released checkpoint is taken at the end of pre-training and has not gone through any mid-training or post-training.
3.1 Data
The pre-training corpus covers a wide range of domains and languages and is curated for both breadth of knowledge and quality. Beyond this broad base, we focused on three areas:
- Web data. Multilingual web data is crawled at scale, extracted with high fidelity and filtered by models that score quality along several dimensions. The result covers a broad range of knowledge and is dense in useful training signal.
- Code data. Code collected from repositories and the web is filtered to remove non-code content, aggressively deduplicated and graded for quality at several granularities. Beyond static code, the corpus includes data on how software evolves and executes: commits, issues, pull requests, code reviews, requirement-to-PR and multi-commit trajectories, generated tests and CI-verified fixes. This data targets repository-level reasoning and agentic software engineering.
- Long-context data. Three complementary sources: natural long documents, selected for long-range dependencies and cleaned with embedding-based deduplication, LLM quality scoring and rules; long sequences built by concatenating natural texts with retrieved, semantically similar distractors; and synthetic data for MRCR-style retrieval, citation-grounded QA and multi-hop QA.
3.2 Training Infrastructure
We built two infrastructure components for this run: a distributed Muon optimizer that stays efficient across thousands of GPUs, and FlashMask-4, an attention kernel for large head dimensions.
Distributed Muon. Unlike element-wise optimizers such as Adam, Muon orthogonalizes the update of each parameter matrix as a whole. This changes how distributed training communicates and how memory is spread across GPUs. Two optimizations make it practical at the scale of thousands of GPUs:
- Communication-efficient updates. Conventionally, dense parameters are synchronized over a single ring that passes through every GPU in the cluster. Data travels across a long chain of inter-node links in many small messages, which leaves the links underused, and latency and jitter grow as the cluster gets larger. MoE parameters are synchronized differently: each GPU exchanges data only with the GPUs that hold the same rank on other nodes. We move dense-parameter synchronization onto this same path and combine the dense and MoE transfers into one collective operation. Messages become larger, so bandwidth is used more fully; the communication pattern becomes more regular and fits expert-parallel communication; and inter-node latency and jitter drop significantly. The optimizer's updates stay exactly the same.
- Memory-balanced sharding. Muon needs large messages to communicate efficiently, so naive sharding groups many parameter tensors together and places them on the first few GPUs. A handful of nodes then hold far more optimizer state than the rest. They are prone to OOM failures and slow to save, upload and download checkpoints, which lengthens failure recovery, and the problem grows with GPU count. Our inter-node balanced sharding spreads these optimizer states over more GPUs, including those later in the order. Memory is then balanced almost evenly across nodes, while messages stay large enough for efficient communication.
FlashMask-4 for large head dimensions. At large head dimensions, FlashAttention-style kernels run up against the limits of on-chip storage such as shared memory and tensor memory: compute utilization drops, and some configurations are hard to implement at all. FlashMask-4 is built on CuTe-DSL for both SM90 and SM100 GPUs. It works around these limits with 2-CTA tiled parallel computation and, on SM100, double-buffer rotation in tensor memory. It keeps FlashMask's compact O(N) column-wise mask representation and still skips fully masked blocks. It supports head dimensions up to qk_head_dim = 576 and v_head_dim = 512, beyond what FlashAttention-4 supports. On SM100 GPUs, it is up to 175% faster in the forward pass and up to 74% faster in the backward pass than FlashAttention-4 MaskMod.
4. Evaluation
4.1 Setup
For comparison, we selected the latest open-source base models of similar size publicly available at the time of release: DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Base (284B-A13B), Hy3-preview-Base (295B-A21A) and MiMo-V2.5-Base (310B-A15B). All four models are evaluated from their publicly released checkpoints with the same evaluation harness, prompts and few-shot examples, and with the same LLM judge for free-form QA.
4.2 Overall Results
ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base performs strongly across all benchmark categories, with reasoning, code and exam benchmarks among its best results. Although 37 of the 43 layers attend over a sequence compressed 128×, the six MLA-DSA layers are enough to keep performance strong on the six long-context benchmarks.
4.3 Detailed Results
The best result in each row is shown in bold. Swipe horizontally on mobile to view the full table.
5. Quick Start
ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base is available on Hugging Face in FP8 and BF16 safetensors (the BF16 version is ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base-BF16), under the ERNIE 5.5 Flash Base Model License Agreement v1.0. The model expects a BOS token at the start of every input, so keep add_special_tokens=True when tokenizing.
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
import torch
model_name = "baidu/ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base-BF16"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto")
model_inputs = tokenizer(["The hybrid attention architecture of ERNIE 5.5 Flash"], add_special_tokens=True, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device)
print(tokenizer.decode(model.generate(**model_inputs, max_new_tokens=256)[0], skip_special_tokens=True))
SGLang and vLLM both serve the model through the completions API; see the model card for deployment instructions. For fine-tuning, please refer to the ERNIE 5.5 example.
6. Conclusion and Outlook
ERNIE-5.5-Flash-Base starts from one premise: a base model meant for further training should be efficient by design. We balanced capability and efficiency in every component, from attention and residual connections to the MoE layers and the output head. The architecture is backed by broad, high-quality pre-training data and by a training system designed together with the model. With 14B parameters activated per token and a compact KV cache, the model performs strongly across a broad range of benchmarks, including long-context ones.
This base model is only a starting point. The post-trained ERNIE 5.5 Flash will follow, and we look forward to seeing what the community builds on top of it, whether for domain adaptation, reasoning or agents.

  author = {{Baidu ERNIE Team}},
