articles.title: Being a kid making games in the early 2000s
articles.body:
it's 1996 or something. 10-year-old me is eating breakfast with the principal in an elementary school cafeteria. this extraordinarily hyped-up breakfast event is my reward for achieving a high score on the FCAT state writing test. i'm disappointed that the food is standard Florida elementary school breakfast fare and not something fancier. they'd played this thing up to be a big deal.
it's fine though, i don't think i deserved the honor. they gave me an expository essay prompt to "explain what makes a Historical figure notable" (or something like that??) and I instead penned a comedy-fantasy with a shoehorned-in Lincoln cameo. my influences were narrow so it probably read like an unserious R.L. Stine short minus the horror. towards the end i threw in a cheeky joke about not following the rules hoping that my judges were amenable to snarky little scofflaws. i guess they were.
Floral Avenue Elementary in Bartow, FL
this was often a thing with me. starting at the age of 8 i simply would (could?) not start assignments i found too challenging (long division destroyed me. it snowballed into never passing pre-algebra by my senior year of highschool) or creative exercises i found pointless (persuasive essays. why would I try to persuade someone regarding a topic I had no interest in or knowledge of?) and instead opted to write short form fantasy and science fiction stories or draw detailed maps of made-up places. 
i was also bonkers about computers and the World Wide Web, though we couldn't afford a PC and i suspected we never would. didn't stop me from picking up the itch from TV, magazines (begging for PC Gamer and PC World mags at the supermarket was a thing i did a lot) and any middle-class acquaintances who'd let me spend the night at their cool houses. the 'information superhighway' metaphor was particularly exciting to me and my young mind took the early ads portraying people flying through cyberspace slightly too literally.
i first 
used
 a computer myself at an unofficial before-school daycare program that this saintly special needs teacher ran. she was often busy so she'd let me use the classroom Mac (a 
Power Macintosh 5200 LC
 to be exact) and it was heavenly. i most often played Oregon Trail, 
The Incredible Machine 2
, and whichever version of 
KidPix
 she had.
in 1997, after like 4 years of incessant begging, my parents took out a bank loan and purchased a Packard Bell Multimedia PC from Best Buy. it looked like this:
source: The Nostalgia Mall (YouTube)
by that time i'd collected enough magazine demo discs and thrift store games (i'd read the manuals for fun) that i had a few things to play, though it would be another two years before i could convince the parents to go in for internet access.
at 11 years old I was diagnosed with ADHD Primarily Inattentive, which in my case means that i don't do (or remember to do) things that i'm uninterested in without a disciplined routine or medication. i did take meds for a few months but stopped because i kept forgetting. my parents were too busy trying to make ends meet to push me on it. i was embarrassed about the diagnosis and wasn't sure if ADHD was real or if I was just being a lazy turd. 
my first year of middle school (i was 11-12?) was my academic downfall. i never did homework and rarely turned in classwork. i was bullied often and made sure to ~stand up for myself~ resulting in embarrassing fights i never won. plenty of detention too. we had parent-teacher meetings every quarter about "turning a new leaf" and getting caught up on assignments but it never took. i soon gave up on school completely. my focus shifted completely to a computer program I had recently discovered called 
The Games Factory
. that and Dragonball Z, Pokemon cards, and Eminem or whatever.
before figuring out how to use The Games Factory to make 
games
, I used its Animation editor to create flipbook-esque animations. stick figures blowing up or shooting anime energy beams at one another, mostly. the Animation editor was my first real taste of frame-by-frame animation, textbook margin animations aside, and thus another grown-up art discipline was demystified.
Gonna mostly call it TGF from now on. 
to my mind, making games was a highly technical thing that only large teams of grown-ups could accomplish, so The Games Factory was a reality-bending discovery. I was never 
not
 thinking about my next game project. I didn't want to do anything else. School notebooks were now for mocking up game concepts, enemy beastiaries, and level designs. I took my backpack to restaurants and other family outings and spent any downtime scribbling notes and sketches.
The Games Factory's Library Graphics. Love 'em now, thought they were a bit cheeseball back then.
though I now have an affinity for the charming library graphics that shipped with The Games Factory, I balked at the idea of using anyone else's art in my games. the appeal of the craft of games for me, even as a kid, was the filling of a virtual realm with minutiae for others to explore and enjoy. i don't think kid-me would've agreed, but the process was more akin to tending a garden or a building a diorama than anything to do with proper game design. or maybe it was closer to building a haunted house in a garage. or planning a theme park. i didn't care about challenge or progression or scoring systems. 
by the end of 1999 I had become a competent Microsoft Paint user and learned the fundamentals of pixel art just through messing around. there wasn't much else to do after i'd exhausted my shareware and demo collection, and we had no internet yet. 
by the way, I wouldn't have known the term pixel art back then. i'm not sure what people called it in 1999 but it wasn't that. i think most Pixel Art terminology was codified by the Pixelation forum, which is a topic for different essay.
in late 1999, two years after buying our first computer, my parents caved again to my computer-related pleading. this time for dial-up internet access. i chose a cool username (Simdrone052) and signed up for the Clickteam forums. i spent most of 2000 learning how to design websites, making and abandoning said websites, downloading screensavers, and probably also downloading naughty Dragonball Z fan art. (actually I just remembered my friend Chris gave me a bunch of those on a floppy. thanks Chris.)
it was early 2001. middle school was almost over. i continued not turning in classwork. i had no idea how to act around girls. i was convinced that i was the ugliest kid on the planet thanks to the pimple constellation dotting my pasty face. typical awkward tween puberty problems i'm sure, but hard nonetheless.  
 
the atmosphere at home was also an uneasy one. we moved to different houses so much that I wasn't able to maintain a real-life friend group and my social world became increasingly online.
 
by the summer of 2001 i only had a single 
real life
 friend left. middle school was over. my 8th grade art teacher (Mrs. Long, she ruled) scored me an audition at a fancy arts-focused high school. it seemed like the perfect place but sadly i decided that the judges would rather see traced pictures of Goku and Starcraft Hydralisks and Gordon Freeman than my own original artwork (which was cool, I was pretty good for my age) and they rejected me. my grades were also likely a factor. THANKS JAPAN. THANKS COMPUTERS.
i remember being convinced that i had already thrown my future away at 13. both my parents and teachers repeatedly emphasized risks of screwing up one's early education, and i was doing as poorly as any kid could while still technically passing. the only real option, to my kid mind, was to keep working on my art and games and hope that it would somday work itself out. and i did! 
by late 2001 i had a 
personal website
 up with downloads of my Games Factory games and graphics libraries. 
Site's Up!
My "RPG Library" for The Games Factory.
i was a regular in the #K&P IRC (basically old Discord) channel. users of Clickteam software called themselves the 'Klik community' after Klik & Play. Mostly anyway. i was one of the early dissenters who prefered "Click" but eventually fell in line.
Confessions of a Game Maker hater. I had to let people know that Game Maker stank. 
2002 was my most active year in the Klik community. i released many "
demo
" and "
beta
" versions of games, which usually meant that the game was stalled by a too-difficult-to-fix bug and I wanted some sort of appreciation for my work before abandoing it. here's one of my three profiles on Create-Games, the most popular Klik community website.
I was constantly deleting my own stuff and making new accounts. Each time I'd improve my old work would seem embarrassing so I'd chuck it. Or that's my assumption anyway, I have no idea why kid me did the things he did.
16-year-old Jay Tholen. 2003. probably around Christmas. probably listening to System of a Down, right on the verge of disocvering Pink Floyd.
2003 marked a move away from games, my attention was divided by a gazillion new influences and microhobbies and teenager things: 
i was devoting more time to prayer and reading scripture. 
i had massive, stupid crushes on girls resulting in embarrassing schemes to get them to notice me. I'll never write an essay on this. 
i was experiencing a life-changing progressive rock phase (Pink Floyd, then Dream Theater, then King Crimson and Genesis, then all the really weird stuff.)
Flash animation! Another new obsession. I was a regular on the Stick Figure Death Theater forum and particularly enjoyed Rob DenBleyker's Joe Zombie series, eventually working on my own never-released series inspired by it.
 
the Something Awful dot com forums had also completely shifted both my self-image and how I saw my peers. i registered in 2004 and quickly became a massive jerk because i suddenly saw myself as part of a savvy in-group. this was new for me. i felt i was on the bottom rung socially in real life. Something Awful was my biggest influence and time sink back then. (i'll def be writing about this later.) 
my game development time was also hampered by No Computer Sunday; a ban mandated by my dad in an attempt to encourage me to occasionally leave my room or do my homework. The result was me skipping tons of class to make up for lost time. at this point the world I cared most about had shifted almost entirely to the internet.
 
 
 
the thing that finally killed game development for me was a visit to 
Full Sail University
's open house. Full Sail was (is?) a private game development school in Orlando, only ~two hours away from our house. they advertised in PC Gamer magazine constantly, so I'd already developed a passing affinity for it. my parents took me there in the hopes that I'd turn my final year of school around enough to land some sort of small scholarship.
the campus tour was impressive. every discipline was represented and their facilities seemed to be state-of-the-art. the tour ended with an "ask a professor" event at their camus coffee place. visitors could mingle with the staff and eat snacks. 
whoever I talked to that night was definitely in the business of smacking down wide-eyed kids with hard industry truths because our conversation was brutal. i explained a little about my experience making smaller games and to him there was no place for that in the industry. in 2004 he may have been right. the shareware era was long dead and the next indie boom wouldn't be for another four or five years. 
he was also thinking of how i'd slot into Full Sail because he advised me to either pursue computer science OR game art but not both. he emphasized that going commercial with my pixelly hobby games was a doomed prospect. i cried on the drive home. 
i would go on to repeat my final year of high school and drop out before the end on the advice of my guidance counselor. my GPA was too low to pass and it'd make more sense to sign up for adult school and earn my GED (General Education Diploma.)

many years later the game thing DID end up working out and none of the experience went to waste. 
THE END!!!!!

articles.title: Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
articles.body:
Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House? (krebsonsecurity.com) 21
			
		 	
				Longtime Slashdot reader bbsguru shares a report from KrebsOnSecurity:  Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder's web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016. The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.
The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into "free" mobile and desktop applications. Infatica's founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia's state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016. [...] Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight. Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.  "This is public access," the Layer3 Intel team wrote. "Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services."

articles.title: Big Tech’s big AI buildout will not end until someone stops it
articles.body:
After four of the biggest competitors in the AI race held quarterly earnings calls late last month, two things are clear: Big Tech is not done spending record amounts on the AI data center buildout, and the AI data center buildout is not any closer to yielding its promised returns.
Big Tech’s big AI buildout will not end until someone stops it
Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Meta are on the hook with their data center plans.
A third thing is also starting to become clear — Big Tech will not be slowing down, at least not on its own.
Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, and Meta told investors they’re planning to spend at least $720 billion on CapEx this year alone. Most of that will go toward AI infrastructure. That’s on top of at least $1 trillion in spending commitments that have been arranged for the coming years.
Big Tech’s spending plans officially spooked Wall Street and triggered a sharp selloff in tech stocks last week that began to taper off as investors shifted focus to Tuesday’s midterm elections. Those spending plans could change after voters across the country elected candidates who favor moratoriums and other restrictions on data centers.
Wall Street might see the new uncertainty around the future of data center regulation as a good thing, given that tech stocks began to rise again on Tuesday. After all, there’s another issue Big Tech companies have to address. Despite enormous amounts of spending, they haven’t really made money from AI yet, and they’re continuing to double down on it anyway.
Until now, investors haven’t really blinked as Big Tech has ramped up its spending to fund the AI buildout. But more than three years in, Wall Street is starting to get antsy about the promised payoff of AI — and exactly when they might expect to see a return on investment.
It’s not that top-line revenue isn’t growing — it very much is. Amazon reported its fastest growth in five years for the quarter, Meta’s ad revenue is surging, and Google Cloud’s revenue more than doubled in a year. But as astonishing as it sounds, it might not be enough to justify the massive amounts Big Tech is spending on AI.
“Would it be more convenient if this type of acceleration and opportunity happened over 25 years and you could spread the CapEx over 25 years? Yeah, it might be more convenient. But that’s not the world we live in, and that’s not the opportunity.”
Alphabet offered the most uncomfortable example of this last week when Philipp Schindler, Google parent Alphabet’s senior vice president and chief business officer, acknowledged on the company’s earnings call that Google Cloud’s revenue growth has come at the expense of its core Search business.
“It’s worth noting that the strong growth in AI Mode queries had an impact because of the lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode,” Schindler said.
Revenue from Google’s Search ads grew 12% in the third quarter, a marked drop from the 17% growth rate the division posted for the same quarter last year.
It’s a weird paradox for Google. The strength of the company’s core business, Google Search, is what previously gave investors the confidence in the company’s aggressive spending agenda for AI. But now, Google’s new AI-enabled search engine is eating into theSearch business before the company has really figured out how to monetize AI Mode.
“To be clear, we feel very good about our trajectory here. Our ad experiments have shown promising results,” Schindler said of Google’s efforts to monetize AI Mode. He did not offer any specific examples.
Wall Street was especially unhappy with Google last week: On Thursday, Alphabet stock saw its worst one-day drop in history, sinking 13% in a single day.
The stock has started to pick back up this week, but it probably isn’t helping that the only thing Big Tech can say with certainty so far is to expect to see more spending.
Alphabet, which plans to spend between $195 billion and $205 billion in capital expenditures this year, is also planning to increase spending “significantly” in 2027, according to CFO Anat Ashkenazi.
Amazon intends to spend “meaningfully more” in 2027 than the $220 billion in capital expenditures it is planning this year, CEO Andy Jassy said on the company’s earnings call last week. He framed the spending — the largest ever in the company’s history — as a “once in a lifetime opportunity” to grow Amazon into a $1 trillion company.
“Would it be more convenient if this type of acceleration and opportunity happened over 25 years and you could spread the CapEx over 25 years? Yeah, it might be more convenient,” Jassy said. “But that’s not the world we live in, and that’s not the opportunity.”
Meta, which is expected to spend between $135 billion and $145 billion this year, didn’t disclose how much it intends to spend next year, but major financial institutions are expecting it to increase its spending from this year.
In touting the company’s rollout of Muse, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg noted that the agentic AI program will only become profitable if Meta can get its compute costs down.
Zuckerberg noted that Meta expects compute efficiency to increase “tenfold” next year, an endeavor he expects will take “significant investment.”
It’s not just Big Tech that is burning cash. Anthropic updated its S-1 prospectus with third-quarter revenue this week, revealing a sharp uptick in computing costs and net losses. The AI startup’s revenue grew to $17 billion in the quarter, a more than 1,000% increase from last year, but its compute costs came in at $17.5 billion — not quite enough to cover the impressive gains.
Anthropic has also committed nearly $900 billion in future compute and infrastructure costs, and it plans to begin the costly endeavor of building its own data centers.
Some of that $900 billion will go to Google, which is selling its TPU chips to Anthropic. Two different analysts on Google’s call pressed executives on the TPU business. After all, Google, like the other hyperscalers, has said it is capacity-constrained. If that is true, why would Google spend its resources selling its own capacity to other labs?
When asked if the money made from selling TPUs would help Google tamper some of its own spending, Ashkenazi didn’t give a clear yes or no answer. However, the answer seems likely to be no. Google is fronting the costs of building the hardware it sells to AI labs like Anthropic. Those contracts are supported by financial obligations that will come due when the hardware is ready to be used, but they don’t represent cash in Google’s pocket right now.
It may be worth noting that Microsoft was the only Big Tech company to escape Wall Street’s ire last week. The company posted $45.2 billion in capital expenditures for the quarter, down from an expected $50 billion. However, the lesser spend wasn’t due to any austerity on Microsoft’s part, but rather “third party capacity delays.”
Until last week, Microsoft had been the only hyperscaler that hadn’t taken on debt to fund its AI buildout. “We are fortunate to have access in the debt markets, given where our ratings are, and we have not yet, I would say, tapped that,” CFO Amy Hood said on the company’s earnings call Wednesday night.
That had changed by the next morning, when news of Microsoft’s $25 billion, 10-part bond sale broke.
By the time of this writing, Big Tech stocks were back up. Maybe Wall Street is banking on the “blue wave” of the midterms to force Big Tech to slow down some of its spending in the coming years. A slowdown might also give Big Tech a little more time to figure out how to make AI profitable.
Then again, despite the midterm elections looming last week, they did not come up on any of Big Tech’s earnings calls.

articles.title: TikTok launched a dedicated TikTok Shop app
articles.body:
TikTok has released a standalone app for TikTok Shop in a few countries, as spotted by social media consultant Matt Navarra. According to its App Store listing, the TikTok Shop app offers:
TikTok launched a dedicated TikTok Shop app
The new TikTok Shop app is now available in a few countries, but not the US.
- Personalized picks inspired by your interests
- LIVE streams & short videos to see products in action
- App-only deals, free shipping offers & exclusive first-order benefits that make every order feel worth it
- Secure payments for safe checkout
- Easy order tracking & 24/7 support from purchase to delivery
But it appears the app, which is also available on Android, hasn’t launched widely yet. Navarra says it’s currently listed in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia, and the Philippines, and not in the UK or US App Store. (I’m personally not seeing it on the US App Store on my iPhone.) Still, the fact that the dedicated app exists at all could signal that TikTok is planning to make an even bigger push into online shopping.
TikTok didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.

articles.title: Offline survival assistant – local LLM and Kiwix, runs from a USB stick
articles.body:
A survival assistant that works 100% without internet — on Windows, Linux and macOS.
🇧🇷 Português · 🇺🇸 English · 🇪🇸 Español
If the internet, power and services go down, this kit keeps working on a laptop or USB drive:
- 📚 Practical guides with cited sources (EN, PT, ES): water, fire, shelter, food, gardening and livestock, foraging/fishing/hunting, first aid and medicine, hygiene and homemade soap, alcohol (fermentation, distillation, antiseptic and fuel), solar power, radio and navigation, tools and knots, mental health and community, and checklists for 72 hours and 1 year.
- 🤖 Local AI that answers any question in natural language, citing its sources — it runs on your own computer (llama.cpp or Ollama); nothing goes to the internet.
- 🌐 Kiwix offline libraries: medical Wikipedia, post-disaster manuals, Where There Is No Doctor, wikiHow, iFixit and more — the AI searches them too.
- 📱 Web interface in your browser, shareable over the local network (other phones connect via Wi-Fi, even with no internet).
- 🔍 No-AI mode: even without a model, guide search works on any PC with Python.
⚠️ Disclaimer: educational content. It does not replace doctors, firefighters or emergency services. Health guidance follows public guidelines (WHO, Red Cross/IFRC, AHA, CDC, Hesperian…) cited in each section.
 Question ──► search kit guides (BM25) ──────┐
          └─► search Kiwix (.zim files) ──────┼─► local language model ──► answer with [1] [2] sources
                                              └─► (no model? shows the most relevant passages)
Large files are not committed to git (see .gitignore): the repository stays small and everyone builds their own kit with the preparer.
git clone https://github.com/sdalberto/ia-da-sobrevivencia.git
cd ia-da-sobrevivencia
The preparer asks for:
- AI model: leve (light, 1 GB, 4 GB RAM), padrao (default, 2 GB, 8 GB RAM — recommended), forte (strong, 4.7 GB, 16 GB RAM).
- Kiwix libraries: minimo (~3–5 GB), recomendado (~25–40 GB) or completo (100+ GB, full Wikipedia).
- Systems: this computer only, or Windows + Linux + macOS (universal USB kit).
- Portable Python: so the kit opens on computers without Python.
Non-interactive:
python sobrevivencia.py --lang en prepare --model padrao --zims recomendado --os all --python
Your browser opens http://127.0.0.1:8090. Switch language anytime with the PT/EN/ES buttons. To make English the default, create config/settings.local.json with { "language": "en" }.
Copy the whole folder to a USB drive or external disk formatted as exFAT (works on all three systems and supports files over 4 GB).
python sobrevivencia.py --lang en chat                   # terminal chat
python sobrevivencia.py --lang en ask "how do I make oral rehydration solution?"
python sobrevivencia.py --lang en search burn
python sobrevivencia.py status
python sobrevivencia.py start --host 0.0.0.0             # share on the local network
python sobrevivencia.py prepare --search survival        # find more Kiwix libraries
Ollama: if you use Ollama, run ollama pull qwen2.5:3b — it is detected automatically. Any local OpenAI-compatible server (LM Studio, llamafile, KoboldCpp, Jan) also works: set llm_url.
Kiwix Desktop: Kiwix Desktop can open the .zim files in zim/. To let the AI use its Local Kiwix Server, set { "kiwix_url": "http://127.0.0.1:<port>" } in config/settings.local.json. The Windows Kiwix Desktop package (~150 MB) exceeds GitHub's 100 MB per-file limit — publish it as a Release asset instead of committing it.
Drop .md or .txt files in knowledge/extra/ (family recipes, local maps, contacts, equipment manuals). They are indexed and cited by the AI.
- Minimum (search only): any PC with Python 3.8+.
- With AI: 4 GB RAM (light model), 8 GB recommended; x86-64 CPU with AVX2 or Apple Silicon/ARM64. No GPU needed.
- Disk: 3 GB (minimal kit) to 100+ GB (full kit).
python -m unittest discover -s tests
Code: MIT. Guides in knowledge/: CC BY-SA 4.0. Models, Kiwix, llama.cpp and ZIM files downloaded by the preparer have their own licenses. The default model (Qwen2.5 3B) uses the Qwen Research License; for commercial use choose leve or forte (Apache 2.0).

articles.title: American Voters Overwhelmingly Reject AI Data Centers
articles.body:
People across America rejected data centers during last night’s midterm election. Proposals related to data centers were explicitly on the ballot in more than 40 races across 13 states. People voted against data centers in 38 of them and counting. Six cities voted to ban data centers outright and 12 put limits on the amount of megawatts such buildings could draw. In addition to specific ballot measures, candidates who supported data centers lost across the country.
One of the most striking repudiations of pro data center politicians was in Texas, where Gregg Abbott lost a bid for a fourth term as governor. Abbott had made Texas a data center friendly place. The state has more than 300 working data centers and there are plans to double that number. “Texas is the epicenter of AI development,” Abbott said in 2025 at a press conference with Google CEO Sundar Pichai. “We must ensure that America remains at the forefront of the AI revolution, and Texas is the place where that can happen.” He went on to accept more than $9 million from data center-related donors.
When public sentiment turned against data centers, Abbott attempted to ride shifting political winds by issuing a “pause” on new projects. The pause wasn’t real. Texas regulators continued to approve data center projects after Abbott’s announcement and only shut down the state’s permitting web portal when 404 Media reported it.
Gina Hinojosa, Texas’s Democratic governor-elect, made Abbott’s stance on data centers a central part of her campaign. Abbott’s words about making Texas a data center-friendly AI state played on TVs and the internet over and over again. He lost by more than 700,000 votes.
Anti-data center candidates overwhelmingly won statewide races across the country. In Burgin, Kentucky, mayoral candidate George Hensley lost his bid after voting to approve a hyperscale project—to a write-in candidate. Hensley was the only name on the ballot, and he lost to Joe MonroeTK, who ran an anti-data center write-in campaign. Emporia, Kansas — where police arrested a school teacher for clapping during a data center related city meeting — passed a ban on high impact data centers. In Yukon, Oklahoma the mayor lost a recall election after he supported a hyperscale data center project.
"These midterms sent a clear message — people don't want to see data centers in their backyards,” Michael Whitesides, the deputy communications director for Local Progress, told 404 Media. “Across the country, people do not see the promised benefit of these data centers, and the AI they power, playing out in their daily lives. They're seeing basic goods and services get more expensive while these billionaire backed monstrosities take up space in their community, poison their air, and drive up their utility bills.”
Local Progress is a network of local elected officials. Over the past year, its members have become increasingly focused on data centers as a top political issue. “Last night, we saw local, state, and federal officials who backed data center deals lose their seats,” Whitesides said. He noted that Kim Rooney in Asheville, North Carolina and Amanda Rodrigues in San Marcos, Texas (both members of Local Progress) were elected mayors in their cities after running anti-data center campaigns.
“Big Tech will continue its typical playbook of trying to buy and bully local officials into complying with their demands for more data center development, but our hope is that last night's results are a clear signal to local leaders that they can resist and their community will back them up,” Whitesides said.
American voters in the communities where they’re being built hate data centers. They run up power bills, burn through water, and power Silicon Valley’s AI apparatus. America rejected data centers last night as both symbols of the big tech oligarchy and a physical manifestation of the future it wants to build. It’s a future Americans seem willing to fight.
Elon Musk, one of the night’s big losers, took a break from a weeks-long posting spree on X as the election results rolled in. Musk spent half a billion dollars on the midterms, $224 of it in Texas, the state where he lives and does a lot of business. The world’s richest man wanted to cover the state in data centers. Those plans aren’t looking good now that Abbott is out and Hinojoa is in.
Musk broke his election day posting silence a little after 1 am. “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” he said on X. Chased off the land by its people, the billionaire looks to the sky.

articles.title: Introducing Images 2.6
articles.body:
We’re introducing Images 2.6 in ChatGPT, Codex, and the API, bringing your ideas to life faster. With this, you can bring motion to your images with GIFs — from animating a brand mascot or character to turning a product shot into an eye-catching loop. You can also create polished visuals faster and refine them with greater precision — keeping characters, products, and brand details consistent as you edit.
People around the world now create 4 billion images per week across ChatGPT, Codex, and the API. On average, that’s more than half a billion images created per day.
Images 2.6 generates images 50% faster than before. In the API, we offer GPT‑Image‑2.6 Flare and Sunburst for developers to choose from. When quality is set to low, Flare can generate images in as little as six seconds. For work that calls for greater detail and precision, GPT‑Image‑2.6 Sunburst brings higher-quality image generation and even greater image consistency across edits when quality is set to medium or high. Flare also improves layout quality for posters, product imagery, and other professional visuals.
For moments that call for motion, GIFs bring another dimension to your ideas. Marketers and creators can animate a brand mascot for a campaign, create reactions and memes for social media, or use animated storyboards to explore character movement before video production.
And you don’t need a polished design to get started — even a simple sketch can become an expressive, animated character for videos, games, and more.
From personal reactions to brand mascots and product visuals, GIFs give people and businesses a playful way to communicate. Town, a startup building an AI work assistant, used Images 2.6 in the API to explore how animated characters could bring more personality to everyday interactions at work.
With Images 2.6, developers get more control over how images are created, edited, and carried into the next stage of a project. Image markup, already available in ChatGPT, comes to the API so teams can pinpoint exactly where to make specific changes. SVG exports make designs ready to use across websites, apps, and print.
A new complexity parameter lets developers adjust how much planning the model does to meet a request, with lower settings suited to quick edits. Image quality controls visual detail and fidelity, while complexity guides how much goes into the scene.
For most editing tasks, we recommend low complexity for faster edits, paired with the image quality your workflow requires. For scenes with many elements or constraints, try medium or high complexity effort.

Images 2.6 is available globally today in ChatGPT and Codex across all subscription tiers on desktop, mobile, and web.
GPT‑Image‑2.6 Sunburst and GPT‑Image‑2.6 Flare are available in the API. See pricing details here.(opens in a new window)

articles.title: Local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Linux
articles.body:
A thousand fewer paths to root
We've developed an autonomous vulnerability discovery, exploitation, and patching pipeline. In one run with our cyber model, it validated and generated patches for 948 local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Linux at an API cost of $1.2 million.
Security research that once required a separate, sustained investigation for each finding can increasingly be run as a systematic process. This document explores one of our efforts in this area.
Vulnerability discovery is becoming easier to scale, but prioritization and validation remain operational bottlenecks. We built a prototype to look for security flaws in the Linux kernel inside a controlled research environment. Our prototype identified and analyzed 2,308 candidate Linux kernel findings, dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and produced 948 local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits that could allow an unprivileged local user to gain root access.
We used this evidence to prioritize vulnerabilities for reporting and developed candidate patches for maintainer review. Following guidance from the Linux kernel community, we began with critical vulnerabilities and are working with Patch the Planet partners on further reports and patches.
In June, as part of our Patch the Planet initiative, we shared that GPT‑5.5 Cyber had identified Linux kernel vulnerabilities and developed 24 local privilege escalation exploits to validate and report them. We expanded that work into a pipeline, powered by an upcoming cyber model, covering vulnerability discovery, dynamic validation, exploitability assessment, and patch generation. When it finished, human researchers reviewed the outputs and reported found vulnerabilities alongside patches.
Summary
Methodology
- At a high level, our pipeline works as follows: first it identifies security-relevant parts of the Linux kernel, statically scans those audit targets for candidate findings, dynamically reproduces those findings in an isolated environment, creates a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit to demonstrate exploitability, generates patches, and finally a human security researcher reviews the results.
- The output of the pipeline includes a root cause analysis, a minimal crashing proof-of-concept, a candidate patch, and a full exploit to assist human researchers in assessing the severity of the vulnerability and upstreaming the fixes.
Findings
- In a run in mid-October 2026, our pipeline using an upcoming cyber model dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and generated PoCs for 291 information leak vulnerabilities and 948 working local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits for a commonly used Linux distribution. The total run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, or $1,279 per LPE exploit.
- The target virtual machines ran a stock desktop operating system, not a weakened target, under the same threat model used by cybersecurity competitions (e.g. Pwn2Own(opens in a new window), TyphoonPWN(opens in a new window)). Historically, Pwn2Own and TyphoonPWN offered a $20,000 and $70,000 bug bounty for Linux kernel LPE exploits. Applying those historical bounty amounts to the 948 exploits produces a hypothetical valuation of $18.9M—$66.3M, approximately 16x to 55x our pipeline’s cost.
- On an adapted kernelCTF(opens in a new window) environment, which is a version of the Linux kernel with reduced attack surface, our pipeline obtained 25 information leak PoCs and 21 LPE exploits. For comparison, 26 confirmed 0-day LPE exploits have been accepted by kernelCTF in 2026 at the time of writing. 
  - The campaign cost roughly $32,936 in API credits. If the 21 vulnerabilities were accepted by the program, it would lead to around a $1.5M bounty award, ~45x the scanning cost.
- To the best of our knowledge, the agents in this pipeline discovered and used at least 10 novel Linux exploitation techniques.
Reflections
- The Linux maintainers and security community are working hard to rapidly discover and fix vulnerabilities. Within 10 days while the scan was running, we observed over 100 Linux LPEs had been patched or had staging patches from other contributors, with ~300 more being publicly discussed.
- Given the rate of vulnerability discovery by frontier models, we believe automated patch generation is essential to secure software at the pace required, and to limit the exploitation window. With human expert-guided iteration, we believe AI-generated patches can be functionally correct, aligned with existing coding styles, and robust to attack variants. This is an important area for further research.
- More capable models are able to discover new vulnerabilities in existing code, often including ones that have been around longer and are more complex to identify. Our analysis pipeline using the newer cyber model in mid-October discovered >5x more novel LPEs than a GPT‑5.6 Sol run in July, despite three months of hardening between the scans.
- Large, complex software projects likely require multiple rounds of scanning and fixing vulnerabilities to “bottom out” latent bugs. Ideally this process is repeated with each subsequent generation of frontier models. This applies to both proprietary and open source software.
- For the near and medium term, having access to a low-privileged account on an operating system, that isn’t up-to-date on its latest available patches should be considered functionally equivalent to root access for a well-resourced threat actor. Defense in depth, using sandboxes and isolation approaches like Firecracker and gVisor are important for limiting the blast radius of exploited vulnerabilities.
- Within the next few years, we believe that if there are vulnerabilities in a given software project, frontier models will likely be able to discover them and even less capable models may be able to develop exploits once disclosed. In a world of no unknown vulnerabilities, it will be critical to build and maintain high assurance software, especially core software such as operating systems, browsers, image parsing libraries, the TCP/IP stack, and more. Investing in training models to write secure code by default, minimizing attack surface by removing unnecessary features, and formal verification are promising areas of future research to effectively scale software security, in addition to finding and fixing existing vulnerabilities.
The Linux kernel underpins Android devices, cloud infrastructure, supercomputers, and other systems used by billions of people. With more than 40 million lines of code, the kernel exposes a broad attack surface through system calls, networking, filesystems, and device drivers. We chose Linux to study how effectively frontier models could find vulnerabilities and demonstrate their security impact in a codebase of this scale and importance.
The initial vulnerability discovery stage produced thousands of candidate findings, too many for security researchers to manually review and triage. The operational challenge of our vulnerability discovery pipeline was not discovery, but determining which findings could be reproduced, what security boundary they crossed, and which warranted the earliest maintainer attention.
The mission of OpenAI’s Cyber team is to help secure the software the world relies on. We report API costs for each stage to help researchers assess the resources needed to reproduce and extend this work. These costs reflect the models, target configurations, and workflow used in this evaluation. Our broader goal is to help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities, reducing the opportunities available to attackers and raising the cost for them to exploit software.
Finally, note that we focused on methodology and measuring model capability in this research, not cost. We expect that sufficient harness engineering could meaningfully reduce the cost at each stage; thus, the costs we report are more an upper bound.
Our vulnerability research prototype is a pipeline of five stages, which uses an upcoming cyber model at its core:
- Vulnerability discovery: Agents identify security-relevant parts of the codebase and scan them for candidate findings.
- Dynamic validation: Agents attempt to reproduce each candidate in an isolated environment and preserve runtime evidence. This step outputs the reproduced and validated vulnerabilities.
- Exploitability assessment: Agents test whether validated vulnerabilities could enable information disclosure or local privilege escalation.
- Patch generation: Agents generate patches that address each identified vulnerability.
- Human review: Security researchers review the exploit, patch, and proposed severity before reporting to the maintainers.
At the end of the pipeline, the system bundles a root cause analysis, a minimal crashing proof-of-concept, a candidate patch, and a full exploit to assist human researchers in assessing the severity of the vulnerability and upstreaming the fixes.
Not every line of code in the Linux kernel is security-relevant. Our pipeline used a team of Scout agents to identify high-value audit targets, which were then passed to Analyst agents for vulnerability scanning.
Scout agents read through each folder and file and determine what targets to audit based on their reachability (reachable by low-privileged users) and security relevance.
This stage identified 5,034 audit targets, about 2.8 million lines of code, which is roughly 7% of the whole Linux kernel code base, significantly reducing the cost of the security audit when compared to a full codebase analysis. This step cost $3,426 in API credits.
Next, analyst agents analyzed each audit target and produced candidate findings using a workflow similar to that of the Codex Security plugin(opens in a new window). At a high level, the analyst agents read the assigned audit target’s code to understand how it works, identify its threat model, and look for vulnerabilities in it.
Within 12 hours, the analyst agents produced 2,308 candidate findings after deduplication. This stage cost $316,549 in API credits.
A candidate finding is not the same as a validated vulnerability. At this scale, manually investigating every report is impractical for our research team.
We therefore focused on validating findings that a) were reachable by a low-privileged user, b) required no special capabilities, and c) produced measurable evidence of memory corruption.
For each candidate, a triage agent generated a proof of concept and ran it in an isolated virtual machine running a Linux kernel with Kernel Address Sanitizer (KASAN). The agent observed both the program output and system console, then iteratively refined the proof of concept until it reproduced the reported behavior or exhausted the potential ways of triggering it.
Within 30 hours, our system reproduced 1724 vulnerabilities, ~74.7% of the 2,308 candidate findings. Static code review alone can be prone to false positives, so we were impressed by the accuracy of the analyst agents and the effectiveness of the triage agents in autonomously creating working proofs of concept for almost three quarters of the candidate findings.
Most remaining findings either required elevated privileges or failed to reproduce within the time budget because of difficult race conditions, specific trigger conditions (e.g., a required allocation failure at a specific line), or time-consuming validation (e.g., refcount wraparound). Only 3.1% reflected incorrect analysis by the model, where the reported vulnerability assumed an impossible condition.
The validation stage cost $73,330 in API credits in total. We observed that in our validation pipeline, which needed to generate a proof-of-concept to confirm if a candidate is a real vulnerability, this process was more expensive than making a recommendation based only on static analysis, and the costs of attempting to validate a true positive and false positive were similar. Thus removing false positives earlier in the pipeline makes the process meaningfully more cost-efficient.
Validation establishes that a vulnerability is real, but not how urgently it should be addressed. A vulnerability that could enable local privilege escalation, for example, warrants greater priority than one that could only cause a local denial of service. With 1,724 validated vulnerabilities, the next task was to identify the findings with the greatest potential security impact.
An initial screening agent reviewed each report, crash log, and relevant source code statically. It was deliberately permissive to avoid discarding potentially serious findings, while filtering out cases without a plausible exploitation path. This narrowed the results to 313 information leak candidates and 1,238 local privilege escalation candidates.
Exploit-development (ExploitDev) agents then tested those candidates in isolated virtual machines configured with the protections enabled by a standard Linux distribution, including Supervisor Mode Execution Prevention (SMEP), Supervisor Mode Access Prevention (SMAP), Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR), and HARDENED_USERCOPY. This helped prevent unrealistic assessments that depended on protections being disabled.
The agents produced 291 proofs of concept for information leaks and 1,169 working local privilege escalation exploits that could give unprivileged local users root access.
We performed variant analysis and developed 948 distinct patches for the vulnerabilities behind those exploits. We use that number to determine the overall number of unique LPEs. Successful exploits cost an average of $359 in credits to develop. That makes it relatively inexpensive for defenders to test the exploitability of found vulnerabilities.
The initial vulnerability screening agent cost $44,194 in API credits. The exploitation stage cost $775,929 in API credits in total, $84,929 for processing information leak candidates and $691,000 for local privilege escalation candidates.
On average, processing a local-privilege escalation candidate ($558) was roughly two times more expensive than processing an information leak candidate ($271). This is because information leak PoCs were carried forward from the validation stage and required less modification to become usable in an exploit. On the other hand, developing an exploit from an LPE candidate required many extra steps such as exploitation strategy planning, identifying vulnerable objects to use, mitigation bypasses and more. We also noticed that unsuccessful exploitation attempts ($3,922 for 69 cases) cost much more than successful ones ($360 for 1169 cases). This was caused by a few hard-to-exploit vulnerabilities (e.g. race conditions). Defining a reasonable give-up condition, such as stopping the attempt after making no progress for one hour, would have reduced the cost of ExploitDev significantly.
For each validated vulnerability, the system also generates a patch. We provide the model with the relevant source code and prompt it with best practices in patch writing, such as performing static checks on the patch, following the software development practices used in nearby code, and performing variant analysis to make sure the patch is complete.
Following the Linux kernel community’s suggestion, we have already sent out hundreds of reports and patches for critical vulnerabilities and are working with Patch the Planet partners to gradually send out patches for the rest. This work is part of our broader Daybreak commitment to support open-source projects.
In this section we share learnings, reflections, and additional analysis from this research.
During this research, we observed the Linux maintainers moving quickly to fix vulnerabilities and protect users. The scan was performed on the latest Linux kernel in mid-October 2026. When the autonomous scan and manual analysis finished after 10 days, 61 LPEs had already been patched upstream, 43 had staging patches, and 299 were being reported and discussed publicly.
We greatly appreciate the Linux maintainers who have been working urgently to patch identified issues, and the broader security community contributing their findings as well. This collective response is what’s needed to secure the world’s software. The rapid rate of vulnerability disclosure and patching also emphasizes the criticality for users and companies to keep software up to date.
Takeaway: Automated triage should take the rapid patching cycle into account. Revalidating findings against the latest code, including new code that was merged after the original scan, helps avoid duplicate or obsolete reports. This focuses attention on unresolved vulnerabilities and gives maintainers evidence that they can act on without adding unnecessary review burden.
While we were developing the pipeline, in late July 2026, GPT‑5.6 Sol found and exploited 166 unique LPE vulnerabilities for an end-to-end $513,690 cost in API credits.
In the second scan, in mid-October 2026, the newer cyber model found and exploited 948 unique LPE vulnerabilities for an end-to-end $1,213,430 cost in API credits. For both campaigns, we scanned the latest Linux kernel master branch at the time.
Takeaway: Rescan previously audited code as model capabilities improve. A more capable model may uncover vulnerabilities that earlier models missed, even when using the same research harness.
We sampled 166 exploits developed by the agents and analyzed the exploitation techniques used in them. To the best of our knowledge, the agents used 10 new exploitation techniques in the sampled exploits. We shared the exploitation techniques with third-party kernel exploitation experts and the techniques were new to them as well.
Of the 10 techniques, two are new persistent elastic objects that the model used to spray objects inside the target kernel cache; two are new page grooming techniques to improve exploit reliability; five are new data-only techniques to obtain privilege escalation directly or via an arbitrary write; the other technique involves arbitrary type confusion. For safety reasons, we omit sharing the full technical details of these new exploitation techniques in this post.
Takeaway: Frontier models do not just pattern match known vulnerable code patterns or solely use known exploitation techniques; they demonstrate creativity and novel approaches.
An important part of our team’s mission is to measure the cost of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities and use that evidence to guide defensive investment. Our goal is to help defenders fix vulnerabilities before attackers can use them, and make it cost prohibitive for attackers to exploit software. Measuring exploitation costs helps us assess how that challenge changes as model capabilities improve. In this section, we compare our pipeline run’s cost with bug bounty program rewards for the vulnerabilities identified.
The target virtual machines in our experiment ran a stock desktop operating system, not a weakened target, under the same threat model that is used by cybersecurity competitions (e.g. Pwn2Own(opens in a new window), TyphoonPWN(opens in a new window)). Historically, Pwn2Own and TyphoonPWN offered bug bounties of $20,000 and $70,000, respectively for Linux kernel local privilege escalation exploits. Applying those historical bounty amounts to the 948 exploits produces a hypothetical valuation of $18.9M—$66.3M, approximately 16x to 55x our pipeline’s cost.
We also tested our pipeline against Google’s kernelCTF(opens in a new window) vulnerability reward program, which features a hardened Linux kernel with reduced attack surfaces as the target. We ran the pipeline on the latest version of the Linux kernel (incompatible with the SLAB_VIRTUAL mitigation in kernelCTF so we dropped it from the config) under kernelCTF’s environment and obtained 25 information leak proofs of concept and 21 local privilege escalation exploits. For comparison, 26 confirmed 0-day LPE exploits have been accepted by kernelCTF in 2026 at the time of writing. The whole campaign lasted 112 hours in total, costing roughly $32,936 in API credits, with vulnerability discovery accounting for 83.7% of the API cost. If the 21 vulnerabilities were accepted by the program, it would lead to around a $1.5M bounty award, approximately 45x the cost.
Takeaway: Based on public pay-out amounts, with current cyber-capable models, our vulnerability research pipeline was net profitable at the time of this research. Defenders should proactively analyze their software so that it becomes cost prohibitive for attackers to exploit.
During exploitability assessment, ExploitDev agents were given a vulnerability report and tasked with creating a fully functional exploit. Our pipeline marked a vulnerability as exploited if a root shell was successfully obtained. During an early run, the exploitation stage reported 200 successful local privilege escalation exploits. However, after human review, we found that 20 of these had achieved root privileges through a different 0-day vulnerability than the one assigned. This suggests that even successful exploitation by agents needs proper validation.
We subsequently tightened the task constraints and added an independent check confirming that each final exploit used its assigned vulnerability.
Takeaway: For autonomous security research, verify the path to a result in addition to verifying the result itself; isolation, monitoring, and independent checks are necessary controls.
Early in this research, we explored the design decision of whether to build heavy orchestration around the agent to improve its cyber capability. Our result suggested that stronger models require lighter orchestration and hand-holding. And the marginal improvement does not justify the maintenance cost. As a result, we decided to remove the heavy orchestration.
The experiment compared GPT‑5.5 Cyber and GPT‑5.6 Cyber. In our observation, GPT‑5.5 Cyber did not consistently identify when and how to apply existing Linux kernel exploitation techniques. We then assembled 103 techniques in a model-friendly format, made them available in the agent’s environment, and prompted the agent to use them. Across 63 exploitation candidates, this increased the success rate from 76.2% to 88.9%.
When we repeated this with GPT‑5.6 Cyber, the model was better able to find, select, and apply relevant techniques on its own. We removed the technique/skill orchestration and this lightly orchestrated GPT‑5.6 Cyber workflow outperformed the more heavily scaffolded GPT‑5.5 Cyber workflow. Adding back the additional technique layer for GPT‑5.6 Cyber provided only a marginal 1.5 percentage-point improvement.
Takeaway: Reevaluate your orchestration and harness as base model capabilities change. Scaffolding that materially improves one model generation may add little value for a stronger model and should be evaluated for the maintenance tradeoff.
Initially, when directly prompted to generate candidate patches, the model would create functionally correct patches that mitigate the proof of concept but occasionally introduce other issues: more code than necessary, introduced potential performance tradeoffs, deviated from coding conventions, or failed to examine related code for variants of the same vulnerability, leading to incomplete patches.
Additional instructions and iterations on the patch generation process improved the quality of patches, which suggests that with proper handling, it is possible for AI-generated security patches to be correct, minimal, and consistent with existing code conventions. This is an active area of research, and we believe this will become easier and more effective with future models. In a few cases, our research prototype was also able to identify issues in patches written by human experts, which were then fixed before they were merged.
Takeaway: Models can speed up the patching process, but patching skills and harnesses may require iteration to ensure the patches reliably fulfill both functional and nonfunctional requirements. Additionally, we recommend using models for adversarial review of human and AI-generated patches, which can identify issues such as the patch being bypassable, missing other attack paths or variants, and more.
In our kernelCTF run, besides the 21 Linux kernel 0-day exploits, our research prototype also found and exploited a QEMU TCG vulnerability. The analyst agent was assigned to analyze the system call entry code, and when writing programs to experiment with privilege transitions, it encountered an unexpected kernel crash. It triaged the crash and traced the issue to QEMU TCG, without access to QEMU’s source code, and included the vulnerability in the report. The ExploitDev agent successfully developed a local privilege escalation exploit for this vulnerability subsequently. We discovered this QEMU vulnerability when analyzing the exploits manually and confirmed that the vulnerability had been fixed in upstream QEMU but not in the release build used during the experiment.
Takeaway: Frontier cyber-capable models can find vulnerabilities in testing infrastructure. We recommend testing each part of the infrastructure before carrying out offensive vulnerability research. We have proactively tested our infrastructure, disclosing and patching many vulnerabilities in Kata, Moby/Docker, gVisor, and other projects.
Our goal is to turn increasing model capability into a lasting advantage for the people securing the Internet. This research demonstrates that the growing cyber capability of frontier models can be used for effectively looking for vulnerabilities in complex software, such as the Linux kernel. Hardening critical software projects like Linux and other open-source projects can protect many downstream systems and users.
Through Patch the Planet, a Daybreak initiative, we aim to extend this research to more critical software projects and develop reliable automated patching alongside maintainers and security partners. We want to steadily reduce the opportunities available to attackers and raise the cost of finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, until the expected payoff no longer justifies the attack.
Every generation of models should help us build software that the next generation finds harder to compromise. We will continue working towards building a secure Internet that anyone can joyfully build on.

articles.title: Local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Linux
articles.body:
A thousand fewer paths to root
We've developed an autonomous vulnerability discovery, exploitation, and patching pipeline. In one run with our cyber model, it validated and generated patches for 948 local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Linux at an API cost of $1.2 million.
Security research that once required a separate, sustained investigation for each finding can increasingly be run as a systematic process. This document explores one of our efforts in this area.
Vulnerability discovery is becoming easier to scale, but prioritization and validation remain operational bottlenecks. We built a prototype to look for security flaws in the Linux kernel inside a controlled research environment. Our prototype identified and analyzed 2,308 candidate Linux kernel findings, dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and produced 948 local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits that could allow an unprivileged local user to gain root access.
We used this evidence to prioritize vulnerabilities for reporting and developed candidate patches for maintainer review. Following guidance from the Linux kernel community, we began with critical vulnerabilities and are working with Patch the Planet partners on further reports and patches.
In June, as part of our Patch the Planet initiative, we shared that GPT‑5.5 Cyber had identified Linux kernel vulnerabilities and developed 24 local privilege escalation exploits to validate and report them. We expanded that work into a pipeline, powered by an upcoming cyber model, covering vulnerability discovery, dynamic validation, exploitability assessment, and patch generation. When it finished, human researchers reviewed the outputs and reported found vulnerabilities alongside patches.
Summary
Methodology
- At a high level, our pipeline works as follows: first it identifies security-relevant parts of the Linux kernel, statically scans those audit targets for candidate findings, dynamically reproduces those findings in an isolated environment, creates a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit to demonstrate exploitability, generates patches, and finally a human security researcher reviews the results.
- The output of the pipeline includes a root cause analysis, a minimal crashing proof-of-concept, a candidate patch, and a full exploit to assist human researchers in assessing the severity of the vulnerability and upstreaming the fixes.
Findings
- In a run in mid-October 2026, our pipeline using an upcoming cyber model dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and generated PoCs for 291 information leak vulnerabilities and 948 working local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits for a commonly used Linux distribution. The total run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, or $1,279 per LPE exploit.
- The target virtual machines ran a stock desktop operating system, not a weakened target, under the same threat model used by cybersecurity competitions (e.g. Pwn2Own(opens in a new window), TyphoonPWN(opens in a new window)). Historically, Pwn2Own and TyphoonPWN offered a $20,000 and $70,000 bug bounty for Linux kernel LPE exploits. Applying those historical bounty amounts to the 948 exploits produces a hypothetical valuation of $18.9M—$66.3M, approximately 16x to 55x our pipeline’s cost.
- On an adapted kernelCTF(opens in a new window) environment, which is a version of the Linux kernel with reduced attack surface, our pipeline obtained 25 information leak PoCs and 21 LPE exploits. For comparison, 26 confirmed 0-day LPE exploits have been accepted by kernelCTF in 2026 at the time of writing. 
  - The campaign cost roughly $32,936 in API credits. If the 21 vulnerabilities were accepted by the program, it would lead to around a $1.5M bounty award, ~45x the scanning cost.
- To the best of our knowledge, the agents in this pipeline discovered and used at least 10 novel Linux exploitation techniques.
Reflections
- The Linux maintainers and security community are working hard to rapidly discover and fix vulnerabilities. Within 10 days while the scan was running, we observed over 100 Linux LPEs had been patched or had staging patches from other contributors, with ~300 more being publicly discussed.
- Given the rate of vulnerability discovery by frontier models, we believe automated patch generation is essential to secure software at the pace required, and to limit the exploitation window. With human expert-guided iteration, we believe AI-generated patches can be functionally correct, aligned with existing coding styles, and robust to attack variants. This is an important area for further research.
- More capable models are able to discover new vulnerabilities in existing code, often including ones that have been around longer and are more complex to identify. Our analysis pipeline using the newer cyber model in mid-October discovered >5x more novel LPEs than a GPT‑5.6 Sol run in July, despite three months of hardening between the scans.
- Large, complex software projects likely require multiple rounds of scanning and fixing vulnerabilities to “bottom out” latent bugs. Ideally this process is repeated with each subsequent generation of frontier models. This applies to both proprietary and open source software.
- For the near and medium term, having access to a low-privileged account on an operating system, that isn’t up-to-date on its latest available patches should be considered functionally equivalent to root access for a well-resourced threat actor. Defense in depth, using sandboxes and isolation approaches like Firecracker and gVisor are important for limiting the blast radius of exploited vulnerabilities.
- Within the next few years, we believe that if there are vulnerabilities in a given software project, frontier models will likely be able to discover them and even less capable models may be able to develop exploits once disclosed. In a world of no unknown vulnerabilities, it will be critical to build and maintain high assurance software, especially core software such as operating systems, browsers, image parsing libraries, the TCP/IP stack, and more. Investing in training models to write secure code by default, minimizing attack surface by removing unnecessary features, and formal verification are promising areas of future research to effectively scale software security, in addition to finding and fixing existing vulnerabilities.
The Linux kernel underpins Android devices, cloud infrastructure, supercomputers, and other systems used by billions of people. With more than 40 million lines of code, the kernel exposes a broad attack surface through system calls, networking, filesystems, and device drivers. We chose Linux to study how effectively frontier models could find vulnerabilities and demonstrate their security impact in a codebase of this scale and importance.
The initial vulnerability discovery stage produced thousands of candidate findings, too many for security researchers to manually review and triage. The operational challenge of our vulnerability discovery pipeline was not discovery, but determining which findings could be reproduced, what security boundary they crossed, and which warranted the earliest maintainer attention.
The mission of OpenAI’s Cyber team is to help secure the software the world relies on. We report API costs for each stage to help researchers assess the resources needed to reproduce and extend this work. These costs reflect the models, target configurations, and workflow used in this evaluation. Our broader goal is to help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities, reducing the opportunities available to attackers and raising the cost for them to exploit software.
Finally, note that we focused on methodology and measuring model capability in this research, not cost. We expect that sufficient harness engineering could meaningfully reduce the cost at each stage; thus, the costs we report are more an upper bound.
Our vulnerability research prototype is a pipeline of five stages, which uses an upcoming cyber model at its core:
- Vulnerability discovery: Agents identify security-relevant parts of the codebase and scan them for candidate findings.
- Dynamic validation: Agents attempt to reproduce each candidate in an isolated environment and preserve runtime evidence. This step outputs the reproduced and validated vulnerabilities.
- Exploitability assessment: Agents test whether validated vulnerabilities could enable information disclosure or local privilege escalation.
- Patch generation: Agents generate patches that address each identified vulnerability.
- Human review: Security researchers review the exploit, patch, and proposed severity before reporting to the maintainers.
At the end of the pipeline, the system bundles a root cause analysis, a minimal crashing proof-of-concept, a candidate patch, and a full exploit to assist human researchers in assessing the severity of the vulnerability and upstreaming the fixes.
Not every line of code in the Linux kernel is security-relevant. Our pipeline used a team of Scout agents to identify high-value audit targets, which were then passed to Analyst agents for vulnerability scanning.
Scout agents read through each folder and file and determine what targets to audit based on their reachability (reachable by low-privileged users) and security relevance.
This stage identified 5,034 audit targets, about 2.8 million lines of code, which is roughly 7% of the whole Linux kernel code base, significantly reducing the cost of the security audit when compared to a full codebase analysis. This step cost $3,426 in API credits.
Next, analyst agents analyzed each audit target and produced candidate findings using a workflow similar to that of the Codex Security plugin(opens in a new window). At a high level, the analyst agents read the assigned audit target’s code to understand how it works, identify its threat model, and look for vulnerabilities in it.
Within 12 hours, the analyst agents produced 2,308 candidate findings after deduplication. This stage cost $316,549 in API credits.
A candidate finding is not the same as a validated vulnerability. At this scale, manually investigating every report is impractical for our research team.
We therefore focused on validating findings that a) were reachable by a low-privileged user, b) required no special capabilities, and c) produced measurable evidence of memory corruption.
For each candidate, a triage agent generated a proof of concept and ran it in an isolated virtual machine running a Linux kernel with Kernel Address Sanitizer (KASAN). The agent observed both the program output and system console, then iteratively refined the proof of concept until it reproduced the reported behavior or exhausted the potential ways of triggering it.
Within 30 hours, our system reproduced 1724 vulnerabilities, ~74.7% of the 2,308 candidate findings. Static code review alone can be prone to false positives, so we were impressed by the accuracy of the analyst agents and the effectiveness of the triage agents in autonomously creating working proofs of concept for almost three quarters of the candidate findings.
Most remaining findings either required elevated privileges or failed to reproduce within the time budget because of difficult race conditions, specific trigger conditions (e.g., a required allocation failure at a specific line), or time-consuming validation (e.g., refcount wraparound). Only 3.1% reflected incorrect analysis by the model, where the reported vulnerability assumed an impossible condition.
The validation stage cost $73,330 in API credits in total. We observed that in our validation pipeline, which needed to generate a proof-of-concept to confirm if a candidate is a real vulnerability, this process was more expensive than making a recommendation based only on static analysis, and the costs of attempting to validate a true positive and false positive were similar. Thus removing false positives earlier in the pipeline makes the process meaningfully more cost-efficient.
Validation establishes that a vulnerability is real, but not how urgently it should be addressed. Exploit-development (ExploitDev) agents then tested those candidates in isolated virtual machines configured with the protections enabled by a standard Linux distribution, including Supervisor Mode Execution Prevention (SMEP), Supervisor Mode Access Prevention (SMAP), Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR), and HARDENED_USERCOPY. This helped prevent unrealistic assessments that depended on protections being disabled.
The agents produced 291 proofs of concept for information leaks and 1,169 working local privilege escalation exploits that could give unprivileged local users root access.
We performed variant analysis and developed 948 distinct patches for the vulnerabilities behind those exploits. We use that number to determine the overall number of unique LPEs. Successful exploits cost an average of $359 in credits to develop. That makes it relatively inexpensive for defenders to test the exploitability of found vulnerabilities.
The initial vulnerability screening agent cost $44,194 in API credits. The exploitation stage cost $775,929 in API credits in total, $84,929 for processing information leak candidates and $691,000 for local privilege escalation candidates.
On average, processing a local-privilege escalation candidate ($558) was roughly two times more expensive than processing an information leak candidate ($271). This is because information leak PoCs were carried forward from the validation stage and required less modification to become usable in an exploit. On the other hand, developing an exploit from an LPE candidate required many extra steps such as exploitation strategy planning, identifying vulnerable objects to use, mitigation bypasses and more. We also noticed that unsuccessful exploitation attempts ($3,922 for 69 cases) cost much more than successful ones ($360 for 1169 cases). This was caused by a few hard-to-exploit vulnerabilities (e.g. race conditions). Defining a reasonable give-up condition, such as stopping the attempt after making no progress for one hour, would have reduced the cost of ExploitDev significantly.
For each validated vulnerability, the system also generates a patch. We provide the model with the relevant source code and prompt it with best practices in patch writing, such as performing static checks on the patch, following the software development practices used in nearby code, and performing variant analysis to make sure the patch is complete.
Following the Linux kernel community’s suggestion, we have already sent out hundreds of reports and patches for critical vulnerabilities and are working with Patch the Planet partners to gradually send out patches for the rest. This work is part of our broader Daybreak commitment to support open-source projects.
In this section we share learnings, reflections, and additional analysis from this research.
During this research, we observed the Linux maintainers moving quickly to fix vulnerabilities and protect users. The scan was performed on the latest Linux kernel in mid-October 2026. When the autonomous scan and manual analysis finished after 10 days, 61 LPEs had already been patched upstream, 43 had staging patches, and 299 were being reported and discussed publicly.
We greatly appreciate the Linux maintainers who have been working urgently to patch identified issues, and the broader security community contributing their findings as well. This collective response is what’s needed to secure the world’s software. The rapid rate of vulnerability disclosure and patching also emphasizes the criticality for users and companies to keep software up to date.
Takeaway: Automated triage should take the rapid patching cycle into account. Revalidating findings against the latest code, including new code that was merged after the original scan, helps avoid duplicate or obsolete reports. This focuses attention on unresolved vulnerabilities and gives maintainers evidence that they can act on without adding unnecessary review burden.

In the second scan, in mid-October 2026, the newer cyber model found and exploited 948 unique LPE vulnerabilities for an end-to-end $1,213,430 cost in API credits. For both campaigns, we scanned the latest Linux kernel master branch at the time.
Takeaway: Rescan previously audited code as model capabilities improve. A more capable model may uncover vulnerabilities that earlier models missed, even when using the same research harness.
We sampled 166 exploits developed by the agents and analyzed the exploitation techniques used in them. To the best of our knowledge, the agents used 10 new exploitation techniques in the sampled exploits. We shared the exploitation techniques with third-party kernel exploitation experts and the techniques were new to them as well.
Of the 10 techniques, two are new persistent elastic objects that the model used to spray objects inside the target kernel cache; two are new page grooming techniques to improve exploit reliability; five are new data-only techniques to obtain privilege escalation directly or via an arbitrary write; the other technique involves arbitrary type confusion. For safety reasons, we omit sharing the full technical details of these new exploitation techniques in this post.
