articles.title: OpenAI is already trying to shape the 2028 election
articles.body:
OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane thinks the 2028 presidential election could be a defining moment for AI. And he wants politicians to start developing policies that address Americans’ concerns about the technology, rather than simply paying lip service to anti-AI sentiment and the backlash against data centers.
In a new essay, Lehane compares AI’s potential to reshape the economy to President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal, the 1930s set of federal programs and reforms enacted after industrialization and the Great Depression shattered the old economic order. He observes that Americans today feel similarly anxious about losing control over their economic futures and urges politicians to find a “compelling third path” that allows people to share in AI’s benefits. He lays out five policy priorities, spanning worker protections and education to AI safety and data center development.
The essay comes on the heels of a stunning Democratic victory in the midterm elections, in which Democrats flipped control of Congress amid widespread voter frustration over the cost of living. Kate Brennan, who leads AI and corporate power policy at the AI Now Institute, told TechCrunch that Lehane’s rhetoric marks a notable shift from OpenAI’s policy agenda last year, which focused on accelerating AI development, reducing regulatory barriers, and expanding infrastructure.
Unsurprisingly, many of Lehane’s proposals would encourage wider AI adoption and support the infrastructure expansion companies like OpenAI need to grow. The original New Deal established protections for workers and placed constraints on corporate power. It’s less clear how Lehane’s vision would hold AI companies accountable for the economic disruption their technology could create.
“Invoking a New Deal metaphor is to invoke state capacity to actually benefit the public,” Brennan said. “This is written by a private company that is trying to advocate for policies for its own benefit. It is ahistorical at best and harmful at worst.”
While AI wasn’t a dominant issue in the midterms, opposition to data centers emerged as a major bipartisan concern in several races in the midterms. And Lehane may be right that AI will become a bigger part of the conversation over the next two years.
Affordability is already shaping up as a key issue for the 2028 election as Americans grapple with inflation, tariffs, and the rising cost of living. AI could become an increasingly large part of that conversation as voters stress about data centers hiking up electricity bills, AI replacing their jobs, and technology’s economic gains flowing only to a handful of wealthy companies.
Lehane acknowledges many of these concerns, but he offers few concrete proposals to prevent AI’s gains from becoming concentrated. Instead, he largely pitches AI as a path to greater prosperity for Americans willing to embrace it.
Take his proposals for the tax code. He suggests incentives for workers to learn AI skills, easier capital access for entrepreneurs, and new approaches to employee ownership and profit-sharing. Those are not the same as binding requirements that would ensure workers share in AI-generated wealth or that companies pay the costs of displacing workers.
“I was struck by how much of this policy is for a future…that is already predicated on mass AI adoption and AI benefiting society, which we have yet to see,” Brennan said. “All of it is predicated on benefiting from AI’s upside.”
Brennan said it would make more sense to see things like a revised corporate tax rate or tax incentives for hiring human beings rather than automating jobs, as well as ways to keep companies from amassing outsize market power.
Lehane’s emphasis on expanding AI’s economic opportunities, rather than limiting potential harms, extends to data centers. He notes concerns about data centers while emphasizing the construction jobs and local tax revenue they could generate. He then warns that politicians who support a data center moratorium could jeopardize America’s lead over China, going so far as to compare that stance to the 2002 vote to authorize the Iraq war.
Lehane also makes child safety and education central to his proposed agenda, stressing the importance of age-appropriate protections and safeguards around AI companions for minors. He also warns against keeping AI out of classrooms, arguing that doing so could lead to inequality between wealthy students and “children in rural communities.” But the argument takes for granted that AI improves learning, a claim that remains unproven and one critics say deserves more examination than more funding or individualized attention from human teachers.
Lehane also calls for enforceable AI safety standards, independent evaluations, public oversight, and the ability to restrict AI systems or use a kill switch to shut them down — though recent studies show that OpenAI and other AI labs haven’t published comprehensive plans for what they would do if a model escaped human control.
Brennan called these stances “disingenuous,” pointing to OpenAI’s history of opposing legislation designed to impose such measures. In 2024, for example, OpenAI opposed California’s AI safety bill, SB 1047, which would have mandated catastrophic risk evaluations and shutdown capabilities. Last year, OpenAI also sought to limit state regulation, arguing that states could undermine American innovation. The company has more recently shifted some of those positions, backing several state safety laws and saying it would be open to independent evaluators embedded in the company.
Lehane also argues that people should maintain control over consequential decisions made using AI, rather than handing off judgment entirely to machines. But that raises the question of what human control really looks like in a society where humans are increasingly being required to use AI in education, work, healthcare, and government.
Throughout his essay, Lehane frames AI as a technology that could give Americans back their sense of agency and economic opportunity. But he ties average Americans’ “middle class” success to participation in an economy increasingly shaped by companies like OpenAI. Whether his policies will meaningfully redistribute power or subtly entrench it is less clear.
TechCrunch reached out to OpenAI for more specifics on Lehane’s proposals and the company’s stances, but it did not respond by the time of publication.

articles.title: Axon Sued Over AI-Powered License Plate Reader Network
articles.body:
Axon Sued Over AI-Powered License Plate Reader Network 31
			
		 	
				Axon has been sued in a proposed class action accusing the Taser and police body-camera maker of illegally collecting and storing license plate data on millions of California drivers through its AI-powered surveillance network. Reuters reports the details:  - The lawsuit (PDF), filed on Tuesday in federal court in San Francisco by law firms Hausfeld and Gibbs Mura, alleges Axon has failed to comply with a California privacy provision by not disclosing how it collects, uses and shares plate data gathered through its camera systems
- "Axon has created a mass-surveillance infrastructure that is practically impossible to avoid," the lawsuit said
- Scottsdale, Arizona-based Axon did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The lawsuit said the company has more than 1,000 cameras in California and alleges millions of drivers may have been affected
- Some Axon cameras are installed in high-traffic areas and collect plate information as vehicles pass by. Other cameras are placed inside police vehicles, the lawsuit said
- The proposed class covers drivers whose vehicle plate information was captured by an automated license plate reader in California and processed or stored by Axon's system since 2023
- The lawsuit seeks more than $5 million in damages, in addition to a court order stopping Axon from its allegedly unlawful practices

articles.title: Netflix Launches First AI-Branded Content Recommendations Feature on TVs
articles.body:
Netflix Launches First AI-Branded Content Recommendations Feature on TVs 18
			
		 	
				Netflix is testing its first consumer-facing feature explicitly branded as AI-powered. Called "AI Discover," the feature generates personalized TV and movie recommendations in real time based on viewing history, preferences, trending content and selectable themes like "Something Light" or "Quick Watches." Variety reports:  The streamer will begin rolling out AI Discover in the U.S. to customers who use Netflix in English on supported smart TVs. If you have access to it, you will see a "Discover" tab with a red gem-shaped icon and a "New" label in the top navigation bar on your TV. The company plans to expand the feature to more regions and customers in the coming weeks.
Netflix has long used machine-learning and AI technologies to personalize content recommendations, but AI Discover is the first user-facing application that the company is branding as powered by artificial intelligence. The hope is that the AI-recommended titles will be another tool to drive up Netflix's total watch time among viewers, especially in the U.S.

articles.title: Grimes is going to star in an AI movie that’s coming to theaters
articles.body:
The AI-generated sci-fi film Gods Don’t Give Gifts has added a bit of star power: Pop star Grimes is going to appear in the movie. Billed as “the first AI film to come to theatres,” Gods Don’t Give Gifts is a notable test case for the commercial potential of AI films, and it releases on December 4th. Grimes — who will be lending both her likeness and vocal performance to the movie, which you can see in the clip above — potentially gives the project some legitimacy.
Grimes is going to star in an AI movie that’s coming to theaters
The sci-fi anthology, titled Gods Don’t Give Gifts, releases in December.
AI studio Fable, which is producing the film, claimed in a press release that “casting the likeness of an actor with their spoken vocal performance will become more common with animated films using AI: audiences will see actors, athletes, musicians giving vocal performances with their likeness in films.” Gods Don’t Give Gifts is being directed by Jack London, better known under the online handle Gossip Goblin.
Gods Don’t Give Gifts is an anthology that’s set in a future “where bodies are disposable and consciousness has been commoditized” and depicts what happens when “four interconnected stories collide with the horrifying consequences of humanity’s attempt to transcend the flesh.” Those themes seem to fit pretty snugly with Grimes’ interests, as she has explored themes of transhumanism and artificial intelligence in the past. It’s also not the only AI project she’s working on, with an AI-themed album called Psy Opera in the works.
Here’s the trailer for Gods Don’t Give Gifts:
While there has been plenty of hype around the potential for AI in Hollywood, there’s yet to be a project that shows that the technology is actually a vital storytelling tool. Previous examples, like two different takes on The Odyssey — including one made with Elon Musk’s Grok — have left plenty to be desired.

articles.title: Ember’s smallest self-heating mug is on sale for just $33
articles.body:
We’ve been fans of Ember’s temperature-controlled mugs for years, though given the price tag, we admit that they’re somewhat of a luxury purchase. Thankfully, if you’ve been looking for a more affordable option, Woot is selling the Ember Cup in black for $32.99 ($67 off) with a 90-day warranty through November 7th. You can potentially save even more as part of Woot’s larger Home and Kitchen Sale, which lets you save an additional $20 off orders of $100 or more when you use code COOK at checkout.
Ember’s smallest self-heating mug is on sale for just $33
It may only hold six ounces, but it offers the same customizable temperature settings as Ember’s pricier drinkware.
Granted, six ounces isn’t much, but the smaller, handle-free cup is well-suited for cappuccinos, cortados, flat whites, and other espresso-based drinks. It’s also a perfectly fine option if you don’t mind refilling your cup of coffee, cocoa, or tea throughout the day. I’m actually tempted to pick one up myself at this price, especially since I’ve been trying (with varying degrees of success) to cut back on coffee.
Like Ember’s larger mugs, the smart cup lets you choose and set your drinking temperature between 120 and 145 degrees Fahrenheit using a companion app, then remembers your setting for future drinks. It can then maintain that temperature for up to 95 minutes on a charge, up to four hours with a lid, or even all day if you leave it on the included charging dock. The cup also automatically enters sleep mode after two hours of inactivity to conserve power. Just keep in mind that, despite its IPX7 water-resistance rating, the cup is hand-wash only.

articles.title: Major Digital Bank In Paraguay Collapses With Half of Population's Savings
articles.body:
Major Digital Bank In Paraguay Collapses With Half of Population's Savings (apnews.com) 58
			
		 	
				Paraguayan President Santiago Pena resigned Thursday amid mass protests and impeachment threats following the collapse of Ueno Bank, a major digital lender with close ties to his administration and more than 60% of the country's adults as customers. Regulators seized the bank after uncovering risky insider lending and accounting irregularities that left its capital below legal requirements, locking millions of customers out of their savings. The Associated Press reports:  Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium. Government money poured into Ueno's coffers under Pena. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender. As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.
Even as retirees' savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad. On a single day in September 2025, nearly $39 million had gone to three such companies. Pena repeatedly brushed off the warnings. As recently as last month, he defended Ueno and the central bank's oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.
But on Monday, it all came crashing down. Regulators investigating Ueno's loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending, the central bank said, as well as expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets. Once the books were corrected, Ueno's capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, fell to less than half the legal minimum. The central bank seized the lender Tuesday and announced plans to move customers' accounts, along with whatever assets still hold value, to other banks before liquidating what's left. Ueno's app, cards and transfers went dark and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside with no way to cash out their savings. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks' mobile apps, fueling public panic.  Officials say they had begun repaying depositors and opening accounts at other banks for the roughly 280,000 customers who had banked exclusively with Ueno.
"The banking system is sound," insisted Pedro Acosta Bernal, appointed interim central bank president Wednesday after Carvallo resigned at Pena's request.
Meanwhile, eight senior Ueno executives have been detained, including founder Miguel Vazquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale. "Prosecutors also charged 27 bank officials and business associates with offenses including breach of trust and attempted fraud," reports the AP.

articles.title: Microsoft's Imagine Cup 'Evolves' From Student Competition To AI Startup Contest
articles.body:
Microsoft's Imagine Cup 'Evolves' From Student Competition To AI Startup Contest (geekwire.com) 6
			
		 	
				theodp writes:  That Was Then: The Imagine Cup competition, Microsoft explained in a 2003 press release, "seeks to provide students [aged 16-and-up] around the world with resources to use technology and Web services to solve everyday problems [...] Imagine Cup is about empowering students to apply their creativity and knowledge toward making the world a more-connected place."
This Is Now: "Building is Hard. Selling is Harder." begins the "Why Imagine Cup?" promo video for the 2027 Imagine Cup competition, which is pivoting to an AI startup-first focus in recognition that "A new era for founders is here." "Since 2003, Imagine Cup has empowered emerging innovators to turn ambitious ideas into real-world solutions with Microsoft technology," Microsoft writes of the Imagine Cup Evolution. "Now part of Microsoft for Startups, Imagine Cup enters its next chapter in 2027, opening the competition to eligible early-stage startups and founders everywhere."
An Eligibility FAQ drives home the point that Imagine Cup is no longer a student-only competition: "Imagine Cup 2027 welcomes eligible early-stage startups across seven categories; founders do not need to be students." And if you think making high school students compete against seasoned full-time employees of startup companies seems a tad unfair, Microsoft advises: "Eligible student-led startups are encouraged to enter the Student Startup category but may choose an industry category instead." The #1 overall startup will win a $250,000 cash award and $1,000,000 in startup credits. However, Student Startup category entrants are ineligible for the open category prizes (where the 2nd-place winner gets $50,000 cash and $350,000 in credits, while 3rd place is good for $25,000 and $350,000 in credits); they will instead compete for a single prize of $25,000 cash and $250,000 in credits. The Official Rules (PDF) note that all startups must have a valid Azure Subscription ID and a Microsoft for Startups account.

articles.title: Box taps Nvidia’s Nemotron for new agent-first content retrieval system
articles.body:
At its developer conference on Thursday, Box showed off a new feature that will build Nvidia’s Nemotron embedding system into the core of its product.
Called Box Content Retrieval, the new feature allows agents to answer queries far more effectively by relying on the embedded metadata created by Nemotron.
Box says the upshot for users is faster, more accurate, and less expensive queries. Nvidia’s VP of generative AI software, Kari Briski, told TechCrunch that she expects queries to be answered four times faster, with 20% fewer errors and 90% fewer tokens used.
The system will be available to all of Box’s Enterprise Advance customers, rolling out early next year.
“This dramatically boosts both the relevance of our search technology for agents,” Box CEO Aaron Levie said. “Instead of an agent having to kind of read through each document, we can send back chunks from the documents that are most relevant to the user’s query or whatever the task is that the agent is doing.”
The feature is an implementation of Nvidia’s Nemotron Embed project, which offers open-weight embedding models to improve automated retrieval systems. Major labs have often overlooked such models, which use LLMs to pre-process data so it can be better used by agents. The sector has been a focus for Nvidia’s open source model project, with its recent Nemotron release in July topping the RTEB benchmark, which measures retrieval quality.
The system will be most useful when paired with active agents, Box says, giving the example of lawyers, who will ostensibly be able to find relevant clauses and precedents more easily under the new system. Because Nemotron’s embeddings go beyond simple keywords to map underlying concepts, a search tool can surface related legal themes even when different wording or language is used.
While the Nemotron models are freely available, the system also relies heavily on Box’s pre-existing metadata and permission controls, which will make it challenging to recreate from scratch. “We’re probably packing in five different technologies into one simple API,” Levie told TechCrunch.

articles.title: Playstation and Spider-Man performance see Sony profits surge
articles.body:
Sony is enjoying a sharp profit spike in its latest quarterly financials, largely driven by its PlayStation business and the blockbuster success of Spider-Man: Brand New Day. According to the company’s September earnings, Sony’s net profits climbed to 449.60 billion yen (about $2.84 billion) for the three months ended September — a 44 percent increase compared to the 311.4 billion yen ($1.96 billion) it reported for the same period last year.
Playstation and Spider-Man performance see Sony profits surge
Sony reported Q2 net profits of $2.84 billion, a 44 percent jump from the same period last year.
Spider-Man: Brand New Day was a notable contributor, which released in July and became the third-highest grossing movie in history by earning $2.52 billion at the global box office. That’s a huge boost for Sony Pictures Entertainment, which posted earnings of $581 million for the three months ended September — a 527 percent jump from the $93 million it reported for the same period in 2025.
Sales of Playstation 5 consoles have fallen, with 2.6 million units reported this second quarter compared to the 4 million that were sold in Q2 2025. While the Sony-exclusive Marvel’s Wolverine sold 2.4 million units against a reported budget of $300 million, PlayStation game sales generally have increased for both digital downloads and physical discs. That’s in spite of the week-long player blackout that took place in August to protest Sony’s plan to ditch discs entirely. Looking forward, PlayStation is now looking at its next generation console, which developers are making “solid progress” on according to Sony CFO Lin Tao, and is “progressing as scheduled.”

articles.title: Meta’s warns that election backlash against data centers could make AI expansion harder
articles.body:
Meta president Dina Powell McCormick said that the Democratic wins in the midterm elections are going to make it a lot harder for companies to build data centers, adding that the industry has “not done as good a job as we needed to explain the benefits of these investments.”
Speaking at the WSJ Tech conference on Wednesday, the Meta exec pointed out that the backlash against data centers — which was very much on the ballot during this election season — was also tied to people’s feelings about AI technology overall.
“The visible sort of manifestation of AI is a data center, and it’s something that people can say, ‘I don’t want this in my community,’” she explained. “I think there’s an underlying bigger issue, which is how people feel about AI in general.”
Meta believes it could turn around the negative consumer sentiment around AI if it’s able to demonstrate the value, not only of the data centers coming to local communities, but also in the technology itself.
“The stakes of who builds the technology that cures cancer, that gives access to education, that is also a very fundamental difference … Mark [Zuckerberg, Meta CEO] is very ‘long human,’ and he’s betting on humans more than machines,” Powell McCormick explained. “And that’s what we mean when we say the future is for everyone. That people should not be left behind. But the way to ensure that is that this technology is democratized, that people have access to it in a very fair and transparent way,” she said.
The exec also touted Meta’s experience in building data centers, saying that the company has been doing so for 20 years, as it takes a lot of compute power to offer the products it does in the social networking space. Today, the company has data centers in 23 states, she said, and five of them, including one in Texas, are planned as projects of 1 gigawatt or more.
But Meta is now worried that it could lose some of its investments after politicians ran on anti-data-center platforms during the midterms.
“I think it’s going to be harder,” Powell McCormick said, describing what the future of building data centers looks like. “It has been hard, I should say, but I also think that it’s becoming clear what models work, and the states want those models that work.”
Specifically, communities only want data centers when it benefits them in some way, she explained, laying out the approach that Meta today uses to close its data center deals in local communities.
Successful projects see Meta paying for its own electricity, directing any tax surpluses as a result of the data centers toward teachers and first responders, keeping the labor force local, and getting bipartisan support for the project, among other things.
Going forward, she expects data center projects to come under more review and be weighed against whether the constituents actually want them.
Meta has pinned its hopes on its AI investments, particularly its consumer AI agent Muse scaling far beyond the 10 million users it has today, to become a business that one day serves billions. But even if that’s not the case, it believes that its investments in data centers will not be for nothing, as the compute itself will be valuable.
“We’re getting calls every day to lease that compute [we’ve built], and so one way or another, we’re seeing a path to monetization,” Powell McCormick said.

articles.title: The Hackintosh Reborn
articles.body:
The Hackintosh Reborn... with AI
Almost a decade ago, I released a hackintosh guide on running macOS 10.14 through a VM with an x86 host. A "Hackintosh" is the feat of running macOS on non-Apple hardware, and has a history dating back to the late 1980s. At the time KVM and PCI passthrough were relatively new technologies, and this guide provided near-native performance with GPU acceleration.
A few years passed by, and we saw Apple release the first ARM-based Mac in 2021, the M1 MacBook Air. The timing was impeccable, Intel was unable to create competitive processors (due to being stuck on the 14nm node), and Apple had powerful and efficient ARM chips already being shipped in their iPhones. The long battery life, the fanless design, the instant wake, what's not to like? The benefits of switching to ARM were clear, however to most, this was thought to be the final chapter in the hackintosh community. x86 versions of macOS would soon be discontinued, and the hackintosh community would slowly fade away. That day has come and the latest version of macOS 27 (Golden Gate) released this year is no longer compatible with x86...
Just a few days ago, I decided to create an iOS app for the first time. It required XCode 26 for development, so I used my spare ThinkPad T490 as my development machine and installed macOS 26 using a posted guide. The installation was smooth and painless. XCode 26 has integrations with Claude Code and OpenAI Codex, and this was my first foray into AI-assisted coding. After some initial tinkering with x86 workarounds, I was pleased that I had a functional iOS app within a day, without touching a single line of code!
So how does this all tie in? Well, this is exactly what the Hackintosh community could hardly envision five years ago: the rise of AI. Waiting patiently and gently until now, the hackintosh and the hackios community has seen an absolute explosion in development, activity, and success in the past few weeks! As one person aptly wrote, this is the power of Claude Code with Ghidra on steroids. Just to list a few recent developments, we have:
macOS 27 running on the Snapdragon Laptop:
macOS 27.2 Beta on an ARM SBC RK3588 with Mali drivers:
iOS 17 running on the Nintendo Switch OLED:
Support for 50-series Nvidia GPUs with nullmoth:
I'm barely scratching the surface, with further developments in AirDrop, accelerated video decode, and even running translated macOS 27 on x86. As much as we lament the cost of AI, there are some glimmers of hope: you just might be able to have your hardware and own it too.

articles.title: NTS: Authenticated Time at Meta
articles.body:
- Meta’s public time service now speaks NTS (Network Time Security, RFC 8915) at nts.meta.com. Packets are authenticated, so a device can verify the time came from us and was not modified on the way.
- Our NTS servers hold no per-client state. Cookie keys are derived, not stored and not replicated.
- We’ve open sourced everything, including the protocol, server, client through Meta’s Time library on GitHub.
- We’re also encouraging everyone, particularly those who maintain an NTP client on Android or iOS, to join us in enabling NTS support.
We’ve previously written about building a more accurate time service at Meta scale – migrating from ntpd to chrony, going from 10 milliseconds to 100 microseconds, and opening time.meta.com to everyone.
That work made time precise. This work makes it verifiable.
Why NTS?
NTP has been unauthenticated since 1985, like a lot of the internet’s foundational protocols. But it is also the one every certificate, token, and signature is checked against. The client sends 48 bytes, something sends 48 bytes back, and the client believes it. There is no signature and no identity.
It is not alone in that. Plenty of the internet’s foundational protocols were designed for a network where nobody was assumed to be hostile, and the industry has been retrofitting them ever since. What makes time different is that it is not just another protocol to secure. It is the input every other security decision is measured against.
For most of NTP’s life that did not matter much, because a clock being a few seconds off was an operational annoyance. Today it is load-bearing:
- Certificate validation: notBefore and notAfter are compared against the local clock. Wrong clock, wrong answer.
- Token and credential expiry: “Valid for 15 minutes” is a claim about a clock.
- Replay windows: Rejecting a request older than N seconds requires knowing what time it is.
- Log correlation and ordering: Two hosts that disagree produce a timeline that never happened.
And the check itself is circular. You can’t do X.509 notBefore/notAfter validation without knowing the current time. Effectively you’d have to disable cert time validation, or implement one of the suggested work-arounds.
There are two common workarounds. Both are bad. You can skip validation until the clock is set, which leaves a device unprotected exactly when it is most exposed. Or you can build in-slack: A certificate issued at 12:00:00 is rejected by a client whose clock reads 11:59:30, so issuers backdate notBefore by a few minutes and validators quietly widen the window at their end. Both sides are guessing at how wrong the other one is.
That was survivable when a certificate lasted 398 days. CA/Browser Forum ballot SC-081v3 changed that. The cap on newly issued publicly trusted TLS certificates dropped to 200 days in March 2026, falls to 100 days in March 2027, and reaches 47 days in March 2029 — with domain validation reuse dropping to 10 days at the same point.
At 47 days, manual certificate management stops being viable at any scale. Renewal moves to roughly monthly, and it happens unattended — usually over ACME. An automated renewal loop on a host with a skewed clock does not raise a ticket. It reissues, or it fails, on a schedule nobody is watching.
How NTS Works
NTS works in phases, and separating them is what makes it deployable.
Phase 1 – Key Establishment (NTS-KE): TLS 1.3 over TCP/4460, negotiated with ALPN ntske/1. The client and server agree on an AEAD algorithm, then derive two directional session keys (C2S and S2C) straight from the TLS session using the RFC 5705 exporter. The server issues eight cookies, tells the client which NTP server to actually use via a server negotiation record, and closes the connection. This happens once, not per packet.
We negotiate three AEADs: AES-SIV-CMAC-256 (ID 15), which RFC 8915 makes mandatory to implement and is what an unknown client is most likely to ask for; AES-SIV-CMAC-512 (17); and AES-128-GCM-SIV (30). Client preference wins.
Phase 2 – Authenticated NTP: Standard NTPv4 over UDP/123 to the advertised server, with NTS extension fields. A request carries a unique identifier, a cookie, and an authenticator; the authenticator covers everything before it, but encrypts nothing. The server opens the cookie to recover the session keys, verifies that authenticator, and replies with the unique identifier echoed back plus an authenticator of its own – and that one does carry a payload: the fresh cookies, encrypted inside it.
A forged packet fails verification and is dropped. We do not send an NTS NAK, so a failure is indistinguishable from packet loss and cannot be used to push a client into a fresh key exchange. A replayed response carries the wrong unique identifier and matches no outstanding request. Because the replacement cookies ride inside the response authenticator rather than in the clear, an observer sees a different opaque blob every exchange and cannot follow a client between networks. Spending each cookie once is the client’s side of that bargain – the server is stateless and does not track them.
Cookies Without State
A cookie is a server state handed to the client for safekeeping. It holds the session keys, sealed with AES-SIV so only the server can open it. The obvious implementation is a key ring replicated to every server, which turns time service into a distributed state problem.
We do not replicate keys. Each server derives the sealing key from a shared master secret and the current day:
Since the Unix epoch, day is measured as whole 24-hour periods,  not a calendar day. So there is no timezone and no DST, and every host computes the same integer for the same instant. That integer is the cookie’s key ID and travels in the clear. A server that has been handed a cookie it has never seen or sealed by a host it has never talked to, re-derives the key and opens it. We accept two days back and one forward to cover skew around a rotation boundary.
The result is no key ring, no replication, no session table, no shared state to fall out of sync, and nothing for an attacker to exhaust. It is also what makes the split above work – the KE server and the NTP servers it hands you off to are different machines in different places, and they never exchange anything. Adding a server is adding a server.
The plain NTP path is untouched. The responder parses extension fields only when they are present, so unauthenticated clients hit the same code as before at the same cost.
Using NTS
One line of chrony config:
nts.meta.com terminates key exchange only. During the handshake it advertises an NTP responder in a server negotiation record, so the client is steered to time.meta.com and sends its authenticated NTP there. The host you configure is not the host you end up talking to.
That indirection is why we use pool rather than server. A single server line gives you one association and one responder, which is a single point of failure – and NTP is a protocol that wants several sources so it can outvote a bad one. pool asks for maxsources independent associations. Each runs its own key exchange over its own TLS session, so each ends up with a distinct pair of session keys:
Five rows, five independent authenticated sources, from one line of config and one KE endpoint.
Reading across: Type 30 is the negotiated AEAD, AES-128-GCM-SIV, with KLen 128 bits of session key — chrony lists it first and client preference wins. CLen 68 is the cookie: 36 bytes of envelope around the two 16-byte keys inside. Cook 8 is cookies in hand and NAK 0 means none has been rejected.
The more interesting half is not in the table. Each row’s session keys came out of its own TLS handshake and work only for that association. The key that seals them into a cookie is the shared one – the epoch day number from the derivation above, identical on every responder we run, stamped inside each cookie and never visible to the client. That split is what lets a single key exchange hand a client five different responders that have never spoken to each other.
When a pool member completes key exchange and moves to its negotiated responder, the freed KE address is handed to the next unresolved member, repeating until maxsources responders have answered. Five sources come up in about 20 minutes as each member completes its own key exchange in turn.
NTS Protects Against Attacks
Unlike NTP, NTS stops a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack from forging the answer. A classic MITM attack doesn’t need to break any cryptography, it just has to answer a client before a real server does. If an attacker rolls the clock backward they can make expired certificates validate again or revoked tokens work again. Any control that relies on something having expired is reset. If they roll the clock forward everything expires at once. This is the more difficult direction to address because beyond a certain point the failure stops being recoverable.
Let’s look at an example of what happens to a device that gets convinced it is the year 2037. NTP counts seconds in a 32-bit field that wraps in February 2036, and a client stranded on the far side of that boundary computes its correction into the wrong era – so the mechanism that exists to fix a wrong clock now moves it further away. Meanwhile every certificate the device holds is long expired, so TLS fails, therefore it cannot reach anything that might help, including its own update service. The patch that would fix it cannot be delivered, because delivering it needs the clock that is broken.
The device is not damaged. Every component works exactly as designed. It is simply holding a number that puts it outside the reach of the network. And no amount of waiting or rebooting fixes it. Recovery means a factory reset, or a trip to a service center. Multiply that by a fleet and the cost of a wrong integer becomes a logistics problem.
Now, consider a clock forward attack on a host that issues credentials. Short-lived credentials are considered safe because they expire quickly, which means short lifetime is doing the job revocation would otherwise do. That property is entirely a function of the issuing host’s clock. An issuer convinced it is next year signs credentials that outlive the window you designed for.
What NTS Does Not Fix
Delay attacks. RFC 8915 is explicit. An attacker who holds your packets shifts your clock by up to half the delay introduced, and no cryptography in the protocol detects it, because every byte is genuine. Authentication tells you who wrote a packet, not how long it spent in flight. Mitigations are the usual ones – multiple independent sources, sanity limits, bounded steps.
So the claim is narrow: An on-path attacker can still delay your packets and can still drop them. What they can no longer do is lie about the contents.
Bootstrapping. NTS-KE runs over TLS and TLS wants a working clock, which is the same circular problem as above. A device with a dead RTC still has to get roughly correct before its first handshake.
Wrong servers. NTS authenticates the path, not the answer. A server that is correctly configured, correctly authenticated, and simply wrong will hand you the wrong time with a perfect signature on it. Quorum, sanity checks, and monitoring are still required.
Monotonicity. Authenticated time is still wall-clock time, and wall clocks move backward — at a leap second, or whenever a correction lands. Cloudflare’s authoritative DNS hit this at the end of 2016: a resolver round-trip measured across the leap second came out negative, propagated into upstream selection, and panicked Go’s rand.Int63n(). Nothing was forged and nothing was misdelivered. If your code measures elapsed time, use a monotonic clock.
Adoption
RFC 8915, Network Time Security for the Network Time Protocol, was published on the IETF Standards Track as a Proposed Standard in September 2020. Cloudflare had launched time.cloudflare.com with NTS 15 months earlier, in June 2019, against the then-current draft, and showed it works at scale.
Server-side, the public NTS list today runs to a few dozen entries, mostly national metrology institutes and internet infrastructure operators such as PTB, Netnod, and time.nl. We are adding one more.
The bigger gap is on the client. NTS support exists where you would expect it in the server world – chrony and ntpsec implement it. It is absent entirely from the stock time client on the platforms that account for most of the endpoints on the internet.
Android’s platform time sync is plain SNTP over UDP/123 – a fixed 48-byte packet with no extension-field handling, alongside NITZ and GNSS – so there is no NTS path in it. Apple devices sync through timed against time.apple.com, where we are not aware of any NTS support either.
Those two stacks set the clock on billions of phones, watches and headsets, and every one of them is trusting an unauthenticated UDP packet. A device vendor can ship a separate NTS-capable client today — chrony runs perfectly well on Android – but that is a workaround for something the platform should do itself.
The protocol is finished, the servers are appearing, the client implementations exist.
What is missing is mobile.
Join Us in Enabling NTS
nts.meta.com is live and free. The code is in github.com/facebook/time.
If you run a public time service, turn NTS on. If you maintain an NTP client, implement RFC 8915. If you own the time stack in a mobile OS, this is the gap – Android and iOS are where most of the world’s clocks get set, and both of them are still doing it over an unauthenticated packet.
We have spent years making time more precise. Precision without authenticity only gets you a very accurate number from an unknown source. Now it can be both.
Acknowledgements
We’d like to thank Sofia Scalzo, Pablo Mazzini, Vadim Fedorenko, Patrick Cullen, and Yixin Wei for their support on this project.

articles.title: Building a Multi-Agent System from Scratch: Architecture Patterns
articles.body:
Building a Multi-Agent System from Scratch: Architecture Patterns
Orchestrator-worker, blackboard, and pipeline patterns for coordinating multiple AI agents — with the failure modes that only show up once you go past a single-agent demo.
A single well-tuned agent is easy to demo. Give it a clear goal, a handful of tools, and a generous system prompt, and it'll look impressive in a five-minute walkthrough. I wrote about exactly that kind of agent in an earlier post — a single agent that turned natural-language restaurant queries into structured search filters. It worked well because the problem had one shape: understand the query, call some tools, format the answer.
Multi-agent systems are a different animal. The moment you have more than one agent, you've introduced a coordination problem on top of the reasoning problem, and coordination is where almost all of the real engineering effort goes. Nobody warns you about this in the demos, because demos are built to succeed once, not to run in production for six months against inputs nobody anticipated.
This post is about the three architecture patterns I keep coming back to when splitting work across multiple agents, and — more importantly — the failure modes that only show up once you're past a single-agent demo and into something that has to run unattended.
Why split into multiple agents at all?
Mostly for the same reason you split code into functions: a single agent juggling retrieval, domain reasoning, validation, and formatting in one prompt tends to do all four things a little worse than four agents each doing one thing well. Narrower responsibility means a shorter, more focused system prompt, which means more predictable behavior and easier evaluation.
Pattern 1: Orchestrator-Worker
This is the pattern most people reach for first, and for good reason — it maps cleanly onto how a human manager delegates work. One orchestrator agent receives the task, breaks it into subtasks, dispatches each subtask to a specialized worker agent, and aggregates the results into a final answer. Workers don't talk to each other; they only talk to the orchestrator.
Task → Orchestrator
              ├─→ Worker A (research)
              ├─→ Worker B (code generation)
              └─→ Worker C (validation)
                     ↓
             Orchestrator aggregates → Final answer
This pattern fits when the task decomposition is clear upfront — you know in advance that answering the question requires "look something up," "generate something," and "check it," even if you don't know the specifics until runtime. The orchestrator's only job is planning and aggregation, which keeps its prompt small and its behavior predictable. The tradeoff is that the orchestrator becomes a bottleneck: every piece of context has to flow through it, and if it misjudges the decomposition, every worker downstream inherits that mistake.
Pattern 2: Blackboard
The blackboard pattern drops the strict hierarchy. Instead of a central orchestrator directing traffic, agents read from and write to a shared state store — the "blackboard" — and each agent decides for itself when it has something useful to contribute. There's usually a lightweight scheduler that decides which agent gets to act next based on what's currently on the blackboard, but there's no single agent that owns the plan.
         ┌────────────────────────┐
         │   Shared Blackboard    │
         │  (partial state,      │
         │   hypotheses, facts)  │
         └───────────┬────────────┘
        read/write    │    read/write
     ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
     ↓                 ↓                 ↓
 Agent A           Agent B           Agent C
(hypothesis)      (evidence)        (critique)
I reach for this pattern when the solution path genuinely isn't known ahead of time — debugging a subtle production issue, for instance, where one agent proposes a hypothesis, another gathers evidence for or against it, and a third critiques the reasoning. Nobody could have written that as a fixed sequence of steps beforehand, because the next useful action depends entirely on what's already been discovered.
The cost of that flexibility is that blackboard systems are much harder to reason about and to test. There is no single place where "the plan" lives, so debugging a bad outcome means reconstructing the entire sequence of reads and writes after the fact — closer to debugging a race condition than debugging a function call stack.
Pattern 3: Pipeline
The pipeline pattern is the simplest of the three, and it's the one I default to whenever the workflow is well-understood and repeatable. A fixed sequence of specialized agents, each handing its output to the next: retrieve, extract, validate, format. No delegation logic, no shared scratch space — just a chain.
Input → Retrieve Agent → Extract Agent → Validate Agent → Format Agent → Output
Pipelines are the easiest of the three patterns to evaluate, because each stage has a well-defined input and output contract, which means you can test and version each agent independently. The obvious limitation is rigidity: if a task doesn't decompose into a fixed sequence — if step three sometimes needs to loop back and redo step one — a pipeline will either fail outright or you'll end up bolting ad hoc branching logic onto it until it quietly turns into an orchestrator with extra steps.
Picking a pattern
If you can write the decomposition down as a checklist before you start, use a pipeline. If the decomposition is knowable but the specifics depend on the input, use orchestrator-worker. If you can't know the solution path until agents start finding things out, use a blackboard — and budget more time for evaluation.
Failure Modes You Won't See in a Demo
Every one of these showed up for me only after moving past a controlled demo into something running against real, messy inputs.
Infinite delegation loops
Two agents that can each decide "this isn't my job, pass it back" will occasionally pass a task back and forth indefinitely. An orchestrator delegates to a worker; the worker decides it needs clarification and delegates back to the orchestrator; the orchestrator, seeing an unclear request, delegates it right back out. Neither agent is wrong in isolation — the loop only exists at the system level, which is exactly why it's invisible when you're testing agents individually.
Runaway cost from re-invocation
Every agent-to-agent call is a model call, and model calls cost money and time. A blackboard system with three agents each re-checking the board after every write can spiral into dozens of model calls for a task that a human would resolve in three steps. This is easy to miss in development, where you're running one task at a time and eyeballing the transcript. It's very much not easy to miss on the invoice.
Conflicting concurrent writes
When two agents can act on shared state at the same time — two workers both trying to update the same record, two blackboard agents both trying to "resolve" the same open question — you get the same class of bug as an unguarded race condition in concurrent code, except the two writers are language models instead of threads, which makes it much harder to reproduce reliably.
Error propagation between agents
The most insidious one. If Agent A hallucinates a fact and passes its output to Agent B, Agent B has no way to distinguish that hallucination from a verified fact — it just sees text in its context window and reasons from it as if it were true. In a single-agent system, a hallucination is a wrong answer. In a multi-agent system, a hallucination is an input that gets compounded by every downstream agent that trusts it.
Guardrails That Actually Work
None of the failure modes above are solved by "better prompting." They're solved by hard limits enforced in code, outside the agents' control.
Hard caps on delegation depth
Track how many times a task has been re-delegated and refuse further delegation past a fixed limit — typically 3 to 5 hops in my experience. When the cap is hit, escalate rather than loop.
A token or cost budget per task
Set a hard ceiling on total tokens or dollars spent per task, tracked centrally, not per agent. When a task hits the ceiling, it stops — it does not get "one more try."
A defined human-escalation path
When confidence is low or a cap is hit, the system needs a real exit that isn't "let the agents keep trying" — surface the partial state to a human, don't let the system quietly retry into a low-quality answer it presents as confident.
The Honest Summary
Multi-agent architecture buys you task decomposition — the ability to break a large, fuzzy problem into smaller, more tractable pieces that are each easier to prompt, test, and reason about. It does not, on its own, buy you correctness. A system of five agents that each hallucinate 5% of the time doesn't average out to more reliable behavior; it compounds. The pattern you choose determines how the work is split. The evaluation harness and the guardrails you build around it determine whether the system is safe to actually put in front of users. Spend your engineering time accordingly.
Continue Reading
Explore more articles on software engineering and technology

Give it a budget and a diet preference, and Combo Maker assembles the best meal combo it can afford from a sample menu — a live demo, how the allocator works, and an honest look at what a real AI-backed version would need.

articles.title: Exporting tables from a SQL Server backup (.bak) to Parquet without restoring it
articles.body:
FastBCP 1.6: Export Tables from SQL Server Backups
FastBCP 1.6 exports a table from a SQL Server full backup to Parquet, with no restore and no SQL Server instance. On a 320 GB production backup, the first open took 2 min 29 s and later ones 0.3 s. With 24 threads, a 175-million-row table then went to Parquet in 29.6 seconds. FastTransfer can load the files into SQL Server, on any version, or into PostgreSQL.
FastBCP 1.6 reads a table straight out of a SQL Server full backup. You point it at a .bak file, name a table, and get Parquet files. There is no restore, no SQL Server instance, and no credentials to manage.
Parquet is the only output for now. That is enough to close the loop, though: FastTransfer loads those files into the SQL Server instance of your choice, and that instance can run an older version than the one that took the backup. RESTORE cannot do that.
A first export
The new connection type is backup_mssql.
- --server is the directory that holds the backups.
- --database is the backup file, or a pattern that matches it (tpch_*.bak for a striped backup). The stripes can also be listed, separated by ;.
- Windows
- Linux
.\FastBCP.exe `
--connectiontype backup_mssql `
--server "D:\Backups\MSSQL" `
--database "tpch_full.bak" `
--sourceschema "dbo" `
--sourcetable "orders" `
--directory "D:\export\orders" `
--fileoutput "orders.parquet" `
--parallelmethod Physical `
--paralleldegree 8
./FastBCP \
--connectiontype backup_mssql \
--server "/var/opt/mssql/backup" \
--database "tpch_*.bak" \
--sourceschema "dbo" \
--sourcetable "orders" \
--directory "/export/orders" \
--fileoutput "orders.parquet" \
--parallelmethod Physical \
--paralleldegree 8
With a backup as the source, --parallelmethod Physical cuts the table into as many slices as --paralleldegree. Each thread reads its own slice and you get one file per chunk (orders_chunk_000.parquet, orders_chunk_001.parquet…).
To export a subset of columns, use --query with a column list: SELECT o_orderkey, o_orderdate FROM dbo.orders. That is the whole grammar, SELECT * | col1, col2, … FROM [schema.]table. A WHERE clause is not accepted.
Here is where the files go next:
What it reads
The driver behind backup_mssql, ArpeMSBackup, reads the backup file on its own, with no SQL Server component involved.
- 2017
- 2019
- 2022
- 2025
- Full
- Copy-only full
- Several backups in one file
- None
- MS_XPRESS
- ZSTD
- Any block size
- Pattern
- List
- Any order
- Several data files
- Several filegroups
- Heaps
- Clustered indexes
- Partitions
- Data compression
- Clustered columnstore
- Archive compression
- Open delta store
- Deleted rows
Data types
bigint✓int✓smallint✓tinyint✓bit✓decimal✓numeric✓money✓smallmoney✓float✓real✓date✓time✓datetime✓datetime2✓smalldatetime✓datetimeoffset✓char✓varchar✓varchar(max)✓nchar✓nvarchar✓nvarchar(max)✓text✓ntext✓binary✓varbinary✓varbinary(max)✓image✓uniqueidentifier✓rowversion✓xml✓sql_variant✓hierarchyid✓geography✓geometry✓vector(n)✓vector(n, float16)✗json✗
The full mapping is in the datatypes conversion page.
Restrictions
Copy-only included. Differential and log backups are not applied. A file that holds no full backup is refused.
Backups of TDE databases and encrypted backups (WITH ENCRYPTION) are refused: their pages cannot be read without the server certificate.
Backups compressed with Intel QuickAssist are not supported. MS_XPRESS and ZSTD are.
On Windows x64 and Linux x64.
One more thing to keep in mind: a RESTORE replays the part of the transaction log stored in the backup to make the database consistent. FastBCP does not. If a table was being written to while the backup ran, you get its pages as they were copied. For an exact image, back up while the table is quiet.
Use cases
Restore n-tables
Someone dropped a table, or needs last Tuesday's version of it. The usual answer is to restore the whole database next to production, which means as much free disk as the database and hours of restore for a 2 TB backup, all to get one table back.
With FastBCP and FastTransfer, you export that one table from the backup and load it wherever you want: a scratch database, the production server under another name, or an instance running an older version. SQL Server cannot restore a backup on an older version than the one that created it, while Parquet files do not care.
The load step uses FastTransfer, one chunk per Parquet file. The target table must exist.
- Windows
- Linux
.\FastTransfer.exe `
--sourceconnectiontype duckdbstream `
--sourceserver ":memory:" `
--query "SELECT * EXCLUDE filename FROM read_parquet('D:\export\orders\*.parquet', filename=true)" `
--targetconnectiontype msbulk `
--targetserver "sql2019\restore" `
--targetdatabase "tpch_restore" `
--targettrusted `
--targetschema "dbo" `
--targettable "orders" `
--loadmode Truncate `
--mapmethod Name `
--parallelmethod DataDriven `
--distributekeycolumn "filename" `
--datadrivenquery "SELECT file FROM glob('D:\export\orders\*.parquet')" `
--degree 8
./FastTransfer \
--sourceconnectiontype duckdbstream \
--sourceserver ":memory:" \
--query "SELECT * EXCLUDE filename FROM read_parquet('/export/orders/*.parquet', filename=true)" \
--targetconnectiontype msbulk \
--targetserver "sql2019,1433" \
--targetdatabase "tpch_restore" \
--targetuser "FastUser" \
--targetpassword "FastPassword" \
--targetschema "dbo" \
--targettable "orders" \
--loadmode Truncate \
--mapmethod Name \
--parallelmethod DataDriven \
--distributekeycolumn "filename" \
--datadrivenquery "SELECT file FROM glob('/export/orders/*.parquet')" \
--degree 8
Migrations
A migration starts with a bulk copy of the existing data. Reading it from last night's full backup puts no load on the source server, and the backup is often already on a share the migration team can reach. If you have to stay on a newer-to-older path, Parquet removes the version constraint too.
Say you are moving from SQL Server to PostgreSQL. FastBCP exports each table from the backup to Parquet, then FastTransfer loads the files through PostgreSQL's COPY protocol:
Run this pair of commands once per table. Create the target tables first: FastTransfer loads into tables that already exist.
- Windows
- Linux
.\FastBCP.exe `
--connectiontype backup_mssql `
--server "D:\Backups\MSSQL" `
--database "tpch_full.bak" `
--sourceschema "dbo" `
--sourcetable "orders" `
--directory "D:\export\orders" `
--fileoutput "orders.parquet" `
--parallelmethod Physical `
--paralleldegree 8
.\FastTransfer.exe `
--sourceconnectiontype duckdbstream `
--sourceserver ":memory:" `
--query "SELECT * EXCLUDE filename FROM read_parquet('D:\export\orders\*.parquet', filename=true)" `
--targetconnectiontype pgcopy `
--targetserver "pgserver:5432" `
--targetdatabase "tpch" `
--targetuser "FastUser" `
--targetpassword "FastPassword" `
--targetschema "public" `
--targettable "orders" `
--loadmode Truncate `
--mapmethod Name `
--parallelmethod DataDriven `
--distributekeycolumn "filename" `
--datadrivenquery "SELECT file FROM glob('D:\export\orders\*.parquet')" `
--degree 8
./FastBCP \
--connectiontype backup_mssql \
--server "/var/opt/mssql/backup" \
--database "tpch_*.bak" \
--sourceschema "dbo" \
--sourcetable "orders" \
--directory "/export/orders" \
--fileoutput "orders.parquet" \
--parallelmethod Physical \
--paralleldegree 8
./FastTransfer \
--sourceconnectiontype duckdbstream \
--sourceserver ":memory:" \
--query "SELECT * EXCLUDE filename FROM read_parquet('/export/orders/*.parquet', filename=true)" \
--targetconnectiontype pgcopy \
--targetserver "pgserver:5432" \
--targetdatabase "tpch" \
--targetuser "FastUser" \
--targetpassword "FastPassword" \
--targetschema "public" \
--targettable "orders" \
--loadmode Truncate \
--mapmethod Name \
--parallelmethod DataDriven \
--distributekeycolumn "filename" \
--datadrivenquery "SELECT file FROM glob('/export/orders/*.parquet')" \
--degree 8
The final cutover can use the same path: stop the application, take a COPY_ONLY full backup, export, load. With the application stopped, the backup is consistent and no log replay is needed. Whether it beats a direct transfer depends on the size of the database and on the cutover window, so measure both.
Feeding a data warehouse or a data lake
Most production databases are backed up every night, and those backups already sit somewhere outside production. FastBCP can turn them into Parquet files for a data lake, or for a warehouse load, without opening a single connection to production. No read replica, no extraction window, no read locks on busy tables.
Why it is fast
The driver reads the backup file itself and goes straight to the data of the table. The first open is kept in a cache for the next exports.
With Physical, each thread reads its own share of the table from the same opened backup.
No SQL Server process and no other session: nothing waits on anything, and production never sees the export.
The file is read in place, never loaded. Since 1.6.5, memory also stays bounded on wide columnstore tables.
Straight to the table
The driver reads the backup as a plain binary file. It understands it well enough to go straight to the data of the requested table and skip everything else in the file. Values are decoded straight into Apache Arrow columns, which FastBCP writes to Parquet.
The first export from a backup pays a one-time cost: the whole file is read once, decompressed if needed, so the driver can find its way in it. FastBCP keeps what it learned in a small local cache. The next exports from the same backup, whatever the table, skip that step. On the 320 GB production backup measured below, the first open took 2 min 29 s and the next ones 0.3 s. A new backup file gets a fresh read.
Parallel reads, when you want them
With --parallelmethod Physical, each thread takes its own share of the table. All threads work on the same opened backup, so it is opened once whatever the degree. For a compressed backup, they also share the decompressed data.
No locks, no latches
There is no lock manager, no buffer latch, no other session, and no SQL Server process. A thread reads its pages and nothing waits on anything. The production server does not see the export at all.
Memory does not grow with the backup
The backup is read in place and is never loaded into memory. Data goes once from the file to an Arrow batch. What stays in memory is a small amount of metadata, one batch per thread and, for a compressed backup, a shared decompression cache (256 MB by default). Exporting a 15-million-row rowstore table with 8 threads peaked at 674 MB for the whole FastBCP process from the uncompressed backup, 979 MB from the ZSTD one.
Columnstore tables are the exception, and today the weak spot: a rowgroup of up to a million rows is decoded whole, so memory grows with the number of threads and the number of columns. On the real tables below, 24 threads peaked at 26 GB for 62 columns and 44 GB for 124 columns, where the live export of the same table stayed at 4.5 GB. We are working on it. Until then, lower --paralleldegree on a machine with less memory.
FastBCP 1.6.5 keeps memory bounded on columnstore tables. Exporting a wide clustered columnstore table with 8 threads peaked at 42 GB before this version and peaks at 5.9 GB with it. The figures in this article were measured with 1.6.3 and 1.6.4. See the release notes.
The speed depends on two things: how fast your disk reads, and how fast the export tool decodes and writes. A local NVMe drive delivers several GB/s and a decent SSD several hundred MB/s. A USB key, or a small cloud disk whose throughput is tied to its size, will be the bottleneck. On a good disk, the limit is the export tool, and that is the part FastBCP is built for.
Performance
Real columnstore tables, FastBCP 1.6.3
These runs come from a real production database, not a benchmark schema: two clustered columnstore tables, one with 62 columns and one with 124, both well over 100 million rows. The source is the nightly full backup of that database: 383 tables, 320 GB striped over 16 files of 20 GB. The server is an Intel Xeon Gold 6430 machine with 128 logical processors and 1 TB of RAM, on Windows Server 2022.
Every run is FastBCP 1.6.3 writing Zstd Parquet with 24 threads: --parallelmethod Physical for the backup, --parallelmethod Ntile on an integer key for the live export through adbc_mssql, from the SQL Server 2022 instance that holds the same database. The first backup run is the cold one, the first time this backup was opened. The second one finds the backup in the cache.
- On the same 124-column table, the backup export takes 72 seconds and the live export 156: 2.2 times faster, and SQL Server did no work for it.
- The cold open cost 2 min 29 s, once for the whole 320 GB backup, about 2.2 GB/s read from disk. After it, the 175-million-row table A went to Parquet in 29.6 seconds, 5.9 M rows/s or 366 M cells/s. Every later export from this backup starts in 0.3 s.
- Wide tables are where cells per second tells more than rows per second: 381 million values decoded and written each second for table B.
- Memory was the price with 1.6.3: 44 GB at the peak against 4.5 GB for the live export. FastBCP 1.6.5 lowers it, see Memory does not grow with the backup.
TPC-H SF10 on a laptop
I ran these numbers on my laptop: an Intel i9-13950HX (8 performance cores, 16 efficiency cores), 64 GB of RAM, one NVMe SSD, Windows 11. The test database is TPC-H shaped, with one 60-million-row lineitem table (16 columns) and three 15-million-row orders tables (9 columns) that differ only in storage. I backed it up three times: uncompressed (9.9 GB), ZSTD (5.7 GB) and MS_XPRESS (3.8 GB).
Each run is FastBCP 1.6.4 writing Parquet with --parallelmethod Physical --paralleldegree 8. For each table and each backup, a cold run comes first: the driver's cache is cleared, so the export opens the backup for the first time. Three warm runs follow, and the tables give their median. For comparison, the same tables are exported from the live database on a local SQL Server 2025 instance, through adbc_mssql (the ArpeMSSQL driver) and mssql (SqlClient). Figures are cells per second (rows × columns), wall clock of the whole FastBCP process.
- Warm, an orders table (15 million rows, 135 million cells) goes to Parquet in 1.5 to 2 seconds from any of the three backups. From the uncompressed backup that is 2.3 to 2.4 times the live adbc_mssql source and 5.4 to 5.8 times mssql.
- The columnstore reaches about 149 M cells/s whatever the backup format: 60 million rows in 6.4 seconds, 2.8 times adbc_mssql and 6.3 times mssql.
- Once the backup is open, compression costs little: ZSTD stays within 5% of the uncompressed backup, MS_XPRESS within 2 to 20%.
- The cold run pays the open once per backup: 0.6 s for the uncompressed backup, about 1.5 s for a compressed one. orders_ci was the first table read from each compressed backup, so its cold run also read the file from disk: 3.1 to 3.6 s. After that, any table of the same backup opens in 20 to 30 ms.
- The live figures include the work of SQL Server, which ran on the same laptop. The backup runs touched no server at all.
The three backups fit in the laptop's 64 GB of memory, so apart from that first read, the cold runs measure the open by the driver, not the disk. With a backup much larger than memory, the open is bound by the disk, as on the 320 GB backup above.

articles.title: Alpine Linux Security advisory: OpenSSH-server password authentication bypass
articles.body:
Security advisory: openssh-server password authentication bypass
If you run sshd on Alpine Linux, update openssh now and restart sshd.
Upgrading the package alone does not replace the running daemon.
If you cannot update yet, at least disable password logins: set
PasswordAuthentication no in your sshd configuration and restart sshd.
Either one closes the hole.
What is the problem?
An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password. It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries.
The attacker needs the name of an account whose password field is *
(an account with no password set, which is normal for key-only accounts), and
needs the machine to have at least one other account with a $5$ or $6$
password hash. The attacker then sends a very long password (257 to 1024
bytes). One user with a password is enough: it makes every account without
one reachable.
Details are in the OpenSSH 10.6p2 release notes. No CVE identifier had been assigned at the time of writing.
Who is affected?
You are affected if all of the following are true:
- You run the Alpine openssh-server package, which is built without PAM, or
you run openssh-server-pam with UsePAM no. (openssh-server-pam with UsePAM yes is not affected.)
- PasswordAuthentication is yes (the OpenSSH default, unless you changed it).
- The machine has an account whose password field is *. This includes:
  - root, which ships as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16.
OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password protects root, so
root is only reachable if PermitRootLogin yes is set. That does not help if
another account that can log in is able to become root, for example
through doas.
  - Any key-only user created with adduser without a password, or with usermod -p '*'.
  - Users coming from a directory service through musl-nscd (nslcd, winbind, sssd), since they have no shadow entry.
  - The alpine user in the official tiny-cloud images (see below).
- At least one local account has a $5$ or $6$ password hash.
Affected releases: every Alpine release we checked, 3.21 through 3.24 and edge, and the older releases that no longer receive regular updates (3.16 to 3.20).
Who is not affected?
- Docker and other container users that do not run sshd in the
container.
- Systems with PasswordAuthentication no.
- Systems using openssh-server-pam with UsePAM yes (with UsePAM no you are affected).
- Locked accounts: those with ! as the password field in /etc/shadow (a line starting user:!:). They cannot log in with a password or a key.
- Systems where no account has a $-style password hash.
- Cloud images configured through cloud-init, which writes
PasswordAuthentication no.
How can I fix it?
1. Update
apk upgrade -U -a
Alpine 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 contain the fixed package (see the release announcement). The fixed package versions are:
Restart sshd after upgrading (rc-service sshd restart). Upgrading the
package does not restart a running sshd, so you must do it after.
2. If you cannot update: disable password authentication
Before you start, make sure your SSH key login works, and keep your current session open until you have tested a new login.
Run these as root. The first two commands create a drop-in file. Alpine’s
default sshd_config reads that directory from 3.19 onward; older releases
ignore it. The sed command changes yes to no on every
PasswordAuthentication line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config, whatever the spacing,
including lines inside a Match block. It also adds PasswordAuthentication no at the top of the file, for the case where there was no such line, and
saves the original as /etc/ssh/sshd_config.bak. The last two commands check
the configuration, restart the daemon, and show the result:
mkdir -p /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d
echo 'PasswordAuthentication no' > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-no-passwords.conf
sed -i.bak -e '1i PasswordAuthentication no' \
  -e 's/^\(\s*PasswordAuthentication[^y#]*\)yes/\1no/i' \
  /etc/ssh/sshd_config
sshd -t && rc-service sshd restart
sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication
The last command should print passwordauthentication no. To undo, delete
/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-no-passwords.conf and copy
/etc/ssh/sshd_config.bak back over /etc/ssh/sshd_config.
Cloud images (tiny-cloud)
The official tiny-cloud images (the qcow2, VHD and AMI artifacts) from
3.18.11 through 3.24.3 ship an alpine user with a * password field and
passwordless doas. They are safe on first boot. They become exploitable as
soon as any $6$ hash exists on the machine, for example when an admin sets a
console password, or user-data adds a user with hashed_passwd. An attacker
then gets a shell as alpine and can use doas to become root.
Images built from 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8, 3.24.4 and later include the fixed
package. Images from earlier point releases do not, so on every running
instance, update openssh or disable password authentication.
Releases that are no longer supported (3.21 and older)
These releases have the same bug. 3.21 reached its end of support on 2026-11-01, but we have published fixed packages for each release all the way back to 3.16.
How do I know if I was attacked?
Look in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for
an account that has no password (alpine, root, or any key-only user).
Review doas use and recently created users, files and authorized keys on
exposed machines. If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as
compromised.
How could this happen?
When sshd is built without PAM, it checks a password by hashing the attempt
with crypt() (the C library function that turns a password into its stored
hash) and comparing the result to the stored password field. For an account
whose stored field is too short to contain a salt (the random prefix of a
hash), sshd borrows the salt of another account.
musl’s crypt() returns the string * as an error indicator when the key is
over 256 bytes long. * is also exactly what the stored field contains for
every account with no password, so the “hash” matches and the login succeeds.
OpenSSH 10.6p2 avoids the problem in sshd. The stable-branch packages above carry a patch for the same problem.
Credits
Reported by Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield. Thanks to Damien Miller and Darren Tucker of the OpenSSH project for the fix and the 10.6p2 release, to Timo Teräs for help analyzing the issue, and to Natanael Copa, who built and uploaded the updated packages.
