articles.title: All-Clad, Our Place, HexClad, and More: The 16 Best Gifts for Home Cooks, According to Our Editors
articles.body:
All-Clad, Our Place, HexClad, and More: The 16 Best Gifts for Home Cooks, According to Our Editors
Our team has lots of experience with (and opinions about) cookware, kitchen gadgets, appliances, and tools. So naturally when it comes time to talk holiday gifts, we’re full of recommendations for great kitchen products you can get for your loved ones.
If you’re shopping for a home cook — whether they’re just starting out or have a longtime love for cooking — then this list is for you. It’s filled with 16 kitchen products our team actually uses and loves, including the best nonstick frying pan set, according to our shopping writer; the food storage containers Food Editor Andrea Rivera Wawrzyn can’t get enough of; and a beautiful new East Fork drop that is absolutely worth the splurge. Happy shopping!
A good nonstick frying pan is a must-have for any home cook. This set from All-Clad is the best Shopping Writer Micki Wagner has ever used, and she’s tested dozens. Not only is this three-piece set great, but it also dethroned her former favorite (a tough feat!). “Its super-slick nonstick surface usurped my all-time favorite fry pan — and All-Clad has retained that title ever since,” she says.
Micki ditched her nearly decade-old slow cooker earlier this year and upgraded to the Ninja HyperHeat. “This super-versatile appliance isn’t just a pressure cooker; it also has a slow cooker function (among seven other functionalities),” she writes in her review. “It has single-handedly reinvigorated my love of slow cooking, and I can do so much more with it.”
“As far as investment-worthy cookware goes, it doesn’t get any more iconic than the Le Creuset Dutch Oven,” writes contributor Abigail Abesamis Demarest in her review. “The beautiful colors, the distinct shape, the longevity — there’s just so much to love about it. It’s my pride and joy.”
Any home cook needs a good set of food storage containers for leftovers — and this 6-piece set is now one of Andrea’s favorites. “I love my stainless steel cookware, but it’s not a material I associate with food storage,” she writes about this set. “I could not have been more wrong. These have fast become some of the most-used containers in my kitchen.” And, get this: They’re microwave-safe.
Assistant Editor Alexandra Foster has been using this colorful cast iron skillet for five months and finds it amazing for sautéing veggies, making frittatas, baking cornbread, crisping up tofu, and even reheating frozen meals. Plus, she writes in her review that it’s great for hosting, too. “You can easily transfer the skillet from the stove to the table for serving. It’s a crowd-pleaser that will get a ton of compliments, no doubt!”
“I can’t sing the praises of this air fryer toaster oven enough,” Micki says. “I’ve tried all three of Our Place’s Wonder Ovens, and this one is the best hands-down. I literally use it every single day. The sleek touchscreen, pretty mint color, and 8-in-1 functionality are my favorite features.” Splurgy? Yes. But so worth it.
For home chefs who love to make burgers, pancakes, and diner-style breakfasts, this double burner griddle is a must-have. Micki reviewed it last year, and instantly fell in love with it: “Every batch of pancakes turned out beautifully — even the very first one.” And if you make pancakes often, you know that’s a big deal.
This is the chef’s knife Anthony Bourdain swore by for decades, and it’s absolutely worth the hype. Micki has been using it for five or six months now, and she says “it’s easily the best knife I’ve ever had in my kitchen.” Enough said!
Looking for a solid nonstick cookware set to help your favorite home cook outfit their kitchen? This 12-piece Caraway set has you covered. “Everything cooked evenly, browned beautifully, needed minimal cooking oil, and didn’t stick at all,” contributor Danielle Centoni writes in her review. “Best of all? Cleanup was so easy, I could wash the pans before we even sat down to eat,” she says.
Our editors are big fans of OXO, and one of our favorite products is this scale (three different editors recommend it!). “This is the best everyday kitchen scale, full stop,” says Andrea. “It’s accurate, durable, and easy to clean. You can change the units easily, and it won’t shut off on you mid-recipe. Everyone should own one.”
Home cooks who are short on time and/or tend to have lots of leftovers will find plenty of use for this microwaveable cookware set. “After a month of use, it was clear to me that the Anyday cookware was going to be sticking around in my kitchen for a while,” writes contributor Julian Plovnick in his review. “As a connoisseur of leftovers and a despiser of dishes, the ability to cook, store, and reheat my food all in one container is a huge plus.”
“The Ninja TWISTi has brought together affordability with a good bit of power,” Micki writes in her review. She loves this blender for how well it crushes up ice and frozen fruit to make delicious smoothies and how it blends chickpeas into smooth, fluffy hummus. Plus, it’s under $100.
Micki has three of these cutting boards in multiple sizes, and she uses at least one every day for slicing fruit, dicing tofu, prepping potatoes and carrots, and so much more. Plus, these paper-composite cutting boards are plastic-free. “I don’t even miss my plastic ones, to be honest,” Micki writes in her review.
This new drop from East Fork is as durable as it is beautiful. It’s microwave-, dishwasher-, and oven-safe up to 450°F, and stunning enough to double as serveware. It’s new to Micki’s kitchen, and she already knows she’ll be using it all season long.
“I finally replaced my clunky old oven mitts with this stylish set,” says Director of Groceries and Shopping Mara Weinraub. “Having dedicated right and left hands makes a huge difference — they fit my small hands comfortably and give me a far more confident grip.” Choose from four colors for just $39.
Former pastry chef and Kitchn contributor Stephanie Ganz “made some of the best crêpes” of her life with this All-Clad pan. “I’ve made hundreds of crêpes over the years, in regular nonstick pans and even fancy copper pans, and this was the most enjoyable experience I’ve ever had making them,” she wrote in her review.
Why You Should Trust Me
I’ve been a journalist for nearly a decade and have tested hundreds of products for the kitchen, home, and beyond since 2022. I only write about the cookware, appliances, and ingredients that truly impress me or come highly recommended from trusted experts. The recommendations below aren’t paid endorsements; they are editorially vetted products from our team.
Which gift(s) are you choosing? Tell us about it in the comments below.

articles.title: The M6 MacBook Pro is probably the last of its kind
articles.body:
On November 6th, Apple will release an all-new MacBook Pro. It’s thinner and lighter and has a beautiful OLED touchscreen. It is very likely what every new MacBook Pro will look like in a couple of years.
The M6 MacBook Pro is probably the last of its kind
The design is starting to show its age next to the lighter, brighter PROLED model, but the entry-level MacBook Pro is still great.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
The M6 MacBook Pro, which is also out on the 6th, is not that laptop. Instead, it’s a straightforward chip bump of Apple’s entry-level MacBook Pro, in basically the same chassis Apple’s been using since 2021. Everything that was great about the M5 MacBook Pro last year, and the M4 the year before, still applies. The M6 MacBook Pro is still a great all-around computer, and a nice step up from the MacBook Air. Processor, screen, speakers, ports, power, battery life: They’re all a little better than the Air’s. The keyboard and webcam are still solid; the trackpad is still best in class. Inside the laptop, only the processor — which bumps up from a 10-core M5 to a 12-core M6 — and the N1 networking chip are new.
There are just two things complicating what would otherwise be the easiest MacBook review of the year. The first is the starting price: $1,999 with 16GB of RAM and 1TB of storage — the same price as the base M5 MacBook Pro since September, but up $200 since its launch a year ago. The other is the actually new MacBook Pro: the one with the OLED touchscreen.
Yes, the OLED model is great. Not that someone who’s considering the base MacBook Pro should spend $900 more to get that screen today. But that design is likely to come to the entry MacBook Pro next year. The question is: Should you wait?
The Good
- Hardware still excellent all around
- 12-core CPU and GPU in base model
- Great battery life
The Bad
- More expensive, like everything else
- Upgrading RAM puts you close to M5 Pro model
- Likely the last pre-redesign MacBook Pro
The entry-level 14-inch MacBook Pro has only existed in its current form for two years. After the 2023 M3 model finally ditched the Touch Bar and butterfly keys, the M4 model brought it up to par with the “real” Pros, most notably by adding a third Thunderbolt port and bumping the minimum RAM from an embarrassing 8GB to a decent 16GB. The M5 version had a faster chip and double the storage speed, and that was enough to keep it among our favorite laptops. The M6 is yet another chip bump, and it adds Apple’s N1 networking chip for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 (and also Thread, for what that’s worth.)
Component report card
- Screen: A
- Webcam: A
- Mic: A
- Keyboard: B
- Touchpad: A
- Port selection: B
- Speakers: A
- Number of ugly stickers to remove: 0
The rest of the hardware is the same as it’s been for two years, which is to say it’s still great. The 14.2-inch miniLED display is bright, beautiful, and color-accurate, with 3092 x 1964 resolution and up to 1,000 nits of brightness in standard mode. The 120Hz adaptive refresh rate (which Apple calls ProMotion) really makes a difference in gaming or even just moving the cursor around. It’s the sort of thing you don’t notice when all your screens are 60Hz, but once you go higher, it’s awfully hard to go back.
Of course, it’s also hard to go back from an OLED screen, like the one on the other new MacBook Pro, once you’ve used one. So it’s a good thing I haven’t used that laptop yet.
The large haptic trackpad remains the best on any laptop, and the keyboard is… still fine. I have never loved Apple’s laptop keyboards, but the keys are large and well-spaced and tolerable for typing on. I’ve used worse. The speakers, on either side of the keyboard deck, are excellent. The “studio-quality three-mic array” is genuinely superb, and noise-canceling is good enough that when I was on a video call using the MacBook’s speakers and mic, my coworker thought I was wearing headphones. That does not happen on my M1 Air.
It still comes in silver and space black. It still has three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, a 3.5mm headphone jack, an SD card slot, and the MagSafe charging port. Again, coming from an Air, that’s just nice. I love not having to find a card reader to import photos. I love having ports on the right side of the laptop. And I’ll never be mad at a headphone jack.
The webcam is the 12MP Center Stage one Apple’s been using for the past few years, and it’s good enough. If I move around too much during a call, it can take a minute to recenter, but the resolution is good. It’s a huge step up from the one in my M1 MacBook Air.
Battery life is still exceptional. The first day I had the MacBook Pro, I kept it plugged in because I was setting it up and running benchmarks. The second day, I unplugged it at 9:30AM and didn’t plug it back in until noon the next day. That’s over 12 hours of screen-on use, including about three hours of video calls and the usual multitasking. Hard to complain about that!
The M6 chip found in the MacBook Pro is the same 12-core chip in the M6 Mac Mini and iMac, with two super cores, four performance cores, and six efficiency cores. It’s more than enough power for regular use, up to and including photo editing, the occasional video editing, and light gaming.
All three M6 machines had very similar performance in nearly all our benchmarks. The exceptions were Premiere Pro, Photoshop, and DaVinci Resolve benchmarks, where the 24GB of memory in our Mini review unit gave it a 5 to 10 percent edge over the iMac and this MacBook Pro, both of which have 16GB of memory.
Apple Silicon remains capable as hell. The MacBook Pro handled everything I threw at it, and I rarely heard the fan except during video-rendering benchmarks and while playing Cyberpunk 2077. Even then, it’s a faint white noise-y whoosh rather than the irritating whine of many laptop fans.
Cyberpunk has recently been updated for Mac, with better MetalFX support and frame interpolation. Gaming on a MacBook keyboard is not really my idea of a good time, but I’ve played a lot of Cyberpunk on my desktop, so I’m familiar with the game. With upscaling and fake frames it’s tolerable on the MacBook in a pinch, but the game really wants more powerful hardware. I also ran into a few graphical glitches, including one that turned everyone’s skin bright green. That was fun.
Last year, we said the base M5 MacBook Pro, with 16GB memory and 512GB storage, was enough for most people. But that laptop cost $1,599 at the time; the M6 MacBook Pro starts at $1,999 with 16GB of unified memory and 1TB of storage. I’m not going to complain too much about the price increase because it’s happening everywhere; that’s just the weather these days. Can’t do anything about it.
It does put the base model MacBook Pro in a tight spot, however. MacBooks last a long time. Apple Silicon in particular holds up very well; every time we review a MacBook, we hear from people who are still perfectly happy with their M1 Pros or M1 MacBook Airs. My work machine is an M1 MacBook Air with 16GB of RAM. It’s getting a little long in the tooth — especially compared with the M6 I’m typing this on — but it’s hanging in there.
Apple Silicon ages so gracefully that if you’re considering this particular MacBook Pro, you’re probably either coming from a very old Intel MacBook, or you’ve outgrown an older Air and you want more ports, a bigger screen, and better everything (or you’re switching over from Windows). If you’re considering spending upward of $2,000 on a new computer, you’re probably going to keep it for a while. And if that’s the case, you should get more than 16GB of memory. You’ll feel the lack of RAM before you feel the processor age.
Now, if you’re running local AI models, doing high-res video encoding or 3D rendering, you should go straight for an M5 Pro or Max model with as much RAM as you can afford. You also don’t need me to tell you that. But if you’re considering the M6 MacBook Pro — this laptop — you should still get more RAM. Even if you don’t need it today, in five years you’ll wish you had it.
But jumping from 16GB to 24GB of RAM without upgrading the storage or the screen puts you at $2,199; going to 36GB costs $2,399. And here’s where you hit the upsell. That’s only $100 less than the M5 Pro model with 24GB of RAM and a more powerful CPU and GPU. And at that point, you’re only $400 away from the one with the OLED.
The best time to plant a tree is 20 years ago, but the best time to buy a laptop is next year.
The M6 MacBook Pro is a fantastic laptop at a good price — RAM and storage shortage taken into account. But it’s also likely the last of its kind, and if you’re considering buying one but it’s not an emergency, you might be exactly the person who should wait for next year.
Mark Gurman reports that next year’s entry M7 MacBook Pro will use the redesigned hardware of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. That chassis is a little bit thinner but nearly half a pound lighter, which makes a difference when you’re carrying around all the time. As my colleague David Pierce points out, the touchscreen part is whatever, but the OLED screen really is good. If you’re considering the M5 Pro or Max model, it’s worth spending extra for the redesigned model.
If you buy the M6 MacBook Pro today, you’re still getting a great all-rounder laptop that’ll last you the better part of a decade. Everything about it is good to great. You can’t go wrong. But if your current laptop still works and you think you’ll want the thinner, lighter OLED model, you might consider holding out just a little longer. Apple has shown us it can make an even better MacBook Pro; I can’t wait to see what next year’s looks like.
Photography by Nathan Edwards / The Verge
Apple MacBook Pro 14 M6 specs (as reviewed)
- Display: 14.2-inch (3024 x 1964) 120Hz Mini-LED
- Processor: Apple M6 (12 CPU cores, 12 GPU cores)
- Memory: 16GB unified memory
- Storage: 1TB SSD
- Webcam: 12-megapixel Center Stage camera with Desk View
- Connectivity: Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6
- Ports: 3x USB-C / Thunderbolt 4, SDXC card slot, HDMI 2.1, headphone / mic combo
- Weight: 3.4 pounds
- Dimensions: 12.31 x 8.71 x 0.61 inches
- Battery: 72.4Wh
- Price: $1,999

articles.title: Obscure audio codec is a perfect fit for the N64
articles.body:
Why this Obscure Audio Codec is a Perfect Fit for the N64
Sorry for the clickbait title. I promise this post delivers: 44100 Hz stereo with near-Opus bitrates using about 4% of the N64’s CPU time.
But first, some history: The options for playing and storing audio data on the N64 were dire. The PlayStation could just stream uncompressed redbook audio straight from the CD. On the N64, cartridge space was at a premium and time on the 93 MHz CPU was limited.
Worse, access to the vector co-processor, the RSP, was guarded by Nintendo for the longest time. Nintendo's own platform library, Libultra, internally used the RSP for various graphics and sound-related tasks, but Nintendo didn't allow third-party developers to directly write code for it.
Libultra provided some functions to transparently play back compressed audio using an ADPCM scheme (adaptive differential pulse code modulation). The RSP handled decompression on the fly, just before the audio was sent to the output buffer.
This works well enough and cuts the space needed for a sample by a factor of 4. Still, a 5-minute stereo audio track at 44100 Hz will land at about 12MB – way too much for an N64 cartridge, even when you cut the sample rate in half. The whole Mario 64 ROM is just 8MB in total. The biggest N64 games were 64MB.
So N64 games produced music similarly to a tracker: short samples were scheduled and played back with some limited effects at the right time. With the space constraints on the cartridge, fully “recorded” audio was pretty much out of the question.
Later in the N64's life, some blessed developers were allowed by Nintendo to directly access the RSP. Most famously, Conker's Bad Fur Day used this to decompress MP3 audio for the myriad of speech samples in the game. Decoding MP3 is quite expensive and the frame rate of the game suffered. It was good enough for cutscenes, but just too much for continuous background music or sound effects during gameplay.
Audio in the Open Source Libdragon
Similar to Nintendo's Libultra, Libdragon, the open source alternative, has a real-time ADPCM decoder running on the RSP. So with ROM space being cheaper these days, I just compressed all music for Xibalba 64 with ADPCM. About 31MB of the 32MB ROM are used for sound and music. Remember that Mario 64 just used an 8MB ROM and Xibalba 64 is a much simpler game with only 15 minutes of music. It worked, but storing music this way is a gratuitous waste of space.
Now, Libdragon also has a real-time, RSP-accelerated Opus decoder. It's a marvel in itself. The Opus format was published 16 years after the N64 and yet Giovanni Bajo managed to make it work on this “obsolete” hardware. Compression and audio quality are excellent, but again – it's too slow to be used during gameplay.
What's the alternative then? We could build an RSP-accelerated MP3 decoder, but the performance gain over Opus would be marginal, and quality and compression would be worse.
QOA would be a slight improvement over ADPCM, but it's just a poor fit for the vector co-processor: each sample relies on the previous decoded sample. Hard to vectorize.
A simple transform codec, something like MP3, but without all the design-by-consortium baggage, may work…
The Ultra Low Complexity Codec
During some late-night “research”, I stumbled across an old Game Boy Advance demo that plays recorded music at just 70kbps. That's less than a typical MP3, but at comparable quality. I repeat: On a GBA. With a 16 MHz ARM CPU. With no vector instructions and, according to the GitHub page, some headroom to spare.
Time-domain codecs (such as ADPCM) need significantly higher bitrates for this quality. Subband codecs, such as MP2, have much worse quality at comparable bitrates, and more “modern” transform codecs, such as MP3, usually need at least an 80–100 MHz CPU. For this GBA demo, no existing codec would fit the bill.
So Aikku93 not only wrote a decoder in ARM assembly, but also created a whole new codec: The Ultra Low Complexity Codec (ULC).
ULC is a transform codec and somewhat similar to MP3. ULC transforms slices of PCM data into the frequency domain. Like MP3, it uses the Modified Discrete Cosine Transform (MDCT) to do so. But unlike MP3, it does not split the signal into multiple bands (ULC's MDCT is “full-band”). Where MP3 uses classic entropy encoding (Huffman specifically), ULC does… not. Instead, transformed coefficients are stored with a very simple nibble-based syntax.
In short: ULC is what MP3 could have been. The same core idea, but without the cruft around it. The “ultra low complexity” does not come from a different algorithm, but by carefully applying and packaging it.
The nibble-based packaging is maybe the most elegant idea of ULC. Each coefficient is stored in just 4 bits, interpreted as a signed integer. Some values are reserved to indicate zero fill, noise fill, or a quantizer change:
- -7 … -2, 2 … 7 - coefficient value
- 0 - zero run, run length (1 … 16) follows in the next nibble
- 1 - long zero run, run length (17 … 288) follows in the next two nibbles
- -1 - quantizer change, value follows in the next nibble
- -8 - noise fill, length and amplitude follow in the next three nibbles
Everything is nibble aligned. This means the whole codec works without any arbitrary bit reads or entropy decoding. Reading and unpacking a block of coefficients takes just ~150 lines of C.
Also note that noise fill is a valuable addition. Cymbals, hi-hats and snare drums greatly benefit from that. MP3 does not have anything similar and needs to encode quasi-random coefficients as is.
ULC can produce usable results even at 16kbps. Quality of course suffers, but it might still be good enough for some applications.
Aikku93 has been working on ULC since 2019 and has steadily improved the encoding quality. All code is permissively licensed. Time to try this on the N64 then!
ULC on the N64
I spent an evening in pre-LLM days compiling the ULC reference decoder for the N64 and producing a small demo. It worked without a hitch.
The only problem: it was keeping the CPU very busy. Nothing was offloaded to the RSP. As a proof of concept, it wasn't doing much: we already knew the 93 MHz CPU was enough to decode a transform-based codec, but we don't need a “music player” that does nothing else. We need this for background music and spoken dialog during gameplay. It cannot hog the CPU.
Float to 16-bit Fixed Point
Obviously the IMDCT needs to be moved to the RSP coprocessor instead. We could just DMA one block of decoded coefficients to the RSP's memory, do the transform and DMA the completed samples back to RDRAM into the output buffer.
That's easier said than done, though. The RSP has only 4096 bytes of data memory (DMEM) and another 4096 bytes for instructions (IMEM). The vector instructions work in 16-bit or 32-bit fixed point, with no floats. The IMDCT will only be efficient if all the data for a transform fits into the RSP's DMEM at once. We also need some of the DMEM for temporary values and – if possible – the lapping buffer: half of the previously decoded block. So with the default 2048-sample block size of ULC, we're out of luck, even with 16-bit fixed point.
While ULC can work with smaller MDCT block sizes, it was optimized for 2048, so
we should keep it as large as possible. On top of that, the ULC reference 
encoder/decoder uses floats, so the obvious choice would be 32-bit fixed point to
maintain quality, but 16-bit may work. So we have two options, both arriving
at 3072 bytes:
- 32-bit values, a 512-sample block size (256-sample lap buffer): (512 + 256) * 4 bytes
- 16-bit values, a 1024-sample block size (512-sample lap buffer): (1024 + 512) * 2 bytes
Using 16-bit fixed point would not only reduce the DMA traffic, but also speed up computation on the RSP. The trade-off would be a higher noise floor. How high? No idea. So I carefully refactored the reference decoder, still running on the N64 CPU, to work in 16-bit fixed point (Q1.14).
After almost blowing my ears off a bunch of times, I got it working and could only hear (or imagine?) the faintest white noise when cranking it up. Case settled: 16-bit it is.
Cramming it into the RSP
Now I just needed to port this C code to the RSP. My knowledge of MIPS assembly is very basic, and writing an RSP decoder would be a serious endeavor.
This is where I took a hiatus from this project – I had a game to finish. When I returned earlier this year LLMs have improved quite a bit. Still, I didn't exactly trust GPT-5 with it. In some previous experiments it did a very bad job, often ignoring delay slots and other intricacies of the RSP, never finishing the job.
(Aside: GPT-6 or Opus-5 would probably one-shot this now)
So instead I opted for a more iterative approach. Max Bebök created a small C-like language to write code for the RSP, aptly named RSPL. Armed with the language documentation, I asked Codex to translate the C code to RSPL piece by piece, always verifying the result. It took a few days to port and land on an API design that made sense. Then in subsequent steps Codex further optimized the RSPL assembly output by first rewriting some parts (directly in assembly this time), then minimizing pipeline stalls by adapting the RSPL's optimizer.
The end result is ~1400 lines of MIPS assembly handling the IMDCT, lapping, stereo interleaving and output scaling. It barely fits into the 4096 byte IMEM of the RSP.
The C side of the decoder is still handwritten, but only because LLMs have no taste. The whole process took me a few weeks, but I'm still amazed that it worked at all.
To make ULC easily seekable, I added a sparse table at the end of the file that contains the byte offset of every eighth frame. The decoder quickly skips ahead from the nearest frame to the desired one. This adds about 20 bytes per second – manageable even for 16kbps audio.
ULC proved to be a very viable alternative to ADPCM and Opus on the N64. Quality and bitrate are close to those of Opus, but complexity is only 4x that of ADPCM. A single 44100 Hz stereo track costs about 4% of CPU time and 5% of RSP time. Perfectly usable for background music, speech, ambience and longer sound effects.
The decoder works transparently in Libdragon, just like all other audio codecs. It has been merged into the preview branch a while ago.
Addendum
A few days ago an excellent port of Half-Life for the N64 was published. 
The README states:
[...] libdragon's ULC audio codec for the 2,500 sounds and 27 music tracks, is what makes everything fit in one 64 MB cartridge image.
~ github.com/ToxyCola/Half-Life-Nintendo-64-Port
Many thanks to Aikku93 for creating ULC. It's a wonderful codec. I merely found and adapted it. I seek simplicity and elegance in everything I do and ULC is something I can truly adore. Kudos!

articles.title: 3M To Pay Over $7 Billion To Settle 'Forever Chemical' Groundwater Claims
articles.body:
3M To Pay Over $7 Billion To Settle 'Forever Chemical' Groundwater Claims (apnews.com) 41
			
		 	
				3M has agreed to pay up to $7.35 billion over nine years to settle claims from as many as 120,000 people who say they were sickened by PFAS-contaminated groundwater near military bases, airports and other locations where firefighting foam was used. The Associated Press reports that 3M "did not admit liability," noting that the settlement comes on top of the more than $10 billion the company previously agreed to pay U.S. public drinking water systems over PFAS contamination. From the report:  3M chairman William Brown called the settlement a "significant milestone" that substantially reduces uncertainty from the litigation. [...] Fred Thompson, an attorney with the Motley Rice law firm that helped negotiate the 3M settlement for the plaintiffs, called it welcome news for "the thousands of victims who have sought answers and accountability for nearly a decade." He said in a news release that the plaintiffs urgently need help covering mounting medical bills and other costs.
Under the terms of the settlement, the payouts will begin with $50 million this year, followed by yearly payments of more than $1 billion each year from 2028 to 2033. 3M could make additional payments if enough plaintiffs participate. If too few sign on, 3M has the option to cancel the settlement and continue fighting the lawsuit.

articles.title: NASA Announces X-70 Experimental Aircraft to Advance Flight Research
articles.body:
NASA Announces X-70 Experimental Aircraft to Advance Flight Research (nasa.gov) 25
			
		 	
				NASA has unveiled the X-70 Fractal, a new crewed experimental aircraft "designed to accelerate the development and testing of advanced aviation technologies." From a press release:  The crewed X-70 features advanced, rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology that will allow NASA to explore aircraft maneuverability in ways never before demonstrated in crewed flight. The aircraft can also accommodate up to 2,000 pounds of experimental payloads in internal and external locations, enabling a wide range of research and flight-testing opportunities.
The X-70 Fractal has a takeoff weight of 10,000 pounds and is designed to cruise at Mach .75, reach altitudes of up to 45,000 feet, and provide an operational range exceeding about 1,726 miles (1,500 nautical miles). These capabilities will enable NASA to conduct demanding flight research across a broad range of operating conditions.
The X-70 joins a storied legacy of experimental aircraft that have helped establish America's leadership in aviation. From the Bell X-1, which first broke the sound barrier in 1947, to the X-15 hypersonic research aircraft and today's X-59 quiet supersonic demonstrator, NASA has spent decades pushing the boundaries of flight. With the X-70, NASA will expand its capacity to conduct experimental flight research, accelerate the testing of emerging technologies, and advance the next generation of American aviation.

articles.title: Vivaldi 8.3 for Desktop: make bad ads sad
articles.body:
We aren’t part of the Big Tech oligarchy, and our business doesn’t depend on knowing all about you to predict when you are ready to buy a new toothbrush. While most browser companies turn your browsing into data for harvesting, and profiles to sell, Vivaldi gives you a European alternative that respects your privacy. With 8.3, we have given our Ad and Tracker Blocker a major upgrade so you can send the surveillance machinery home empty-handed.
We aren’t against respectful advertising. A contextual ad that matches the page you’re reading, and doesn’t follow you around afterwards, is a fair way for a site to pay its writers. The ads we object to are the ones that track and profile you. They follow you from site to site and remember things about you that you never chose to share. The built-in Ad and Tracker Blocker was created to make those bad ads sad. Rad!
How much advertising you want to block depends on YOU, who you are and what you’re reading. Some people want every tracker and ad long gone, and don’t mind if it causes a site to occasionally misbehave. Others want the sites they use to work perfectly every time. Some want a bit of both, depending on the site.
For this release we have given the Ad and Tracker Blocker an extensive rebuild to handle large filter lists more efficiently. We’ve also given it an updated design and new labels.
The updated Ad and Tracker Blocker gives you four default levels of protection to choose from:
- Off: turns the built-in blocker off completely
- Light: blocks most known trackers and some ads
- Strong: blocks more trackers and ads, sites may break
- Aggressive: blocks almost all trackers and ads, sites may break
You can set your default level of blocking from settings or when onboarding to Vivaldi. The level you select from here will be applied to all sites, but in Vivaldi we always give you more. Ad blocking shouldn’t be all or nothing. In Vivaldi, you can decide how much of the web gets through, one site at a time, on every device you use. That’s the kind of control a browser should give the people who use it.
Levels really pay off when you set them per site. Put that dj-set on Youtube on full blast without ads breaking your beat with Aggressive. Keep your bank on Light so every form works as expected. Turn protection down on the small independent site you trust and whose ads you’re happy to see. To set a level for the site you’re on, click the shield icon in the Address Bar. Vivaldi remembers your choice, so each site loads the way you decided.
If you are particularly interested in the topic, we’ve also added the option to create “custom” levels. In these levels you configure everything yourself, giving you full control over which blocklists are used. You can add a custom block list either added from a remote URL or from their file manager.
The new Ad and Tracker Blocker is also available for Vivaldi on Android and iOS today, so your protection looks and works the same way on your laptop, your phone and your tablet.
Expanding our love for vertical tabs
Long before vertical tabs were a talking point in our industry, they were introduced as an option in Vivaldi, and we have continued to improve the workflows for those who prefer to have their tabs on the side. With our 8.0 update this year, we introduced a redesign that really gave the vertical tabbers a sought-after update. With 8.3 we’re stepping it up with two new additions. If you like your Tab Bar stacked the same order as your sandwiches, listen up.
With Expand Tab Bar on Hover, you can keep the vertical Tab Bar slim, with just favicons showing, and give the page as much of your screen as possible until you actually need your tabs. When you’re looking for a tab, move your cursor over the Tab Bar and it smoothly expands to show full titles. Move away and it slides right back. The feature works when the Tab Bar sits on the left or right side of the window.
Pinned tabs on a vertical Tab Bar can now sit side by side in a compact grid at the top, neatly and all in order. Your mail, calendar and project tools stay one click away, and there’s far more room for everything else you have open. This is Vivaldi, so if you instead prefer the “old” way with each pinned tab taking a row, there is obviously a setting (Settings > Tabs > Tab Features > Pinned Tabs > Show Pinned Tabs at Full Width).
If you’re yet to try vertical tabs, this is your sign. If you’re already in love with vertical tabs, you’re welcome.
What else is new in Vivaldi 8.3
Paste and Go, for a whole list of links
Someone sends you a long list of links in an email or a chat, and you want to open every one of them. The desperate times of clicking them one by one are finally over! Copy the whole list, paste it in the Address Field, and Vivaldi opens each URL in its own tab. Research sources, someone’s wishlist, the reading list a colleague shared: all of them open simultaneously in each own tab, ready to stack, tile or work through one by one.
Copy Sanitized Link
Links often carry tracking parameters that tell a site who shared them and where they came from. Copy Sanitized Link strips those out before the link reaches your clipboard, so the person you send it to gets the page and nothing else. It’s an easy habit that keeps a bit more of your browsing to yourself.
Faster Reader Mode
Reader Mode has gotten some tender love and caring for 8.3. It now opens faster and scrolls more smoothly, so you can switch from a busy page to a clean, readable article in a moment and settle in.
Support for Tab Groups API
Vivaldi now supports Chrome’s Tab Groups API for extensions, so extensions built around tab groups can now work in Vivaldi.
This is your browser
We cannot repeat this often enough: Vivaldi is an independent employee-owned European company. That means we don’t answer to advertisers or a VC firm pushing features that benefit them instead of you. We don’t collect data, we just want to make a great browser that helps you explore the web.
Every release we do is built for the people who use Vivaldi. With 8.3 we’re giving you more control over what you see, what follows you, and how your tabs look. As our marketing department said: “this is a really on-brand release”.
If Vivaldi helps you explore more, tell someone about it. Helping a friend, colleague or family member make the switch is one of the best ways to fight for a better web.
Vivaldi 8.3 is ready today!
Vivaldi 8.3 is also out today on mobile. Read what’s new in Vivaldi 8.3 on Android and iOS.
As always, thank you for being part of the Vivaldi community. Together, we’re fighting for a better web, one release at a time.
Changelog
Take a look at the full list of changes from Vivaldi 8.2 to 8.3.

articles.title: The Big Idea: Daryl Gregory
articles.body:
The Big Idea: Daryl Gregory
Posted on November 5, 2026 Posted by Athena Scalzi 1 Comment
Being the middle child isn’t easy, but the bonds you form with your siblings can be some of the closest and most impactful relationships in your life. Author Daryl Gregory shares memories of his sisters from his childhood, and talks about how their bond played a roll in creating his newest novel, The Porcelain Sisters.
DARYL GREGORY:
Is there something wrong with me that I find two sisters fighting with each other to be hugely entertaining? I was the middle child, the boy sandwiched between two girls—one who was seven years older than me, and the other sixteen months younger. We grew up in a small ranch house in the suburbs of Chicago, and we fought what I assumed was a normal amount.
Ninety percent of the time, it was me versus one of them. With my older sister, this was often when she ordered me to do something, and my go-to response was to slam a door and shout, “You’re not the boss of me!” (She was absolutely the boss of me.)
My younger sister and I were closer in age and so spent more time together, which meant more opportunities to torture each other. I liked to hide in her room and jump-scare her. She’s the finest screamer in the family, and terrifying her is extremely satisfying. She knew how to hit back, though. One time she kidnapped my prized possession, a G.I. Joe with lifelike hair and Kung Fu grip, and he reappeared days later with a bald spot, as if his forced marriage to Barbie had driven him into middle age. I still have him—and the damage is outrageous.
So it was a delight—a delight, I tell you—when my sisters fought with each other, and I got sit on the sidelines munching my proverbial popcorn.
But here’s the thing I found amazing—their fights were so short. They’d pivot from shouting at each other to calmly hanging out in their shared bedroom. They didn’t hold grudges. (I, however, was a champion pouter.) Even now, if they have an argument, they repair the damage quickly. I love my sisters, and they’ve assured me that they love me back, but they have a bond with each other that I find mysterious and enviable.
So perhaps it’s not a surprise that sisters turn up a lot in my books. Ruth and Isabel, the two main characters in my new novella, The Porcelain Sisters, are not exactly like my siblings—for one thing, neither of mine is a haunted doll—but let’s just say there are… similarities.
Ruth (the flesh-and-blood sister) and Isabel (the porcelain one) first appeared as teenagers in my YA Lovecraftian horror novel, Harrison Squared. They were my favorite characters to write dialog for, because they operated almost like a vaudeville ventriloquist act—Ruth was shy and soft-spoken, while Isabel spoke the truth and cut everyone down to size.
But in that book I never explained why Isabel could talk, or how they were sisters, or where Isabel came from. That was for a good reason: I didn’t know. I wrote this book to find out—and to get the chance to hang out with them some more.
Ruth, now in her twenties, is trying to make rent while taking college classes, but feeling adrift. She seems to have some latent magical ability, but doesn’t know what her purpose in life is beyond taking care of her sister. She’s never even had a long-term romantic relationship because Isabel deliberately freaks out anybody she brings home.
Isabel’s anger issues stem, of course, from being trapped in a porcelain body. She can’t grow up and may never live on her own. When her body’s accidentally damaged during a fight with Ruth—a seaside cliff is involved—a mundane toy repair shop won’t cut it. They have to go on the road to find the Dollmaker, the French witch who made her.
As I wrote that last sentence I realized the sisters are literally repairing each other. I wish I’d thought of that in time to put it on the back cover copy.
The girls head to Marseille, where they face off with an unkillable assassin with the resilience of a ragdoll, a pair of demons (one a chain-smoking crow, the other a black cat) and their human familiars, as well as a small army of haunted dolls. Oh, and the Dollmaker turns out to be the head of Le Clan des Sorciéres, a kind of witch mafia. I know, it’s a lot.
At the root of the mystery is why their mother, an enforcer for Le Clan called Godless Annie, abandoned them. What the sisters discover about themselves suggests there may be a way for them to live apart—but do they want to?
Another thing occurred to me as I’m typing this: is that ending about my current relationship with my sisters? Since our mom passed we don’t see each other like we used to. We live on opposite sides of the country, and our lives are busy. Did I write this book because I miss them?
I suppose I could talk to a therapist about this. Or write another book about sisters. Or—and hear me out—I could go on the road with the Gregory girls, solving mysteries and fighting the occasional demon.
The Porcelain Sisters: Amazon|Barnes & Noble|Bookshop|Powell’s

articles.title: Claude AI can plug directly into your bank account
articles.body:
Anthropic has a new pitch for managing your personal finances: let Claude do it instead, with a new Personal Finance feature that connects it to your bank and card accounts via the Plaid bank bridging platform. You can ask the chatbot “where did my money go this month,” for example, and it’ll create an overview with a breakdown of spending by category, including rent and utilities, shopping, and food. Claude can also answer broader questions around what bills are left before your next payday, if you can afford big purchases like holiday trips, and how much money you could be saving each month.
Claude AI can plug directly into your bank account
With access to your bank account via Plaid, Anthropic’s chatbot will try to explain where your money is going and what you can afford.
Its access is read-only, and with Plaid facilitating the connection, Claude doesn’t see your banking passwords and your bank doesn’t have to deal with unvetted AI bots crawling around your accounts.
Claude can’t move, manage, or invest your money, according to Anthropic, and it “isn’t designed to give investment advice.”, but it can see the bank’s name, account names, account type, the last four digits of the number associated with it, your balances and credit limits, and up to two years’ worth of your transaction history.
If you choose to give it access to all that, Claude can explain financial terms you don’t understand and answer questions about your balances and transactions.
Personal Finance in Claude is rolling out in beta this week to Claude Pro, Max, and Ultra plan subscribers in the US. Anthropic’s announcement follows OpenAI introducing a similar feature for ChatGPT in May, which also plugs into your bank accounts through Plaid. Allowing AI to have oversight into your finances might ring some alarm bells, but according to the sign-off in Anthropic’s press release, it’s just the beginning:
“Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust. We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it.”

articles.title: Image of our satellite-choked night skies
articles.body:
Stunning Image of Our Satellite-Choked Night Skies
To create this composite image, photographer Brendan Larsen captured almost 600 photographs over a two-hour period and then manually stitched them together.
This is the most time-consuming photo edit I’ve EVER done!
I left my camera photographing the night sky over Mt Taranaki for nearly TWO HOURS, capturing 578 photographs.
The result? An estimated 14,450 satellite trail appearances, representing approximately 1,400 individual satellites! 😱
I manually masked in EVERY SINGLE TRAIL from the original photographs — approximately 45 HOURS of editing to create this one image!
The Guardian has more on how he created the image (which, despite many online commenters’ beliefs, is not AI):
Larsen, 51, says he set his camera up to take an unlimited number of eight-second-long shots, with a two-second gap in between each photo. “I left her running for two hours and captured 578 photos … That was the easy part.”
The hard part came next. Larsen spent about 45 hours layering the individual photos – each of which contained about 25 satellites – over one another, using Adobe Photoshop. Much of the time was spent painstakingly erasing stars, to reveal the satellites.
“I could start to see the pattern emerging and realised: ‘Wow, this looks really awesome.’ I knew if I carried on it would look even better and more impressive in terms of satellite numbers.”
Fellow photographer Vincent Laforet called Larsen’s image “an important photograph”:
I was initially startled. Then confused. Then fascinated all in quick succession.
And then I felt a deep sense of betrayal once I realized that what I was tracking with my eyes were a series of small satellites. And btw: that they likely had ruined my long exposure that I was capturing at the time.
I remember asking in the moment:
Who gave anyone permission do this?

articles.title: Salon.com shutters suddenly after 31 years
articles.body:
Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.
It’s difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.
When Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.
Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.
The history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.
We also want to thank our readers. You came to Salon for the journalism, the dialogue, the essays, the criticism, the unexpected discoveries and the sense that there was a place on the internet where ideas mattered. You read, shared, challenged, subscribed, wrote to us and kept coming back. Your engagement made Salon a publication and a community, and it gave our work meaning. We are so grateful for the time you spent with us.
The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.
Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.
Thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.
Salon

articles.title: Blue Origin’s next launch now won’t happen until 2027
articles.body:
Blue Origin plans to do its next New Glenn rocket launch in January 2027, according to CNBC and the Financial Times, which cite a memo from CEO Dave Limp sent to staff. The new timeline follows a May launchpad explosion that damaged Blue Origin’s New Glenn launchpad ahead of a flight that would have brought Amazon Leo satellites into space.
Blue Origin’s next launch now won’t happen until 2027
Blue Origin had been aiming for a launch at the end of this year after a launchpad explosion in May, but now it’s reportedly targeting January.
In October, Blue Origin founder Jeff Bezos told Fox News that the company was aiming for a December New Glenn launch, joking that it could be “probably December 31st.” The new, revised launch window is “about 10 days later than Blue Origin’s earlier launch target,” CNBC reports. Limp also reportedly cited bad weather as having an effect on the launchpad rebuilding process.
“This small adjustment doesn’t diminish what we’ve accomplished or the importance of the work still ahead,” Limp wrote in his memo, per CNBC and the FT. “Returning New Glenn to flight remains our top priority — it’s worth it.”

articles.title: Vietnam Jails Pirate Football Streamers For Up To a Year
articles.body:
Vietnam Jails Pirate Football Streamers For Up To a Year (torrentfreak.com) 15
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from TorrentFreak: A Vietnamese court has sentenced 14 people who worked on the pirate football streaming site Bun Cha TV, handing out the first prison terms we've seen since the country's piracy crackdown began earlier this year. [...] Four defendants, including the heads of the content, programming and operations teams, were sentenced to 12 months in prison. Five others received ten months, and two were sentenced to eight months. Notably, three of the site's commentators were not sent to prison. Their ten-month sentences were suspended. All 14 defendants reportedly admitted the charges and cooperated with the authorities. According to investigators, Bun Cha TV streamed more than 150,000 sports matches and it allegedly made more than 20 billion dong, roughly $760,000, in illegal profits from betting and gambling ads.
The verdict reports don't mention a total. Instead, they list illegal gains per person or team. The leader of the content team allegedly gained more than 430 million dong, while commentators made from more than 31 million to more than 480 million dong each. The verdict was picked up by Rouse, the law firm that represents the Motion Picture Association in Vietnam. In an article headlined "Strong Vietnam criminal penalties," published on Lexology on November 3, the firm calls the ruling another victory for Vietnam's IP landscape.
"The defendants were all sentenced to terms of 8-12 months in prison," Rouse writes. While Rouse is correct on the length of the terms, it doesn't mention that three of the sentences were suspended. Instead, Rouse stresses that the ruling is part of a tougher enforcement trend. "This ruling reflects a shift in enforcement strategy by Vietnamese authorities, who are increasingly moving past preliminary domain blocking to deliver criminal convictions against the operators of commercial-scale piracy rings," the firm notes. "This perhaps reflects the strength of the national crackdown following the USTR pressure in May," the firm adds. According to the indictment, Bui Ba Hien, who runs a company called S24, allegedly directed employees and collaborators to build and operate Bun Cha TV. However, Hien is not among the 14 defendants named in reports, which also do not identify the affected rightsholders.
"Interestingly, in September, Bac Ninh police issued a wanted notice for a man of the same name, Bui Ba Hien, CEO of esports company Box Vietnam," reports TorrentFreak. "This person is also charged under the same copyright statute."

articles.title: You'll need nerves of steel to work with AI agents
articles.body:
You’ll need nerves of steel to work with AI agents
This post will focus mainly on Composer 2.5 in Cursor. These problems may not be present in opus-5.5 or gpt-6.1-sol-pro-max-ultra-thinking-fast. But gpt-6.1-luna, for example, has all the problems listed here. I’ve also encountered many of these problems before in gpt-5.5 and opus-4.6. I don’t know whether they’re present in the newer AI models released recently.
What I like about Composer 2.5: its usage limits and speed.
For comparison, let’s take two $20 subscriptions, one for GPT and one for Cursor. With gpt-6.1-sol, my 5-hour limit runs out after just a few requests. If I ask it to change a couple of lines in a readme file, that uses up 10% of the limit. If I ask it to change something in a large codebase, the entire limit gets used up just reading dozens of files, without writing a single line of code.
But GPT also offers a $100 plan with five times the usage limits. And how long would that last me? I work with complex monorepo projects. To make changes to one service, the agent has to read dozens of files in other services and several skills. If the $20 plan runs out after reading 20 files, will the $100 plan run out after reading 100 files?
That’s why I don’t use Sol, but use Luna instead. But it’s very slow. Compared to Composer 2.5, it’s dozens of times slower.
That’s why I don’t use GPT Luna, but use Composer 2.5 instead. It’s very fast and very cheap. And in exchange for that speed and savings, I end up wasting my time and getting stressed out. I’ve encountered some of these problems in Deepseek and other open models. Some models have certain problems but not others. The number and frequency of problems vary even when using the same model, depending on the phase of the moon.
Below is a list of problems I’ve encountered over 100+ hours of working with Composer in Cursor.
Removal
The agent writes code and changes dozens of files. I start reviewing the code, and the following conversation ensues:
— Why is this function here?
— You’re right. This function isn’t needed here. (Deletes the function and makes changes to many files)
— Why did you delete it?
— You’re right. I shouldn’t have deleted that function. I’m putting it back. (Makes changes to many files again)
And I still never got an answer to the question of why that function was needed.
Now, whenever I want to ask it something, I have to turn off agent mode or explicitly tell it not to delete anything. But when I forget to do that, it starts deleting parts of the code in response to a simple question.
Sometimes I spend a lot of time reviewing the code and ask it to change just one function. It changes all the files that have already been reviewed. And these changes don’t even relate to that function.
It might even delete all the work done in this chat. And not just in this one. I ask it to make a commit, and it finds changes to other files mixed in. And it just deletes them. Even though that work was done in other chats.
Also, if I ask it to refactor the code — for example, to rename a method in 50 files — it might delete all the comments it finds in those files. Which has absolutely nothing to do with refactoring the method.
And yet, it doesn’t delete what I ask it to delete. When changing a method’s name, it leaves the old method in place and adds a new one with the new name. That’s its entire refactoring process — so it doesn’t have to change all the files where the old method was called. It’ll simply mark the old method as deprecated and leave it accessible. If I point this out, it will finally do the refactoring, but leave the old method name in the tests and documentation. The tests will fail, and it will say the task is complete and the method has been refactored, but the tests are failing. As far as the agent is concerned, failing tests don’t count as evidence that the task is incomplete.
Also, while working on a task, it might remove an important parameter from the config or from a method that has nothing to do with the task at all. When asked why it removed the parameter, the agent claims it didn’t remove anything. You have to explicitly ask it to check the git diff, because it won’t think to do that on its own.
Just do it like the reference
I already have a working service that listens for events, then updates values in the database and writes them to Redis. I ask the agent to do exactly the same thing in another service.
It does it, but forgets to write to Redis. Or it doesn’t update the values in the database. Or it names files and classes completely differently. Or it puts interfaces and types in the wrong places. After that, it says everything is done. I ask it to check everything it’s done. It checks and once again insists that everything is done. And, of course, all the tests are green, which confirms its conclusion that everything is done. I have to go through many rounds, pointing out each mistake so it can fix it. While fixing one mistake, it introduces new ones.
I ask it again to go through the code and make sure everything matches the other service. It changes a lot of files and says everything is done. I open the first file and see that it’s all wrong. I write to it again, and it replies that everything is done. I open the next file, and it’s the same story. What’s more, I can even point out specific functions in a single file and explain how they differ from the reference. It fixes one, we move on to the next function, and it fixes that one too. It can’t even make a single file match the reference.
Let’s go back to the service that listens for events. It has shared, reusable methods for working with the message broker. The agent even does everything right and uses those methods instead of duplicating them. But it forgets to add types, and I point this out. And instead of adding interfaces, for some reason it decides to duplicate hundreds of lines of code from the shared methods.
Testing
It has trouble with tests in general. I give it clear instructions: first, add a test; run the test; make sure it fails; tell me why it failed; then fix the code and run the tests again so that all of them pass.
What the AI agent does: it immediately changes the code. Then it creates a test that does not fail and tells me the task is complete. As a result, I can’t verify whether the test would have failed before the code was fixed. Or whether the code actually fixed anything.
This has happened so many times that I created a separate command for it. And I had to modify it many times before the agent started following the instructions. But it still doesn’t work perfectly. At some random point, depending on the alignment of the planets, it starts editing the code again without creating a test first.
And sometimes, to create a failing test, it uses a clever trick. There’s already a discussion in the chat about a parser for JSON data. I send it a new, small 20-line JSON input and ask it to write a failing test first. It adds the input data to the test along with the expected output from the parser. And to make the test fail, it simply changes a random field in the expected output and reports that the test has failed and the code can now be changed.
The project has a well-established test structure. The test fixtures for each parser method are stored in separate directories. When we need to add a new method to the parser, we simply add a new directory with fixtures and modify the parser code. The tests run through all the fixtures and check that nothing has broken.
All of this is described in the agent’s skills and rules. And when the agent starts working on tests, I can see it reading those skills first. And in most cases, it follows this structure. But at some random point, it stops following it and adds fixtures directly into the test code. I have to point this out, and it moves them to separate files. A few messages later in the same chat, it makes the same mistake again.
If it adds a parameter to API requests, schema validation fails when it runs the tests. It uses another clever trick: it simply disables schema validation or allows any unknown parameters in the schema. And the tests pass again.
There was another case. I asked the agent to write a test for adding data through an API request. The agent spent a long time trying to get the tests to pass. So it decided to simply skip calling the API route in the tests and write the data directly to the database instead. The tests did start passing, and the data was added to the database, but no API request was actually made.
Inability to change the response style
In recent months, I’ve been noticing a new pattern in sentence structure more and more often. Here are some examples:
There’s a difference between "I read the text" and "I understood the meaning of the text".
We too often mistake "I’m used to this" for "I like this".
The path from "I’m afraid of making a mistake" to "I’m ready to try" can take years.
Each sentence contains two phrases in quotation marks that follow the same stylistic pattern. I don’t know where this pattern came from, but I hadn’t seen it before. Now AI models communicate this way, and I’m noticing this style in articles and videos. Maybe it’s an improved version of "It’s not X, it’s Y"? Although these aren’t exactly antitheses.
No matter how much I try to change the rules and skills for the agents, they keep using this technique. What’s more, Composer took the worst of these two techniques and now writes things like this to me:
This isn’t "the API won’t start". It’s "the frontend can’t connect".
It uses quotation marks in almost every reply. Quotation marks are used where they shouldn’t be at all. For example, here:
I "connected the API" to the service.
The service "starts up", but can’t "process" incoming requests.
I added a "status check" before sending the request.
I’m tired of reading this kind of text from the agent. And if I point this out, the following conversation ensues:
— The rules prohibit the use of quotation marks in the text. Why did you use them again?
— You’re right, I shouldn’t have used quotation marks. Now that you’ve pointed this out to me, I’ll never use quotation marks again.
— But your memory doesn’t carry over between chats.
— You’re absolutely right. To ensure I always follow this rule in new chats, it needs to be moved to the very top of the list.
Okay, let’s move the rule to the top. In the next reply, right in the same chat, I get text with quotation marks again.
End of Article
Now you know what to expect if you decide to use Composer 2.5 in Cursor.
And to avoid these problems, you simply need to use the new frontier models that were released a few days ago, regardless of when you’re reading this article.

articles.title: Harbinger raises $240M after expanding into defense
articles.body:
Electric truck startup Harbinger has raised a $240 million Series D funding round as it expands its portfolio of products, including battery storage and defense applications.
The funding comes almost one year to the day after the Los Angeles-based company announced a $160 million Series C, which included an initial truck order from FedEx. Harbinger has now raised more than $650 million to date, according to Bloomberg News, which first reported the round.
The Series D was co-led by Tiger Global, Capricorn’s “technology impact fund,” and defense-focused firm Ridgeline. FedEx invested again after leading last year’s round, and other repeat investors included Maniv, Greycroft, and Leitmotif, a VC firm backed by Volkswagen. Also investing this time was institutional giant Fidelity Management, which tends to invest in pre-IPO startups. (Harbinger is reportedly weighing going public.)
While it didn’t lead this round, FedEx’s relationship with Harbinger continues to deepen. The shipping giant’s senior vice president of safety and transportation, Paul Melander, has joined Harbinger’s board of directors. FedEx also recently placed its first large order with Harbinger — a deal for 2,000 trucks valued at more than $300 million.
Founded in 2022 by former employees of now-defunct EV startup Canoo and battery company QuantumScape, Harbinger started by focusing on making one electric truck chassis. The company has steadily expanded its efforts since. It bought autonomy startup Phantom AI, has begun developing hybrid emergency vehicles, and revealed a driverless hybrid electric platform for the military.

OpenAI says its new cybersecurity model is better at not hacking other companies
articles.body:
OpenAI is launching GPT-6 Cyber, the latest version of its cybersecurity AI model, which it says is better at finding vulnerabilities and less likely to go rogue and hack other platforms in the process. OpenAI says that during testing, GPT-6 Cyber went out of bounds less than 1 percent of the time, down from around 5 percent with GPT-5.6 Cyber.
OpenAI says its new cybersecurity model is better at not hacking other companies
Classified as ‘Critical,’ GPT-6 Cyber outperforms GPT-6 Astra on cyber-related benchmarks.
The evaluation, called ExploitGym HoneyPot, is modeled after the Hugging Face Incident, in which OpenAI’s AI agents breached the open-source AI community to find answers to a problem they were tasked with solving. “With the 6 Cyber model, we were able to make huge improvements on this evaluation,” Fouad Matin, the head of OpenAI’s cyber preparedness and safety team, said during a press briefing. “It’s over 99 percent of the time doing what you ask.”
But evaluation awareness, or when an AI system recognizes that it’s being tested and changes its behavior in response, remains a concern. “Evaluation awareness is super top of mind for us,” Matin said. “Often when we do see evaluation awareness, you’ll see it in the model’s chain of thought.” Matin added that OpenAI is trying to prioritize production-like evaluations, where the model is interacting with real codebases with a real objective to lessen the risk of awareness.
Following a wave of AI cybersecurity incidents, OpenAI has raced to strengthen its safeguards and lock down its most powerful models. The company briefly paused training of its frontier AI models, and it now restricts their access to the internet.
GPT-6 Cyber is classified as Critical in cybersecurity on OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework, which indicates that it “can identify and develop functional zero-day exploits of all severity levels in many hardened real-world critical systems without human intervention.” GPT-5.6 Cyber was previously classified as High under the framework.
GPT-6 Cyber outperforms GPT-6 Astra, OpenAI’s flagship Critical-level model, on most cyber-related tasks. In ExploitGym, an AI benchmark that measures whether an AI model can exploit vulnerabilities, GPT-6 Cyber scored 48.5 percent, about 16 points higher than GPT-5.6 Cyber’s 32.1 percent and a few points higher than GPT-6 Astra’s 42.4 percent score. The model helped find 81 previously unknown vulnerabilities in Firefox, and it played a role in hardening OpenAI’s own infrastructure for training AI models, OpenAI says.
Additionally, GPT-6 Cyber comes with stronger safeguards “to detect and disrupt misuse” while better adhering to user instructions. OpenAI says it’s using new checks to block “high-risk activity,” including attacks on critical infrastructure like power plants and water treatment facilities.
GPT-6 Cyber is rolling out to select members of OpenAI’s Daybreak Red program, which is available to companies and organizations using its models for “authorized defensive cybersecurity work.” It’s expanding GPT-6 Cyber to all Daybreak Red customers in the coming weeks.

articles.title: Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 is $300 off ahead of Black Friday
articles.body:
Android fans with a bit of iPhone Duo envy, take note: The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 is discounted to $1,599.99 at both Amazon and Best Buy, a hefty $300 markdown from its usual price, and just $50 higher than the lowest we’ve seen. Considering the device only launched a few months ago, you’re saving a significant amount of cash on the unlocked device, and you can also opt for the 512GB model, doubling the storage, for just $200 more (Amazon, Best Buy). Best Buy currently has all three colors in stock, while the 256GB model is currently sold out on Amazon in cream.
Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 is $300 off ahead of Black Friday
You can also save on the Beats Pill Bluetooth speaker, a battery-powered Ring doorbell, and a Lego Star Wars droid.
The shorter and wider passport-style shape (similar to the iPhone Duo) quickly became natural and comfortable to handle, according to our reviewer Dominic Preston’s experience with the Z Fold 8. Despite its thin and light construction, it doesn’t skimp on battery life, with a 4,800mAh battery that still had 40 percent charge remaining after a full day of use. The interior 4:3 screen has the same ratio as most Apple iPads, which is great for watching movies or TV, but even better for reading. There’s no telephoto lens on this model (it’s present on the pricier Z Fold 8 Ultra), and it only has an IP48 rating, so you’ll want to be careful near the beach, but those are small compromises to make given the discounted price.
Other deals to consider
- Both Amazon and Best Buy are selling the Beats Pill for a discounted $99.95 and $99.99 respectively, a sizable break from the usual $149.99 price point. The 2024 edition of this iconic Bluetooth speaker adds in lossless audio over USB-C, as well as native feature support for both iOS and Android devices. It’s rated IP67 for dust and water resistance, and comes in three different colors to match your other Beats devices. Read our review.
- The Ring Battery Doorbell 2K is on sale for $39.99 at Amazon, over half off its $99.99 list price. This battery-powered doorbell camera is easy to install, and shoots clear 2K resolution video with a 140-degree field of view and up to 6X digital zoom. You’ll get real-time notifications on your phone for any activity the camera spots, with live view and two-way talk in case you need to have a chat with your neighbors or delivery folks without coming to the front door.
- You can pick up the Lego Star Wars: Ahsoka Chopper set for just $66.99 at Amazon, the lowest price we’ve seen yet for this 1,039-piece building kit. This brick-based droid has great play features, like detachable arms and center wheel for different display positions, and a head that spins and bobs realistically. It stands at over 8.5 inches when fully built, making it a fun addition to your existing Lego display or bookshelf.
