articles.title: Chicken Pomodoro
articles.body:
Chicken Pomodoro
Chicken breasts cooked in a light garlicky sauce made with fresh cherry tomatoes, topped with mozzarella cheese.
Serves4
Prep10 minutes
Cook25 minutes
Why You’ll Love Our Chicken Pomodoro
- It’s simple, but packed with flavor. Pomodoro sauce typically has minimal ingredients, throwing the bright flavor of tomatoes into the spotlight. This recipe proves you can create bold flavors from just a handful of ingredients.
- Weeknight-friendly. This recipe is cooked in one skillet and requires minimal chopping, making it perfect for any night when you need dinner fast.
Every summer I look forward to tomatoes from my garden and the abundance of farmers markets bursting with different shapes, sizes, and colors of the gorgeous fruit (it’s fine if you consider it a vegetable; tomato, tom-ah-to). As peak tomato season fades, my cravings don’t stop. That’s when I turn to tomato recipes, like this chicken pomodoro, that work year-round.
Inspired by classic pomodoro sauce, this one-skillet dinner turns cherry tomatoes, a flavorful choice even in the dead of winter, into a quick, bright sauce that enlivens mild chicken breasts. To keep the sauce tomato-forward, it’s lightly flavored with garlic and basil, but you could also add a sprinkle of chili flakes for heat or oregano for a complementary herbal note. Topping the chicken with fresh mozzarella gives the dish chicken Parmesan vibes, but in a much lighter way.
Straight from Our Recipe Tester
“This was like a lighter, fresher take on chicken Parmesan. I liked the bright flavors in the sauce, and the little bit of butter really brought it all together with some richness. I took the chicken out of the pan, tossed half a pound of cooked pasta in the sauce, and served it alongside. No complaints at the dinner table from my family!” —Christine, October 2026
Why You Should Trust Me
With over 15 years of experience as a professional recipe developer for national print and digital outlets, I have learned how to create recipes that are easy to follow, quick and simple to make, and don’t skimp on flavor, like this skillet dinner. Chicken recipes in particular have been a huge part of my recipe career because chicken is an affordable, versatile, and crowd-pleasing protein that can be spiced and sauced in countless ways. That means I know how to give this lean protein a boost of flavor without overcooking it, because dry, tough chicken is a no-go in my world.
Key Ingredients in Chicken Pomodoro
- Chicken: Boneless, skinless chicken breasts turn this skillet of saucy tomatoes into a meal. To get a good portion size, it’s best to halve larger pieces of chicken versus buying thin-sliced chicken breasts. Those are typically pounded into large, flat cutlets, and 4 wouldn’t fit in a skillet at once.
- Cherry tomatoes: These little round tomatoes are the best type of tomato for this recipe because of their thin skin and flavorful, juicy interior. They’re also easy to find year-round, so you can make this recipe any time you want.
- Garlic: Fresh garlic is one of the few traditional seasonings for pomodoro sauce, so you bet I was going to include it. To keep its sharpness, I add it to the skillet with the tomatoes rather than sautéing it first, which mellows the taste.
- Basil: Basil leaves are a wonderful garnish, but I also love the ease of tossing a whole sprig of basil into a sauce so it can perfume the dish as it bubbles away. Herb stems have so much flavor, so even if you have some without leaves, don’t toss them!
- Butter: I learned from some amazing Italian chefs that butter in tomato sauce is totally legit, and it’s an essential part of Marcella Hazan’s legendary tomato sauce. Here, a small amount goes a long way to add a touch of silky richness to the sauce and balance the natural tang of fresh tomatoes.
- Mozzarella: Fresh mozzarella can be too wet for some recipes, but here it works perfectly, blanketing the chicken and enhancing the dish’s saucy base. For a more rustic look, you can tear the cheese instead of slicing it.
How to Make Chicken Pomodoro
- Brown the chicken. Halve 2 large boneless chicken breasts crosswise, then season both sides with salt and pepper. Cook in olive oil in a large skillet until well-browned on both sides, but not fully cooked through. Transfer to a plate.
- Start cooking the sauce. Stir in about 3/4 of the halved tomatoes, some minced garlic, and a sprig of fresh basil, coating them in the remaining oil and gently scraping up any browned bits on the bottom of the skillet as the tomatoes release liquid.
- Add broth and simmer. Stir in chicken broth and bring to a simmer. Simmer until the tomatoes break down, and the sauce thickens slightly.
- Add more tomatoes and return the chicken to the sauce. Stir in another handful of halved tomatoes and a pat of butter. Nestle the chicken pieces into the sauce, top with cheese, cover, and simmer for a few minutes.
- Finish with cheese and basil. Uncover the skillet and simmer until the cheese is melted, the chicken is cooked through, and the sauce has thickened. Remove from the heat and top with fresh, torn basil.
Helpful Swaps
- Start with smaller chicken breasts. If you have small boneless, skinless chicken breasts (around 6 ounces each) you can skip halving them and cook them whole.
- Lighten up on the cheese. For a less cheesy meal, replace the sliced mozzarella with a sprinkle of grated Parmesan or skip the cheese entirely and top more generously with basil.
- Try a different herb. Fresh oregano is an excellent sub for basil if you are out. Add fresh leaves sparingly as a garnish; they’re more intense than basil.
- Make it extra-creamy. If you are craving penne alla vodka, you can give this dish a similar richness by adding heavy cream instead of broth when adding the second batch of tomatoes. Start with 1/4 cup, taste, and adjust from there to your liking.
Storage and Make-Ahead Tips
- Pomodoro is a quick-cooking sauce, so it’s best to make it fresh, but there are some make-ahead aspects that can trim a few minutes off the prep. Slice the tomatoes and chicken breasts up to 1 day in advance and store them separately in airtight containers in the refrigerator.
- If you want to make this a freezer-friendly meal, cook it all the way through, leaving the cheese off the chicken. Freeze the sauce and chicken in separate freezer-proof containers, thaw overnight in the refrigerator, then assemble and rewarm, covered, in a skillet, topping with cheese in the last few minutes.
What to Serve with Chicken Pomodoro
Chicken Pomodoro Recipe
Chicken breasts cooked in a light garlicky sauce made with fresh cherry tomatoes, topped with mozzarella cheese.
Prep time 10 minutes
Cook time 25 minutes
Serves 4
Nutritional Info
Ingredients
- 2 large boneless, skinless chicken breasts (1 1/2 to 2 pounds)
- 1 1/2 teaspoons kosher salt, divided
- 3/4 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper, divided
- 2 tablespoons olive oil
- 1 1/2 pounds cherry or grape tomatoes (3 pints or 4 cups), halved and divided
- 2 cloves garlic, minced
- 1 sprig fresh basil, plus more for garnish
- 1/2 cup low-sodium chicken broth
- 1 tablespoon unsalted butter
- 4 ounces fresh mozzarella cheese, sliced into 1/4-inch-thick rounds
Instructions
- Slice 2 large boneless, skinless chicken breasts in half crosswise to make 4 thinner pieces. Pat dry with paper towels. Season with 1 teaspoon of the kosher salt and 1/2 teaspoon of the black pepper.
- Heat 2 tablespoons olive oil in a large 12-inch skillet over medium-high heat until shimmering. Add the chicken in a single, tight layer and cook until golden-brown, 2 to 3 minutes per side. Transfer to a plate (the chicken will not be cooked through).
- Reduce the heat to medium. Add three-quarters of the halved cherry tomatoes (3 cups), 2 minced garlic cloves, 1 fresh basil sprig, the remaining 1/2 teaspoon kosher salt, and 1/4 teaspoon black pepper. Cook, stirring occasionally and scraping up any bits from the bottom of the skillet, until the tomatoes start to soften and become juicy, 4 to 5 minutes. Stir in 1/2 cup low-sodium chicken broth and simmer until the sauce thickens and the tomatoes have collapsed, about 5 minutes.
- Stir in the remaining 1 cup halved cherry tomatoes and 1 tablespoon unsalted butter until the butter melts. Return the chicken to the skillet, nestling it into the sauce. Pour in any accumulated juices on the plate. Top the chicken with 4 ounces sliced fresh mozzarella cheese.
- Cover and simmer for 3 minutes. Uncover and simmer until the sauce thickens slightly, 3 to 4 minutes more. Garnish with torn fresh basil leaves.
Recipe Notes
General tip: The halved chicken pieces will inevitably be a little thicker at one end than the other, and that’s totally fine, but if there is a big difference (more than 1/2 inch), take a moment and flatten the thicker end slightly with a meat mallet or rolling pin to even it out.
Substitutions
- Instead of chicken broth, use low-sodium vegetable broth or even water (although if using water, you’ll want to add an extra pinch of salt to make up for the sodium in canned broth).
- Fresh mozzarella offers a lightly creamy taste that doesn’t dominate the tomatoes, but if all you have is low-moisture mozzarella cheese, you can use that. Top the chicken with 1 cup of shredded mozzarella cheese or 1 slice per piece of chicken.
Storage: Refrigerate leftovers in an airtight container for up to 4 days. Reheat the chicken in sauce, covered, in the microwave or in a 350°F oven until the tomatoes bubble and the chicken is warmed through. I like to top the chicken as it warms with a bit more cheese for a fresh, creamy bite, but it’s not essential.

articles.title: I wish tech companies knew more about me
articles.body:
"Tech companies are spying on us" is a truism at this point. Endless articles and investigations have ensured that everybody is aware: they are spying on us, they listen to our conversations, they know more about us than we know ourselves, they know you're going to be fired or become pregnant or become depressed before it happens...
I have never felt anything close to that.
I get shown ads for products I just purchased. All this spying, machine learning, big data result in "he bought a mattress, show him more mattresses". Here, I literally just opened a random website with no adblocker, and I see a purple gamepad I recently purchased, with two other gamepads:
When listening to personalized playlists on Spotify and YouTube Music I skip every single electronic track with vocals. I listen to a lot of techno and related genres, and the moment someone starts singing I skip the track. I've been doing it for years. None of these advanced algorithms have ever noticed this simple pattern.
Using Google Chrome, logged into my Google account, I searched for info about Google AI plan usage limits, got an AI-generated response with a link to the help page, clicked it and ended up, logged out, on a Finnish-language landing page (because I'm located in Finland).
My user account, system locale, browser locale, and keyboard settings are all set to English. I am logged into Chrome and all Google services.
I travel to Germany every few months, and lots of services that I've been using for years suddenly decide I speak German.
The PlayStation online store is in Finnish, while some menus are in English, and even if I switch the website language to English (via a hidden, clunky selector), it resets back after a few clicks or after opening a new tab.
Here's an ad for some smart home wellness system. I click on it: they don't deliver to Finland.
A full page of repeating ads for industrial-grade light-curing, methacrylate-based resin designed for 3D printing. I don't have a 3D printer and have no idea what this is.
I clicked on that ad; now I keep getting other 3D-printing-related ads.
Here's an ad for an email/WhatsApp marketing tool. I never needed any marketing tool, nor do I own a WhatsApp business account.
Now it's a Helsinki hotel. I live in Helsinki, I haven't searched for local hotels since 2014 when I first arrived here.
A fucking asphalt cleaning tractor.
I searched YouTube for installation instruction for a specific appliance "AEG CCS84751", watched a couple of relevant videos and the next day saw my homepage populated with more videos about random ovens and stoves. OK, so, let's see, a user searches for installation instructions for a very specific, concrete model. What could we machine-learn from this, what are the options here?
- The user is into ovens
- The user is into installing appliances
- The user needs this one particular instruction for this one particular oven because the user maybe bought that oven and wants to install it, once, maybe?
My bank keeps sending me offers for car insurance. I have car insurance with that bank. Have had it for years.
An airline, when reminding me of an upcoming trip, send info about visas and border crossing laws which don't apply to my citizenship. They literally have a scan of my passport.
Netflix on Apple TV asks me to select a user every time I launch it. I've had this account for 15+ years, and never had more than one user on it. I always select the only option there is to select. There is no setting to disable this screen.
My mobile provider keeps sending me discounts for children's products and events from their corporate partners. I don't have children.
HBO keeps recommending me foreign movies and shows which I cannot watch as they don't have English subtitles.
I have no doubts that a lot of information is being tracked, stored, and sold. Since that's already done, could you guys at least use some of it?..

articles.title: Sshole
articles.body:
1980
the first star
back in old unix your password hash just sat in /etc/passwd, right next to your username. in a file everyone could read.
in 1980 bill joy put a * there for an account called daemon. nobody's supposed to ever log in as it.
a * isn't a hash, so no password can match it. unix still does this today
3bsd · /etc/passwd · 1980
Addressgithub.com/dspinellis/unix-history-repo/blob/BSD-3/etc/passwd
the next field is the real name. he wrote "the devil himself"
1990s
how sshd checks your password
ok so these days the hash lives in /etc/shadow and looks like $6$abc$k2P9…. the $6$ means sha512, abc is the salt, the rest is the actual hash
you type your password, sshd hashes it with that same salt and checks if it comes out identical. same = you're in. that's it
and if the field is just *? there's nothing to match. type whatever you want, it's never getting you in
1990s
the fine print
one more rule. if crypt() can't do its job, it returns NULL. like if the salt asks for some algorithm the system doesn't have, there's nothing to compute, so you get NULL instead of a hash
the single unix spec · crypt() · 1997
Addresspubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/7908799/xsh/crypt.html
pretty clear.
except a lot of programs never check for NULL. they just compare whatever crypt() gives back with the stored field, hit the NULL, and crash
2012
crypt stops saying NULL
so musl (the libc under alpine) goes ok fine, crypt() just won't return NULL anymore. if it fails, it returns a single character instead. that character can never match a real password, so programs don't crash, they just see a wrong password
now guess which character they picked for that
"?"
yep. the star. again.
musl · b3c4cc12 · aug 2012
Addressgit.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/commit/?id=b3c4cc12
"reportedly."
musl · b3c4cc12 · the diff
Addressgit.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/commit/?id=b3c4cc12
"should not happen" gone, NULL gone, "*" in
2012
three weeks later
then musl adds sha512 crypt. the thing is, sha512crypt gets slower the longer the password is, so someone could send one giant password and keep your server busy for a long time. so musl just caps it at 256 bytes and refuses anything longer
musl · 88bf5a8a · aug 29 2012
Addressgit.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/commit/?id=88bf5a8a
twenty days after the "*" commit btw
musl · crypt_sha512.c @ 88bf5a8a
Addressgit.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/misc/crypt_sha512.c?id=88bf5a8a
so past 256 bytes crypt fails. and when crypt fails… it says "*".
musl · crypt_sha512.c
Addressgit.musl-libc.org/cgit/musl/tree/src/crypt/crypt_sha512.c
literally in the comment the whole time
2016
sshd borrows bob's salt
CVE-2016-6210. ask sshd about a user that doesn't exist and it says no instantly, cause there's nothing to hash. real users take a few ms longer. so just time it and you know who exists
the fix is kinda funny. no real hash to check? sshd grabs some other account's salt and hashes your password anyway, just to waste the same amount of time. still a no, just a slower no
openssh-commits · jul 2016
Addresslists.mindrot.org/pipermail/openssh-commits/2016-July/005428.html
"for invalid users." and also, it turns out, real users with a *.
2019 → 2022
the fix for the fix
2019. turns out alpine's docker images had no root password. at all. CVE-2019-5021. alpine fixes it by locking root with !
but without pam, ! also kills ssh keys. and cloud images log in with keys.
2022. alpine 3.16 switches root to *. still locked, keys work again
alpine aports · fbe926af · shipped in 3.16, 2022
Addressgitlab.alpinelinux.org/alpine/aports/-/commit/fbe926af.patch
narrator: it did not.
2016 → 2026
ten quiet years
why did nobody notice? well, maybe someone did. maybe someone pasted the wrong thing into a password prompt, half a slack message or a whole ssh key, and it just let them in. you've never pasted the wrong thing into a password prompt?? amazing. a fresh box with no passwords set isn't affected. a * in shadow needs a wrong try first. openssh tests on openbsd and glibc, musl doesn't test sshd, and most distros go through pam, which never even calls crypt for a *.
so as far as anyone knows, nobody noticed. as far as anyone knows.
some people got really close though
libc-alpha · debian #714219 · 2013
Addresssourceware.org/legacy-ml/libc-alpha/2013-07/msg00046.html
a debian dev asks glibc to copy musl's "*". six years later debian moves to libxcrypt, which says "*0", and closes the bug. one character away.
musl mailing list · dec 2024
Addressopenwall.com/lists/musl/2024/12/31/2
this thread is about busybox passwd breaking on a 257 character password. same "*", same limit. nobody says "sshd"
openssh-commits · 30 oct 2026
Addresslists.mindrot.org/pipermail/openssh-commits/2026-October/013271.html
a security review fixes pick_salt(). the bug is four lines below it. four days before i found it.
nov 2026
how i ran into it
i was messing around with openssh, mostly the boring parts where it talks to libc, like the password code. people don't really look at that stuff, they look at the crypto. so i built sshd every way i could think of (glibc, musl, pam, no pam, shadow, no shadow) and threw like 17,600 weird logins at it. weird hashes, broken accounts, passwords way too long
oh did i say "i"? sorry. i had agent swarms. a lot of them. let's not get into it
every build agreed on every login. except musl without pam. that one said yes to things it shouldn't
